content: The control plane for autonomous agents From an image to an agent. Define reusable images, work with coding agents directly, and let Autopilot carry the work forward. Bring agents together when the job needs a team. Get started ↗ Explore the docs ↓ Alpha · macOS 12+ on Apple Silicon · Remote Linux x86 64/aarch64 or Apple Silicon macOS over SSH 01 Image Define the workflow 02 Agent Give it a place to work 03 Interactive Guide the work 04 Autopilot Let work continue 05 Team Coordinate agents 01 / Define Image A reusable definition of how an agent works. An image packages plugins, Agent Skills, and an ordered prompt template . Build it from an original directory containing Tariboyfile.yaml, inspect exactly what the agent will receive, and reuse it across agents. Add the tariboy Store with one click and build tariboy/basic, or build one for a specific role. Export runnable images to other hosts; keep the original source for rebuilds. Harness, model, and effort belong to agent configuration. Explore images → 02 / Configure Agent A named agent, with its own runtime and working directory. Create an agent from an image, then choose where it runs and which harness it uses . Configure its model, effort, working directory, and environment independently of other agents. Use Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, or the Cursor CLI installed on the selected host. Start locally or connect a remote Linux host through your existing SSH configuration. Create your first agent → · Connect a host → 03 / Collaborate Interactive Work with the agent directly. Open Terminal for a live session with the selected harness. Give instructions, follow the work as it happens, and return to the same session after switching away. Start and Stop turn the whole agent on and off. For an ordinary terminal session without image instructions, choose bare:latest, which runs no autonomous iterations. Open Terminal → 04 / Automate Autopilot Keep work moving between conversations. Run bounded iterations on a timer or in response to durable messages . The host daemon manages the loop, so closing the desktop app does not stop it. Inspect triggers, outcomes, usage, and cost in Activity. Set budgets and deadlines, stop the agent, or kill current work when needed. Configure Autopilot → · Understand the controls → 05 / Coordinate Team Independent agents. Shared work. Group agents with a lead, group mail, and individually configured roles . Each member keeps its own image, harness, model, and runtime settings. Native Tasks helps you decompose work, delegate it, track progress, and keep questions and answers attached to the task. Transfer team configuration as compose YAML or a portable archive, and transfer runnable images separately. Build a team → · Organize tasks → Start small. Grow when you need to. Your first agent in ten minutes. Get the alpha DMG and checksums from the release owner. You need an Apple Silicon Mac running macOS 12+ and a supported harness on the host where the agent will run. Install the app → Choose a host and image → Create an agent. Follow the quickstart → Tariboy is under heavy development. APIs, workflows, and configuration may change without notice. Building from source? Go further Explore the documentation Package your workflow and inspect the prompts and tools agents receive. Configure timers, message triggers, deadlines, and iteration controls. Bring agents together and coordinate their work. Run agents on Linux servers through system OpenSSH. Understand trust boundaries, limits, and safe operator controls. Build, test, and contribute with isolated environments. Architecture · CLI reference · Plugins · Support
description: Define reusable images, run coding agents interactively, and grow into autonomous teams.

content: Each GitHub Release attaches Tariboy X.Y.Z android-arm64.apk, signed with the project's release key, and its .sha256 file. This page tells you how the APK is built and signed, how to build it on your computer, and which values you must add to GitHub before the next release tag. How a release builds the APK When you push a vX.Y.Z tag, .github/workflows/desktop-release.yml runs the android job on ubuntu-latest in parallel with the macOS job. The job: 1. Rejects the tag when it differs from internal/version/version.go or scripts/release-version.txt. 2. Stops with NAME is required when one of the four ANDROID Secrets is empty. 3. Decodes the keystore into the runner's temporary directory and writes desktop/src-tauri/gen/android/keystore.properties. Only this step can read the Secrets. 4. Runs make desktop-android. Gradle signs the release APK with the key. 5. Checks the APK and stops the release when any check fails: - exactly one APK exists and its name does not end in -unsigned.apk; - apksigner verify --print-certs accepts the signature; - the certificate is not the Android debug certificate (CN=Android Debug); - the APK carries exactly one signing certificate, and its SHA-256 fingerprint equals the ANDROID CERT SHA256 repository variable. scripts/apk-cert-sha256.sh reads the fingerprint from both apksigner formats: Signer #1 certificate SHA-256 digest: and the per-scheme V2 Signer: certificate SHA-256 digest:. 6. Renames the APK to Tariboy X.Y.Z android-arm64.apk and writes its .sha256 file. The publish job waits for both the macOS and the Android job. It creates a draft release, writes the Android note with the certificate fingerprint into the release text, uploads all files, and then makes the release public. When the Android job fails, no release is published, also not the macOS files. GitHub settings You do these steps one time, before the next release tag. Without them the android job fails and the release is not published. | Name | Kind | Value | | --- | --- | --- | | ANDROID KEYSTORE BASE64 | Secret | the keystore file, base64-encoded on one line | | ANDROID KEYSTORE PASSWORD | Secret | the keystore password | | ANDROID KEY ALIAS | Secret | the key alias, for example tariboy | | ANDROID KEY PASSWORD | Secret | the key password; in a PKCS12 keystore it is the keystore password | | ANDROID CERT SHA256 | Variable | the SHA-256 fingerprint of the signing certificate | The fingerprint is public information, so it is a variable and not a Secret. The workflow ignores colons, spaces, and letter case in it. 1. Create the signing key You need a JDK with keytool: keytool asks for a password and for the owner's name. Keep tariboy-release.jks and its password in a safe place, for example a password manager. Do not commit the file to the repository. Android does not update an installed APK with an APK signed by a different key. If you lose or replace the key, users must uninstall the app and install it again. 2. Read the fingerprint The output looks like SHA256: 5F:A1:8B:...:30:A9. Copy the value after SHA256:. 3. Add the Secrets and the variable In the browser: 1. Open the repository on GitHub and go to Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions . 2. On the Secrets tab, click New repository secret one time for each of the four ANDROID Secrets in the table. For ANDROID KEYSTORE BASE64, paste the output of base64 < tariboy-release.jks | tr -d '\n'. 3. On the Variables tab, click New repository variable , enter the name ANDROID CERT SHA256, and paste the fingerprint from step 2. Or with the GitHub CLI, from the directory with the keystore. The commands without --body ask for the value, so the password does not go into your shell history: 4. Check the settings gh secret list must show the four ANDROID names. gh variable list must show ANDROID CERT SHA256. Nothing else is necessary: the runner has the Android SDK, the NDK, and Java, and the workflow sets its own permissions. When you replace the key, update all four Secrets and ANDROID CERT SHA256 together. Build the APK locally You need a JDK 17 or newer, the Android SDK with a platform and build-tools in ANDROID HOME, and an NDK in NDK HOME: The APK is in desktop/src-tauri/gen/android/app/build/outputs/apk/universal/release/. Without a keystore the file is -unsigned.apk, which is good for local checks only. To sign it, write desktop/src-tauri/gen/android/keystore.properties (the file is ignored by Git): Verify a released APK Download the APK and its .sha256 file into one directory, then: The certificate SHA-256 digest line must show the fingerprint in the release text. When the Android job fails | Message | Cause and fix | | --- | --- | | ANDROID ... is required | A Secret is missing. Add it as in step 3. | | ANDROID CERT SHA256 is required | The variable is missing. Add it as in step 3. | | does not match ANDROID CERT SHA256 | The keystore and the variable are from different keys. Set the variable to the keystore's fingerprint. | | expected one APK signing certificate SHA-256, found N | apksigner printed no certificate digest, or the APK is signed with more than one certificate. Read the apksigner output printed above the message. | | release APK is signed with a debug certificate | The keystore holds the Android debug key. Use the release keystore. | | make desktop-android fails in the Gradle signing task | The password or the alias does not match the keystore. Check the Secrets. | | release APK is unsigned | Gradle did not read keystore.properties. Look at the Restore signing keystore step output. | After the fix, open the failed run in Actions and click Re-run failed jobs , or push a new release tag. For how the phone app connects to a daemon, see Remote hosts.
description: Build the signed Android APK locally and configure the GitHub Secrets and variable that let each release attach it.

content: The daemon (tariboyd) tariboyd is the long-running process at the center of the system (cmd/tariboyd, internal/daemon). It owns: - the agent lifecycle — create, start/stop the loop, run iterations, reap, and remove in one of three modes (see Agent-owned tables); - the mailbox — letters between agents, the customer, plugins and daemon components; - native Tasks — queues, recursive task trees, comments, dependencies, per-agent sticky goal selection, agent pools, queue triggers, events, and a durable notification outbox; - the SQLite store — tariboyd.db, all durable state; - the plugin supervisor — spawns, health-checks, and restarts plugins; - the AI proxy — every LLM call flows through it; - API and WebSocket surfaces for clients. The Desktop UI is shipped by Tauri, not embedded in the daemon. System context and trust boundaries The daemon is the one durable control plane on a host. Desktop and the operator CLI are clients; harnesses are supervised workers; plugins are supervised integrations. None of them owns a second copy of product state. | Surface | Typical client | Boundary and identity | | --- | --- | --- | | Operator API | Desktop, CLI, automation | Unix socket by default; a TCP listener requires the configured bearer-token policy. The optional HTTP/WebSocket listener accepts loopback addresses only. | | Agent capability socket | Skill-local scripts plus the legacy tasks and i-am-done compatibility shims | One Unix socket per agent. The daemon derives the agent and current iteration, so request JSON cannot impersonate another caller. | | AI proxy | Harness or plugin making an LLM request | Loopback listener plus a short-lived iteration- or plugin-scoped token. Upstream provider keys remain in the daemon. | The Android app has no daemon of its own. It reaches a daemon through a port the user forwards to the phone's loopback, or through an HTTPS server, and the loopback listener allows its origin http://tauri.localhost. Remote Desktop access is an SSH local-forward to the remote daemon's loopback listener. System OpenSSH retains host-key verification, agent forwarding, ProxyJump, and interactive authentication. See Security and controls for the full transport and credential rules. Components and ownership | Component | Owns | Does not own | | --- | --- | --- | | Store and migrations | tariboyd.db, configuration, agent/task/message records, and durable outboxes | UI state or a second in-memory source of truth | | Agent store and loop manager | Agent configuration, per-agent engines, iteration adoption, shim refresh, and orphan-session reaping | Harness business logic | | Loop engine and shim runner | At most one iteration per agent, prompt preparation, timeouts, completion, and process supervision | Task state rules | | Image store and builder | Built plugin/prompt artifacts addressed by ref id, source provenance, runnable import/export, and Store path resolution | Harness/model/runtime policy or editable source snapshots | | Mail | Letters, recipient checks, inbox caps, attempts, dead letters, and the wake and hint hooks | Direct process-to-process delivery guarantees | | Assessments | Immutable assessments of iterations and tasks with their image and workflow snapshots. Agents write them through POST /tools/assessment/add (capability assessments). Operators read them through assessment.ls and assessment.show | Updates, deletes, or a write through the operator API | | Native Tasks service | Queues, task trees, comments, relations, pools, triggers, notifications, workflow bindings, queue secrets, transition requests, and script run records | Agent authentication or running script processes | | Workflow script worker | Executing pending check and watch runs: environment, working directory, process group, timeout, run log, and result parsing | What a verdict means for the task | | Plugin host | Plugin process lifecycle, plugin tokens, and delivery of each plugin's inbox to its /deliver | Provider credentials in plugin environments | | AI proxy and pricing catalog | Provider routing, scoped tokens, budgets, immutable request costs, daily model-price refresh, usage, and transcripts | Durable provider keys or proxy leases in SQLite | | API and event hub | Command registry, REST responses, and resumable event hints | State changes outside their owning services | The daemon creates a shared audit recorder for each agent. Loop lifecycle entries, mail actions, proxy decisions, and shim log tails therefore describe one coherent agent timeline, while a WebSocket event remains only a replayable delivery hint. Directories Path resolution lives in internal/paths: - Data dir — $TARIBOY BASE DIR, else /.tariboy. Holds the DB, agent working dirs, built images, and side-by-side external plugin versions. - Runtime dir — $TARIBOY RUNTIME DIR, else /.tariboyd. Holds the control socket (tariboyd.sock), pidfile, and log. Operator PUT /api/files (files upload) accepts a file name and base64 content, stores up to 16 MiB decoded under files/<unique-directory /<name in the data directory, and remains available for compatible clients. Desktop Send files, Attach, terminal-drop, and tariboy cp instead stream raw bodies up to 1 GiB through PUT /api/files/raw?name=.... Both routes return path, absolute abs, and bytes. These uploads belong to the server independently of agents and tasks; agents on the same server can read the returned absolute paths. The former agent-scoped PUT route and agent push command are removed. Uploads are ordinary owner-only files, excluded from support bundles, with no automatic retention. The server rejects path components and control characters in names and confines filesystem operations with os.Root. The raw route rejects a declared oversized body before reading it, also bounds unknown-length streams, and removes its partial file and unique directory after any failed upload. The data directory also holds each agent's working/configuration files and iteration evidence. SQLite owns agents, iterations, mail, tasks, idempotency keys, and durable outboxes. The global agent shell script is the deliberate filesystem-backed exception: <base-dir /global-agent-shell.sh; an agent may additionally have <base-dir /agents/<name /agent-shell.sh. Both are owner-only files, written atomically after Bash validation, rather than SQLite configuration. The owner-only proxy handoff file (aiproxy-handoff.json) intentionally sits outside SQLite, audit logs, and support bundles because it contains active, short-lived proxy leases required to adopt live harnesses after restart. The same data directory contains model-prices-litellm.json, an owner-only cache of validated external pricing data. SQLite remains authoritative for the managed price rows derived from that cache. The cache is also excluded from support bundles; see Security and controls. Startup, execution, and shutdown daemon.Run (internal/daemon) is a short sequence of phases, each in its own function with a typed result: process setup (logger, PATH, paths, the socket guard and PID file), store and telemetry, tasks, AI proxy, plugins, loop manager, runtime start, background workers, and serving. Each phase pushes the stop of every resource it creates onto one shutdown stack right after it creates the resource. The stack runs last-pushed first on every return path, so a resource always stops before the resources it uses. The order is: 1. API servers (Unix socket or TCP, and the HTTP/WS listener), awaited. 2. The access log. 3. The AI proxy, awaited. 4. Background workers, canceled and awaited. 5. Running operations (image and workflow builds), canceled and awaited; each records the status interrupted. 6. Plugins, then the loop manager. 7. Telemetry flush, then the SQLite store, then the PID file. All listeners bind before the daemon reports itself started, so a busy HTTP port fails startup synchronously. If any API listener fails later, the daemon takes the same path as a controlled stop: every server is shut down and its goroutine awaited before the manager and the store stop. An embedder or an in-process test can pass Options.Ready; the daemon calls it once all listeners are bound and the workers run. The daemon fails before serving if it cannot prepare the data directory, bind a safe socket, detects an already-live Unix daemon, cannot parse the requested listener, or receives a non-loopback HTTP address. A shim refresh failure is logged for its agent without preventing unrelated agents from starting. In steady state it runs the schedule publisher, the task notification outbox publisher, the per-agent goal reconciler, the queue-trigger ingress reconciler, the workflow script worker, AI ingestion, the daily pricing catalog worker, budget cache refresh, nightly database maintenance (backup, iteration pruning, cleanup, compaction; see State model), loop engines, and plugin supervisors. The workflow script worker (internal/workflowrun) executes the check and watch scripts of workflow tasks. Before it starts, the daemon records every run that was still running as interrupted. The worker wakes on task changes, when a run finishes, and every two seconds; it schedules due watches, kills runs whose cancellation was requested, and starts pending runs, at most four at once and never two of one task. Each run is its own process group under the daemon account, with no agent tools socket. The tasks service decides what a finished run means in one transaction. On shutdown the worker kills its scripts and leaves their records running for the next start to mark interrupted. See Task workflows. Background operations An image build and a workflow build are operations (internal/operations). POST /api/images/build and POST /api/workflow-images/build check their arguments in the request. An argument error answers at once with its error code. Otherwise the daemon records the operation, starts the build on the daemon's context, not on the request's context, and answers at once with {operation} in the status running. A client that disconnects does not stop the build. With the argument wait: true the request answers only when the build ends: the finished operation, or the build error with its code. Compose and Store automatic builds use wait. Each operation writes its log to <base-dir /operations/<id .log: the build steps, the output of npx skills experimental install, the wait for the image name lock and the result or the error. Each status change and each log line emits an operation event. Clients read operations with these routes: | Route | Result | | --- | --- | | GET /api/operations?page=N&limit=M | One page, newest first, and the total. limit is 1 to 200, 50 by default. | | GET /api/operations/{id} | One operation with its result or error. | | GET /api/operations/{id}/log?offset=N | Up to 1 MiB of the log from byte offset, the next offset, the log size and whether the operation ended. | | GET /api/operations/{id}/log/download | The whole log file. | | GET /api/operations/ws | A hint frame {id, status, ts} for each operation event. The client then reads the operation and the log over HTTP. | The daemon cannot cancel an operation. A daemon stop interrupts running builds, and the next start marks rows that are still running as interrupted. An image build that fails restores the previous image tags, so an interrupted build leaves no partial image. Shutdown stops the API listeners and the proxy first, then cancels and awaits the pricing worker and the other workers before plugins, loops and SQLite stop. That ordering prevents a request, a catalog publication, a final outbox, or a usage write from racing a closed database. Harness model catalog GET /api/harnesses/{type}/models (CLI: tariboy harness models TYPE) returns {harness, models: [{id, label, efforts}], efforts, error} for one harness as installed on the daemon host, so Desktop asks the host the agent will run on, including a remote one behind its SSH tunnel. The daemon runs the harness CLI in its own environment: | Harness | Source | | --- | --- | | Claude Code | Fixed list: fable, opus, opus[1m], sonnet, haiku; efforts low, medium, high, xhigh, max (the CLI has no model list command) | | Codex CLI | codex debug models: models with visibility: list, each with its supported reasoning levels efforts | | Cursor CLI | agent models: id - Name lines; no separate effort list | | OpenCode | opencode models: one provider/model per line; no effort list | Each run is bounded to 20 seconds and 4 MiB of output. A successful catalog is cached in daemon memory for five minutes per harness; refresh=true (CLI --refresh) asks the CLI again. A missing, failing, or unparseable CLI still answers HTTP 200 with empty lists and an error text; only an unknown harness is a bad harness request error. The catalog reflects the daemon environment, not an agent's own environment overrides such as a different CODEX HOME, and codex debug models may refresh its catalog over the network with the account's login. First-run setup The daemon sets up a fresh host by itself. In the worker phase it starts a background routine that registers the default Store tariboy and then builds tariboy/basic through image.build, as an operation with the initiator onboarding. The rules for when it registers and builds are in Images. TARIBOY ONBOARDING=off or tariboyd --onboarding=off skips the routine at start. Every test daemon sets it off. The daemon config key onboarding.default store holds registered, failed or removed. store.remove of the default Store writes removed. Error texts and the starter image state stay in daemon memory, so after a restart the routine tries a failed step again. Two commands read and drive it: | Command | Route | Result | | --- | --- | --- | | onboarding.status | GET /api/onboarding | OnboardingStatus | | onboarding.retry | POST /api/onboarding/retry | OnboardingStatus | OnboardingStatus has these fields: - default store: {state, name, source, error}, where state is registered, failed, removed or pending. - starter image: {state, ref, error}, where state is ready, building, failed, skipped (an image named basic already existed) or pending. - harnesses: {type, found, install} for claude, codex, opencode and cursor. stub is never in the list. - agents: the number of agents on the host. A Store that exists is registered, whatever the config key says. On a daemon with onboarding off, a missing Store is failed with the reason, so a client stops waiting. onboarding.retry starts the routine in the background, also on such a daemon, and returns the current status. A call while the routine runs only returns the status. Harness detection uses the PATH lookup of the missing-tools check. It is cached for five minutes, and refresh=true (CLI --refresh) looks again. When a clone or a build fails and git or npx is missing on the daemon PATH, the error starts with that tool and its install hint. daemon.status does not change. Managed model-price lifecycle The daemon owns one model-price catalog sourced from LiteLLM's fixed published HTTPS document. Startup synchronously reads the local cache because that read is bounded and does not use the network. A missing, stale, or rejected cache does not prevent the proxy from becoming ready: built-in fallback prices and operator-managed overrides remain available, while a missing or 24-hour-old cache triggers a network refresh in the background. The same awaited worker checks again every 24 hours until daemon shutdown. A refresh validates the complete candidate before changing published state. It atomically replaces the owner-only cache, replaces only litellm database rows in one transaction, and finally swaps the complete in-memory generation. Those ordered recovery points ensure requests see one full generation. If database publication fails after the cache rename, the active runtime generation remains unchanged and the next startup reconciles the valid cache. See AI proxy and audit for source precedence, request accounting, and diagnostics. Agent iteration and durable delivery An agent has one on/off switch, enabled , set by Start and cleared by Stop; interactive is a separate setting for the Terminal session. The loop engine launches autonomous iterations only while the agent is enabled, carries no stop policy error reason, and does not use the terminal-only bare:latest image. Its loop engine serializes work: a timer, explicit trigger, or a letter in its inbox may request work, but only one iteration runs at a time. Message-triggered work requires an enabled loop and an open letter in the agent's inbox, but no positive timer interval. Open letters enter the prompt in bounded batches, requests before notices. A request closes only when the agent replies to it; a notice closes only after an iteration that ends done. Any other outcome, including no i am done, a harness error, a timeout, or a kill, leaves both open for redelivery. See Agents and the iteration loop and The shim for the detailed scheduler and watchdog behavior. Failure, recovery, and observability | Condition | Automatic behavior | Evidence or operator action | | --- | --- | --- | | Daemon restart during a live shim | Replacement daemon adopts persisted running iterations and proxy handoff leases. It reaps a tmux session only when no live iteration owns it. | Inspect agent/iteration state and audit; never start a second daemon against the same base directory. | | Daemon restart during a script run | tariboy update and tariboy daemon restart leave the run running, and the replacement daemon publishes its original exit code. tariboy daemon stop, or a process lost at restart, records interrupted. | Inspect the run with script runs and its log; rerun an interrupted run explicitly. | | Harness timeout or error | The shim records a terminal outcome; loop policy may restart or stop future work. Open letters render again. | Review result, shim logs, audit, and agent loop policy. | | Plugin failure | The host health-checks and restarts enabled plugins; open letters to a plugin are delivered again. | Inspect plugin status/logs; never place upstream AI credentials in plugin configuration. | | Model-price refresh failure | The proxy keeps the last valid runtime generation, or built-in fallbacks when none has loaded. The next daily check retries. | Inspect pricing catalog error daemon logs/events; fields are bounded to source, generation time, model count, and a stable error class. | | Missed notification or daemon crash | The durable outbox and the ingress reconciler replay pending intent; task state remains in SQLite. | Inspect task event history; the publisher retries on its own. | | Budget denial | Proxy rejects/reports before provider access and records usage/audit evidence. | Inspect usage, budgets, and the sensitive per-iteration transcript. | Structured daemon logs, per-agent audit JSONL, iteration results, task events, usage records, and optional OpenTelemetry signals make the system observable. The daemon writes two logs in its runtime directory ( /.tariboyd by default). tariboyd.log is the application log: the launcher sends the daemon's stdout and stderr to it. It has startup lines, warnings and errors, and one WARN line slow or failed http request for each API request that takes 500 ms or more or ends with a 5xx status. WebSocket and SSE requests stay open by design and are not slow requests. tariboyd.access.log has one JSON line for every API request: method, path, status and dur ms. The daemon rotates the access log at 50 MB and keeps three old copies (tariboyd.access.log.1 is the newest). The CLI and Desktop launchers move a tariboyd.log that is larger than 50 MB to tariboyd.log.1 before they start a daemon. tariboy daemon logs shows only tariboyd.log. The daemon has one SQLite writer connection for all writes. The reads that the UI polls — daemon status, the agents list, the mailbox, the task list and the image list — use a separate pool of four read-only connections. WAL mode lets those reads see the last committed state while a write is open, so they do not wait behind the writer. OTLP stays off until an endpoint is explicitly configured. Proxy transcripts are sensitive data and support bundles intentionally exclude them. Key daemon flags - --base-dir — override the data dir. - --listen — unix | unix:/path.sock | tcp:HOST:PORT. - --auth-token-file — required for non-loopback TCP. - --http-addr — loopback JSON API/WebSocket listener; pass "" to disable it. --web-addr remains a deprecated compatibility alias. - --log-level, --version. Command registry Every operator command is one registry.Command in internal/commands. The CLI parser, the daemon HTTP router, --help-json and /api/openapi.json are all derived from it. - Arguments are bound once. registry.Call runs registry.Bind before a handler: a missing required argument is answered 400 missing param, and a value of the wrong type ("abc" for a number, a number for a string) is answered 400 invalid param. The HTTP router, the CLI, plugin commands and internal callers all go through it. An empty query value such as ?limit= counts as omitted for a number or a boolean. An argument with an OpenAPI Schema keeps the shape it was sent in, and undeclared keys pass through. - Handlers read typed values. A handler receives registry.Request with the transport context and the bound Params, and reads them through the accessors in internal/registry/params.go (String, Trimmed, Int, Bool, Strings, Has, Decode and the optional forms). A guard test keeps raw map assertions and local coercion helpers out of internal/commands. - Errors map once. internal/api/errors.go maps a domain error to its HTTP answer for both the operator API and the per-agent capability socket: api.UserError, tasks.Error, mail.Error and assessment.Error carry their own status, a parameter error is 400, not-found sentinels are 404, script state conflicts are 409. Any other error is 500 internal with a fixed text, and its detail goes only to the daemon log. Both servers decode JSON bodies with the same size limit and a fixed bad json text. - Some commands run in the CLI. A command with Local runs in the CLI process instead of over HTTP: daemon start|stop|restart|status|logs, update, the compose verbs, image build, workflow build, operation ls, operation log, metrics task and metrics server. daemon status, the build verbs, the operation verbs and the metrics verbs also keep their HTTP routes; the CLI side of a build starts the operation and reads its log over the socket, and the CLI side of a metrics verb reads the report over the socket and prints it as tables. AbsPathArgs names the path arguments the CLI makes absolute, and ExitCodeFrom derives the CLI exit code from a result. - Results are typed Go structs. A handler returns a named struct, never map[string]any, and the command declares it with registry.WithResultT. The helper derives the JSON Schema of T with github.com/invopop/jsonschema, adds T and every named struct it reaches to Schemas under its Go type name, and sets ResultSchema to {"$ref": "#/components/schemas/T"}. For a slice of a named struct, such as []StoreView, ResultSchema is an array of that reference. /api/openapi.json copies Schemas into components.schemas and puts ResultSchema under result in the 200 envelope. The rules follow encoding/json: - the json tag names a property; - a field without omitempty is required, a field with it is optional; - a pointer field must carry omitempty, or registration panics; - every struct schema has additionalProperties: false; - an embedded struct adds its fields to the parent; - an enum is a string type whose JSONSchemaExtend method sets Enum from its Go constants; - a value that can be JSON null, such as a nil slice, carries jsonschema extras:"nullable=true"; - a result whose shape the code does not own, such as a plugin's action result or the daemon config keyed by config name, is a named struct with a MarshalJSON method that keeps the wire format and a JSONSchema method that describes the open shape. Two different schemas under one component name in one command also panic at registration. Every command in internal/commands uses this form. The result types of a domain are in its types.go file, for example agents types.go. The task commands in tasks.go name their result types in the taskResultTypes table. The field descriptions and enums of the internal/tasks types come from jsonschema:"description=..." tags and JSONSchemaExtend methods. No command has a hand-written ResultSchema. - The spec is a checked contract. These tests in internal/commands keep /api/openapi.json and the code together: - TestHTTPCommandsDeclareResultSchema fails for an HTTP command whose ResultSchema is not a component reference or an array of one. There is no exception list. - TestCommandsReturnNoRawMaps (result guard test.go) parses the package's non-test files and fails for a function with the handler result (any, error) that returns a map[string]any literal, make(map[string]any), or a variable filled from one. - TestCommandsDeclareConsistentComponents fails when two commands declare one component name with different schemas. Give result types a domain prefix, such as StoreView, not a generic name such as Item. - TestOpenAPISnapshot compares the served spec with the committed snapshot internal/commands/testdata/openapi.json. The snapshot pins info.version to snapshot, so a release does not change it. A contract change is a change with an updated snapshot. Rewrite it with go test ./internal/commands -run TestOpenAPISnapshot -update-openapi and commit it with the code. - TestTypedResponsesMatchOpenAPI sends a request to every operation whose result is a component reference or has properties, and validates the response against the served spec with github.com/santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6. A new typed operation needs a call in its table or in its domain's typedCallSets entry, or the test fails. The check finds a result that differs from its declared type: an extra field, a missing required field, a wrong type, or null where the schema does not allow it. Error responses are validated against the default error envelope. - TestDaemonOpenAPIContract runs only from scripts/tariboy-tasks-e2e.sh. It reads the spec of the isolated daemon, compares it with the snapshot apart from info.version, and validates the daemon's answers to typed GET routes. The spec stays OpenAPI 3.0.3. Before validation, the tests rewrite nullable: true, which JSON Schema does not know, into a type and enum that allow null. Native task commands have one more table: internal/tasks/wire.go declares each task action's request struct, CLI words, flags and operator route. The ttasks parser, the operator HTTP decoder and the agent socket decoder are all built from it, so a new flag is one tagged field. Version reporting Every HTTP response from the daemon — the operator API and per-agent capability socket alike — carries the daemon's build version in the X-Tariboy-Version response header. It is stamped by one wrapper around each server's handler, so successes, error envelopes and 404s all carry it; clients never need a dedicated version route. The daemon never refuses a request over a version difference: an older client must keep working against a newer daemon. The header is diagnostic only — the reaction to a mismatch belongs to the client, see Binaries & commands. Agent bin shims Provisioning writes only the compatibility shims enabled by the image into <data dir /agents/<name /bin: i-am-done and the legacy tasks shim. The real tariboy-tasks executable is installed globally as ttasks. At startup, a packaged daemon also atomically refreshes one shared bin/ttasks symlink in its runtime directory to its sibling payload and prepends that directory to the resolved account PATH. Fresh Desktop agents therefore have ttasks before optional CLI installation; no agent-local ttasks shim is created. The runtime alias remains across daemon restarts for surviving iterations. An explicit agent PATH override must retain a Tasks command location. When TARIBOY TOOLS SOCKET is non-empty, it uses that identity-bound socket and fails closed; when absent, it uses the host Unix daemon socket as the customer actor. Each compatibility shim execs its owning skill script by an absolute path inside the active image's image/skills directory. Every other capability is invoked through its packaged skill-local scripts/ .sh launcher. The launch gate validates that each required launcher exists inside the candidate image, is regular, and is executable before replacing the current bridge or shims. Failure leaves the previous image and its shims active. Lifecycle is normally driven through the tariboy daemon subcommands rather than launching the binary directly. See The operator CLI. Read on What an iteration is, how the loop wakes, and the whoami / loop / mail core. Letters between principals, requests and notices, and redelivery. One harness iteration under a watchdog. Why the DB is the single source of truth. Queue keys, recursive access, comments, answer tracking, and delegation. Queues bound to workflow images, agent pools, dispatch, artifacts, outcomes, check and watch scripts, queue secrets, and queue triggers. Routing, budgets, usage, and the per-iteration transcript. Where the Tauri UI lives and how it talks to host-local daemons.
description: How tariboyd owns durable state, agent execution, APIs, plugins, policy, and recovery.
title: Daemon architecture

content: Every LLM call an agent or plugin makes is routed through the daemon's in-process AI proxy (internal/aiproxy). The proxy: - routes to the configured provider and model; - enforces cost budgets (tariboy budget …) and records usage and cost into ai requests (tariboy usage); - writes a per-iteration audit transcript (proxy-transcript.jsonl) — the real request/response including thinking and tool calls — so an iteration can be replayed and inspected after the fact. tariboy daemon reindex rebuilds the ai requests metadata from these transcripts. The Cursor harness is the exception to the last two points: its traffic is metered without bodies, prices, or cost budgets. The proxy drops the client's Accept-Encoding header when it forwards a request. The upstream response still travels compressed, but the proxy decompresses it, so the usage parser and transcripts see plain SSE or JSON and the client receives the response uncompressed over loopback. Passing the client's header through would leave compressed bytes that the usage parser cannot read, and requests would be recorded with no model, tokens or cost. Request status Each ai requests row and transcript entry has a status. The HTTP status from the upstream stays in upstream status. | Status | Meaning | | --- | --- | | ok | The upstream answered below 400 and the response arrived complete. | | auth error | The request had no valid attribution token or upstream credential. | | budget block | A cost budget or a task budget refused the request before it reached the upstream. | | quota probe | The upstream answered 429 to the startup quota probe of Claude Code (max tokens 1, one user message quota). This is not a failure. | | rate limited | The upstream answered 429 to any other request, for example at a usage limit. | | client closed | The client went away before the exchange finished. The daemon stops the session after loop.sh done, so an open request at that time gets this status. | | upstream error | Every other failure: an upstream status of 400 or more, an unreachable upstream, or a cut response. | While the newest request of a running iteration is rate limited, the agent status endpoint returns active iteration.rate limited since with the time of that request. The next accepted request clears it. Task budgets A task budget limits the AI spending of a task and its subtree. The proxy checks it after the agent and group budgets, on every request with a task id. The check reads the database on each request. It walks from the task of the request up to its root over tasks.parent id. For each task with budget usd 0, it sums ai requests.cost usd of the subtree and of the old keys in task key aliases. The index idx ai requests task cost (migration 0079) serves this sum. If one subtree spent its limit or more, the proxy answers 429 with budget exceeded: task KEY, in the Connect format for Cursor, and records budget block. The audit event budget block has the scope task:KEY. Then the proxy tells the daemon, which pauses or blocks the task off the request path, once at a time for each key. If that reaction fails, the daemon logs it, and the next refusal tries again. If the check itself fails, the request goes through and the proxy logs a warning. Transcript after iteration close At iteration close the daemon compresses proxy-transcript.jsonl into proxy-transcript.jsonl.gz and removes the plain file. A request that is still open when the session stops finishes later. The proxy then adds its entry to the .gz as a new gzip member, and does not create a new plain file. Go, zcat and Python read the members as one stream. tariboy transcript reads the .gz first and then a plain file, if one exists. Older daemons left such a plain file next to the .gz, and its entries come after the archived ones. Every agent may also have four independent USD limits for the local calendar hour, day, ISO week (Monday start), and month. Each defaults to 0 (unlimited) and is separate from the legacy global/group rolling budgets. When one or more non-zero limits are exhausted from immutable ai requests.cost usd history, the proxy denies the next request before upstream provider access. After token authentication establishes both agent and iteration attribution, the proxy records that iteration's activity timestamp before forwarding the request. This drives the non-blocking stalled-agent signal described in the state model: it never rejects, cancels, or otherwise changes the request or iteration lifecycle, and a recording failure is diagnostic-only. Before starting a harness, the daemon reads its selected Goal once, resolves the task's top-level root through Native Tasks (see Root of a Goal in another queue), and stamps the AI-proxy lease with task id and epic id. All requests in the iteration are therefore attributed without an agent command. An iteration without a selected Goal remains unattributed. An agent that creates or claims work after its iteration starts may use scripts/goal.sh set <TASK-KEY . The daemon validates and persists that Goal, resolves its top-level root, and updates the live lease. Only later requests use the new attribution; already recorded requests remain unchanged. A tagged live lease rejects a different Goal. Root of a Goal in another queue The epic id is the real root of the task tree, also when the agent cannot read it. A Goal can be a child in another queue than its parent (see Subtasks in another queue). The agent then cannot read the parent. The daemon reads the Goal with the rights of the agent. A Goal that the agent cannot read, or reads only as a former workflow holder, is refused with not found. The daemon reads the ancestors of the Goal with the rights of the customer. Thus the cost of the iteration goes to the root of the customer's project. The agent does not get the key of a root that it cannot read. In that case the answer of scripts/goal.sh set has an empty epic id. Only the proxy lease and the recorded requests keep the real root. The operator sees it in tariboy usage --group-by epic. If the daemon cannot read an ancestor, for example because the ancestor was deleted or the store failed, the walk stops. The last ancestor that the daemon read becomes epic id. The daemon writes a warning with the agent, the Goal, that root and the error, and the iteration starts. A cycle of parents still stops the iteration with an error. Pricing catalog and request costs The daemon owns a last-known-good model-price catalog from LiteLLM's fixed published source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BerriAI/litellm/main/model prices and context window.json At startup it loads and validates the bounded local model-prices-litellm.json cache before proxy requests begin. A missing or invalid cache is non-fatal. If the cache is absent or at least 24 hours old, an awaited daemon worker refreshes it after startup without blocking proxy readiness, then refreshes every 24 hours until shutdown. Downloads have a ten-second timeout, an eight-MiB limit, no redirect following, and complete catalog validation before publication. Runtime price resolution uses this precedence: 1. an operator-managed manual database row; 2. the latest valid litellm database row; 3. the built-in fallback for selected models. LiteLLM per-token values are converted to USD per million tokens. When a model does not publish a cache-write or cache-read price, ordinary input pricing is used for that bucket. Provider parsers make the four token buckets exclusive: OpenAI cache-read and cache-write tokens are subtracted from total input, while Anthropic's already-separated values remain separate. Negative values are clamped to zero. One request looks up one complete in-memory price generation and stores the resulting cost usd in ai requests. A later catalog publication cannot mix prices within that request or recalculate its historical cost. Unknown models remain proxyable and are recorded at zero cost with a bounded warning. A successful refresh writes and syncs an owner-only temporary cache, atomically renames it, replaces all litellm database rows in one transaction, and then swaps the complete runtime map. If any candidate, download, cache, or database step fails, the last valid runtime generation remains active; when database publication fails after cache replacement, the next startup can reconcile the valid cache. pricing catalog loaded, pricing catalog refreshed, and pricing catalog error logs/events expose only source, generation time, accepted model count, and a stable error class. They never include the catalog body, credentials, or model request data. Group snapshots and Usage After request attribution is known, the proxy resolves the agent's current group once and stores its identifier and display name with the Usage row. A lookup failure records an explicitly ungrouped request rather than dropping usage. Current groups use their name as both identifier and display name, but the stored fields remain request-time snapshots: later group or membership changes do not rewrite them. The server usage command and /api/usage route apply one group predicate to the aggregate rows, daily series, summary totals, and newest-first request list. An absent group returns all snapshots, a group name selects that saved identifier, and ungrouped selects null snapshots. Recent requests are bounded to 200 rows. The Desktop behavior is described in Web UI architecture. Keys never reach plugins Because the proxy is the only path to an LLM, plugins never receive the upstream provider key: the daemon scrubs ANTHROPIC API KEY / OPENAI API KEY from plugin environments and hands out short-lived scoped proxy tokens instead. Codex harness Codex harness iterations are configured automatically with a per-invocation custom provider that uses this tokenized proxy (including Codex's Responses API). Operators do not need to set OPENAI BASE URL or place an OpenAI provider key in an agent environment for audit attribution. The transcript reader normalizes Responses API messages, reasoning summaries, local shell actions, function and MCP calls, and their results into the same readable Activity timeline used for other harnesses. Activity can copy that readable timeline as Markdown for one iteration or all retained iterations. Its explicit ZIP export contains audit.md for human review and lossless audit.jsonl records for downstream analysis. The JSONL records preserve the raw proxied request and response bodies. OpenCode harness Both OpenCode launch modes prepare provider routes before starting the shim. After the global and agent shell scripts run, bounded opencode debug config and opencode models --verbose probes resolve the main model, small model, and explicitly configured agent models. The main model must be an explicit provider/model selection in the agent settings or OpenCode configuration. When no small model is configured, it uses the main model. Each selected provider's original address is bound to the iteration lease. Address templates such as ${API HOST} use the final launch environment. An unresolved template fails preparation before the harness starts. An in-memory OPENCODE CONFIG CONTENT overlay replaces its options.baseURL with a tokenized local route, limits enabled providers and their model lists, and is checked again with debug config. Image skills keep their existing OPENCODE CONFIG DIR. Original configuration and authentication files are not rewritten, and API keys remain OpenCode's responsibility. The proxy forwards provider authentication only to the bound upstream and removes its own token. For example, kimi-code-plan-global/k3 keeps Kimi's coding endpoint rather than selecting OpenAI from the model name. Supported transports are @ai-sdk/openai, @ai-sdk/openai-compatible, and @ai-sdk/anthropic with API-key authentication. Missing proxy service, failed probes, unresolved models, external OpenCode plugins, OAuth credentials, model transport overrides, and incompatible transports fail preparation. Inline OPENCODE CONFIG CONTENT must be a JSON object; JSONC configuration files remain supported by OpenCode. No direct-provider fallback is installed. After the probes pass, Tariboy can add its own instant mail plugin to the overlay. The probes never see it, and it does not change the provider addresses. Requests use the ordinary usage, budget, attribution, and full transcript path. OpenAI-compatible streams request final usage. Provider routes survive daemon handoff with the lease and disappear when it is revoked. This accounts for new iterations; previous direct requests have no proxy transcript to recover. Pricing uses the exact returned or requested model identifier, including k3, without substituting a similar model. Unknown prices retain token counts and zero cost with a bounded warning. OpenCode's zero Kimi catalog price does not establish a per-token subscription price: a reliable manual or catalog price is needed for nonzero USD accounting. Unknown prices also mean USD budgets cannot cap actual provider spend. Cursor harness The Cursor CLI speaks Connect RPC over HTTP/2, so the proxy listener also accepts cleartext HTTP/2 (h2c) on its loopback address. Requests whose path is /auth… or a method of an agent.v1. or aiserver.v1. service are routed to the cursor provider and streamed unchanged to https://api2.cursor.sh, or to TARIBOY UPSTREAM CURSOR BASE URL when the daemon environment sets it. The same path-safety guard as other providers applies. The proxy never injects a provider key: the client's own Authorization header is forwarded as sent. Cursor metering differs from the other providers: - Request and response bodies are binary Connect frames and are not written to proxy-transcript.jsonl. Each proxied request still produces a metadata row with the path, status, and latency, but zero tokens and no model. - Batch iterations read token counts from the result event of the CLI's stream-json stdout and record one extra cursor row per result. It names the agent's configured model id, or the CLI's display name when the agent uses auto or no model. That row is also appended to the iteration transcript, so tariboy daemon reindex restores it. Interactive Cursor iterations have no machine-readable stdout and record no token counts. - tariboy usage therefore counts the per-request traffic rows plus one usage row per result, so its Cursor request count is higher than the number of model calls. - Cursor reports no price, so cost usd stays empty. Cursor traffic never adds to any USD budget or calendar limit. A budget already exhausted by other spend still blocks Cursor requests; the proxy then answers HTTP 429 with a Connect resource exhausted error instead of the Anthropic error envelope. Daemon restart continuity The proxy listener remains in-process, so a daemon restart creates a brief loopback outage. Its concrete 127.0.0.1:PORT and active per-iteration token leases are atomically stored in the owner-only /.tariboy/aiproxy-handoff.json. The replacement daemon prunes leases whose iteration is no longer running, binds the same address, and accepts the surviving harness's existing token. If that address is occupied while a live lease exists, startup fails instead of silently moving the proxy and marooning the harness on its old URL. Adoption removes the carried lease after the shim produces a terminal result. The handoff file is runtime-sensitive state: it is not part of SQLite, audit logs, transcripts, or support bundles. The pricing catalog cache has a different purpose and lifecycle from this handoff file. It contains external model-price data, not active tokens, but is also owner-only and excluded from support bundles. See Security and controls.
description: Every LLM call routes through the in-process AI proxy, which enforces budgets and writes a per-iteration audit transcript.
title: The AI proxy & the audit log

content: An agent is a configured, named instance of an image with its own working directory and its own loop. It does not run continuously — it runs a series of iterations . On each iteration the daemon: 1. prepares a prompt — a platform-owned Task Processing Order block groups one-shot instructions, messages (including awaiting replies), and Goal in that order. Schema v2 preserves the declared order of the remaining image layers; self-contained legacy schema-v1 artifacts use the same work block; 2. launches the harness (e.g. Claude) under the shim for exactly one pass; 3. records the outcome, iteration logs, AI usage, and audit timeline. What drives the loop The loop is driven three ways, all requiring the agent to be enabled : - Timer — interval s: wake every N seconds. - Schedule — an RFC 5545 RRULE, set with tariboy loop schedule or the Schedule builder on the agent's Configuration tab: start an iteration at each occurrence, with the trigger schedule. See Schedule. - Message — a letter sent to the agent nudges the loop to start an iteration now (only while the agent's inbox holds open letters). A message iteration can end with an error (harness error, or a launch that failed). Open letters then stay open, except the Goal letter of a harness error iteration (see Redelivery after a failed iteration). If the agent still has open letters and on error is not stop, the loop starts a new message iteration after a delay. The first delay is 30 seconds. Each further error doubles the delay, up to 10 minutes. An iteration that does not fail resets the delay to 30 seconds. Each iteration shows a letter again and counts one more attempt. The prompt shows a letter at most five times. The next iteration marks it as a dead letter. With a lasting failure, this happens about 15.5 minutes after the first attempt. A new letter does not shorten a delay that is already running. Loop policy is per-agent: interval, timeout (soft), hard-timeout, on timeout and on error (e.g. restart). An iteration ends when it signals completion, exits, or reaches an enforced deadline. A timeout or hard-timeout of 0 means no deadline, in headless and interactive mode alike. When only timeout is set, the hard deadline is timeout plus 60 seconds. The engine re-reads the agent's saved settings before each iteration it starts, whatever started it: timer, schedule, message, or a manual run (agent exec, Run now ). A change you save, such as the user prompt, applies to the next iteration. An iteration that is already running keeps the settings it started with. Schedule The schedule is an optional RRULE with an optional DTSTART line before it, for example: | Run | Schedule | | --- | --- | | Every weekday at 09:30 | RRULE:FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=MO,TU,WE,TH,FR;BYHOUR=9;BYMINUTE=30 | | The 15th of each month at 08:00 | RRULE:FREQ=MONTHLY;BYMONTHDAY=15;BYHOUR=8;BYMINUTE=0 | | The last day of each month at 23:45 | RRULE:FREQ=MONTHLY;BYMONTHDAY=-1;BYHOUR=23;BYMINUTE=45 | | Once, on 20 October 2026 at 09:30 | DTSTART:20261020T093000 then RRULE:FREQ=DAILY;COUNT=1 | | Every 2 hours | RRULE:FREQ=HOURLY;INTERVAL=2 | The two lines can be separated by a newline or a space. Schedules run at whole minutes: the daemon rejects FREQ=SECONDLY and any BYSECOND other than 0. When the daemon saves a schedule, it stores a normalized form: it adds BYSECOND=0 and, when there is no DTSTART, it adds DTSTART as the current minute. A DTSTART without TZID or Z is in the time zone of the daemon host, also for a remote host. Name another zone with DTSTART;TZID=Europe/Moscow:20261018T000000. An invalid rule is rejected with bad schedule and the previous schedule stays. The engine arms one timer for the nearer of the next interval s firing and the next occurrence. The two sources work independently; set interval s to 0 to start the agent only on its schedule. An occurrence never starts a second iteration while one runs, and missed occurrences are not replayed: after an iteration, or after the daemon or the agent was off, the next start is the first occurrence after the current time. A finished rule (COUNT or UNTIL) stays saved but starts nothing. The agent view reports schedule and schedule next at (RFC 3339, empty when there is no next start). Each row of the agent list (GET /api/agents, agent.ps) also carries current iteration started at, the start of the running iteration, and last iteration at, the start of the newest iteration in any status. Both are the stored started at values and are absent when they do not apply. One query reads them for every agent, through the (agent, started at) index. Agent Goals Goal is per-agent and enabled by default. The reconciler retains one assigned Native Task selection until it is released: done or cancelled, lost assignment or visibility, Goal disabled, a wait customer task whose oldest unanswered customer wait reaches the agent's positive goal wait customer timeout s (300 seconds by default), or eligible assigned work with a strictly higher priority. It orders replacements by priority (P0 through P3), then in progress before open, creation time, and task key. Equal-priority work does not displace a valid selection. A task's pull request URL does not affect Goal selection or release. At startup, relevant task or agent changes, terminal iteration completion, and the bounded one-minute recovery cadence, the reconciler sends one durable task.goal letter from system:goal. The letter wakes the agent like any other; the reconciler never starts an iteration directly. An open Goal letter blocks another one. Dead letters are retained but do not block a new Goal generation; the positive per-agent delivery cooldown (60 seconds by default) still blocks rapid repeats. A wait within its grace period remains the goal but sends no continuation wake. Disabled agents and agents on bare:latest neither select nor receive a goal wake, but preserve a valid sticky key; only disabling Goal clears it. The end of an iteration closes the agent's open Goal and task notices about its Goal task, and stale task notices start no iteration; see Task notifications. After a harness error iteration, the end closes only the Goal letters. The task.assigned and task.answered notices stay open for the next iteration. Redelivery after a failed iteration A failed iteration is an iteration that ended without loop.sh done, with the status harness error, timeout or no i am done. If the newest iteration of the agent failed, the reconciler sends the Goal again after a pause. It does not wait for a new letter. The reconciler counts n, the failed iterations of the agent in a row. It reads the count from the iterations table, newest first, up to the last done iteration. The count therefore survives a daemon restart. A done iteration resets the count. A killed or failed iteration does not change the count and does not reset it. The pause starts at the end of the newest failed iteration: In this formula, c is the goal delivery cooldown s of the agent. The first pause is c. Each further failure in a row doubles the pause, up to 10 minutes. If c is more than 10 minutes, the pause is c: the bound never makes the pause shorter than the configured cooldown. For c = 60 seconds, the pauses are 60, 120, 240, 480, 600 and 600 seconds. Before the pause ends, the reconciler sends no Goal letter and arms one timer in memory for the due time. The timer starts a full reconciliation pass. After a restart, the startup pass reads the due time from the database. If the timer does not fire, the one-minute pass sends the letter up to one minute late. When the pause ends, the reconciler sends one task.goal letter with the reason retry. The usual delivery checks still apply: an open Goal letter blocks it, and so does the cooldown since the last delivery. Each failed iteration gets at most one such letter. For each letter, the reconciler writes the goal redelivered event to the audit log of the agent, with the source system and the ID of the failed iteration. The event data has these fields: - task key: the key of the Goal task. - failures: the count n. - pause s: the pause in seconds. - last status: the status of the failed iteration. These rules apply in special cases: - If the newest iteration is still running, the reconciler sends nothing. The end of that iteration starts the next decision. - If the agent is disabled, it gets no Goal, so it gets no letter and no event. - If a stop policy (on error=stop or on timeout=stop) halted the loop, the reconciler sends nothing. After Start clears the halt, the next pass sends the Goal with the pause of the current count. - If the newest iteration is killed (an operator stop) or failed, the usual Goal delivery applies, with no pause and no event. The engine retry for open letters (30 seconds, doubled up to 10 minutes) still applies after a harness error iteration when other letters stay open. The Goal letter of that iteration is closed, so if it was the only open letter, the engine does not retry and only the reconciler wakes the agent. If other letters stay open, the engine retry can start the next iteration before the pause ends. A Goal letter sent while the engine retry is armed joins that retry and starts no second iteration. When the pause ends, the reconciler decides again from the newest iteration, so one failure gives one new iteration. The engine retry stays in memory and writes no event. Every non-bare agent receives daemon-owned Goal guidance inside Task Processing Order , regardless of image plugins or runtime entries. The guidance has two forms, chosen by the selected task. - Flexible task (a queue with no workflow): the block tells the agent to work through the Native Task workflow, wait for a recorded customer answer while in wait customer, and set wait customer after recording a PR while monitoring it rather than merging. When selected, it also contains the task key, title, priority, status, and description. With no selected task it carries only the general guidance. - Workflow task (a task that follows a workflow image): the block states that the task follows a workflow and that the agent leaves the status only with ttasks advance, then lists the task fields, the status instructions from the pinned image, the outcomes with their requirements, the artifacts, the last rejected or failed transition request of the visit, and the exact ttasks artifacts set and ttasks advance --from STATUS commands. If the workflow data cannot be loaded the agent gets the flexible text and a note to run ttasks workflow get KEY. See The Goal block. The Goal letter is only a durable wake hint. Task title, description, artifact values, and script messages are untrusted task input, not daemon instructions or lifecycle authority; the workflow form renders them as fenced, bounded data. Status instructions are trusted image content. Idle counting. The workflow form feeds the idle iterations limit. The loop manager is the single place that reports an iteration end: every terminal path of an iteration (normal finish, runner error, a manual failure with the tmux session alive, and the adoption and stale-kill recovery paths) calls Manager.iterationCompleted, which first hands the daemon the agent, the iteration, the Goal task key the iteration was prepared with, and its start and end times, and only then wakes the Goal reconciler. A harness error iteration is reported with a harness-error mark: the daemon closes its Goal letters and does not count it as idle. For other iterations, the daemon counts the iteration as idle when the agent held the task's pool status when the iteration began and made no transition request during it, and pauses the task at the limit; see Pauses. The block starts with # Task Processing Order and a fixed instruction to process one-shot, then messages, then Goal. The next paragraph is the iteration mode line. The mode tells the image how the agent works in this iteration, so the image does not guess the process from the Goal text. The line is the same for all images and does not depend on the image template: | Mode | When | Line | | --- | --- | --- | | workflow | A Goal task is selected and its row has a workflow digest | `Iteration mode: workflow. The goal task follows a workflow: the status instructions in the Goal section set the process. | | flexible | A Goal task is selected and its row has no workflow digest | Iteration mode: flexible. The goal task has no workflow: your image instructions set the process. | | request | No Goal task is selected | Iteration mode: request. No goal task is selected: work from the one-shot instruction or the messages. | One function, loop.IterationModeFor, computes the mode from the selected task row alone. The runner and the prompt preview both call it, for schema v1 and schema v2 images. If the workflow data of a workflow task cannot be loaded, the mode stays workflow. In that case the Goal subsection shows the fallback note to run ttasks workflow get KEY. A prompt built without a known mode fails with the error iteration mode is not set, and the iteration does not start. The line appears once, before ## One-shot. Its ## One-shot, ## Messages, and ## Goal subsections always appear. Missing inputs explicitly say that there is no one-shot instruction, no incoming messages, or no selected Goal for this iteration; the agent is told to continue without running commands merely to search for absent input. Outstanding requests remain nested under Messages even when no incoming messages exist. Open letters are listed with their ids, senders, kinds, attempts, threading fields, subject and data, requests before notices, followed by the standing instruction to answer each request with tmail reply; see Mail. Bare sessions still receive no prompt. The operator prompt preview uses the same grouping, Goal selection, and iteration mode line. It keeps placeholders for messages and the one-shot supplied at execution time; viewing the preview does not render letters or increment their attempts. Harness environment and preflight The daemon's own environment is the baseline every iteration starts from, so agents see what the account sees. Desktop starts the daemon inside the account's login shell, which supplies that environment directly; a daemon started without a usable shell instead resolves the account's PATH once, before loop startup, from a bounded interactive-login-shell probe. Per-iteration construction begins with that daemon environment, applies harness-required values, then explicit agent environment and secrets. An explicit agent PATH is therefore an intentional override. Non-bare images prepend the agent bin directory after the override; bare images omit that prefix and otherwise keep the daemon baseline. Each iteration also gets TARIBOY INSTANT MAIL FLAG, the path of the flag file /agents/ /iterations/ /instant-mail. The daemon sets it after the agent environment and the image skill environment, so neither can change it. The daemon creates the file when an instant letter waits for the iteration. Agent scripts and image activation do not get the variable, because they do not run in an iteration. For a Claude Code agent with the mail capability on a non-bare image, the runner also loads the instant mail hooks. After the executable preflight below, it finds tmail on the final PATH and runs claude --version. If the version is 2.1.227 or newer, it writes the plugin /agents/ /harness-hooks/claude/ and appends --plugin-dir to the harness argv. Both the batch and the interactive argv get it, after the image skill bridge. The hooks PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure and Stop call that absolute tmail path. If tmail is missing, the version is older or unrecognized, or the write fails, the runner logs a warning and starts the iteration without the hooks. A codex agent with the same conditions gets the hooks too, but the runner writes no file for them. If codex --version gives 0.141.0 or newer and the daemon codex approval mode is yolo, the runner appends --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust and two -c hooks. =... overrides to the harness argv: PostToolUse and Stop, each with the absolute tmail path. Both codex exec and the codex TUI get the same arguments. The runner does not set CODEX HOME or change HOME. In approve-for-me, with an older or unrecognized version, or without tmail, the runner logs a warning and starts the iteration without the hooks. The mail reference gives the hook output and the limits. For an OpenCode agent with the mail capability on a non-bare image, the runner loads the instant mail plugin during the OpenCode preparation. After the agent shell snapshot, it finds tmail and opencode on the final PATH and runs opencode --version. If the version is 1.19.5 or newer, it writes /agents/ /harness-hooks/opencode/tariboy-instant-mail.js. After both routing probes pass, it adds the file:// URL of that file to the plugin key of OPENCODE CONFIG CONTENT. The probes never see this plugin, so they still refuse every other plugin. The batch and the interactive mode run the same command with the same overlay. If tmail is missing, the version is older or unrecognized, or the write fails, the runner logs a warning and starts the iteration without the plugin. With a plugin, OpenCode installs @opencode-ai/plugin into each of its configuration directories before it starts. The first start after an OpenCode update can take about 70 seconds longer. Without network access, each start waits about 72 seconds until an install succeeds. The routing probes have a timeout of 20 seconds, and this wait does not affect them, because they run without the plugin. Before starting the shim, the runner checks the adapter's actual executable against this final environment. For a non-bare image it also resolves python3 there and supplies that absolute interpreter path to the packaged skill launchers. A missing or non-executable harness or Python interpreter fails preparation through the normal harness error path without including environment values, prompts, secrets, working directories, or user files. This preflight improves the diagnosis but cannot remove the normal race in which an executable disappears before process launch. Immediately before the unchanged harness command is executed, Bash sources /global-agent-shell.sh, then /agents/ /agent-shell.sh. Missing or empty files do nothing; exports and filesystem effects from either script are available to that iteration. A source-time failure prevents the harness from starting and follows the existing harness error lifecycle. OpenCode sources these scripts once during preparation, before discovering its providers. It carries their exported environment, resulting working directory, and umask into the launch instead of sourcing them again. Script output is discarded during this bounded preparation; failures report a fixed diagnostic without shell output or environment values. Original provider environment URLs remain available for discovery. The final routing overlay takes precedence over inline configuration exported by either script, and a second effective-config probe checks it before launch. Missing proxy routing or unsupported OpenCode configuration fails preparation with harness error; see OpenCode routing. The same scripts, in the same order, are sourced before every command the daemon runs as the agent outside an iteration: each durable script run, where a source-time failure fails that run, and each run as: agent workflow check, which starts with the environment the scripts export and fails without running when they fail. Every harness error iteration writes an iteration finished audit event whose error field states the cause, which the audit timeline shows next to the status. A failure before or during launch, such as a configured agent CWD that does not exist, records the launch error. A harness that exits non-zero records harness exited with code N, followed for non-interactive agents by up to 20 trailing lines (2 KiB) of harness.stderr.log; the same lines are already teed into the audit as harness output. After loop.sh done, the daemon waits for the done grace and then stops the session itself. The harness then exits with 143 or 137, or the shim records -1 because tmux wrote no exit status. A done iteration therefore stores exit code 0, and the daemon log keeps the raw code as harness exit after done. A non-zero stored exit code means that the harness failed or was killed before loop.sh done. The claude adapter starts every iteration with CLAUDE CODE ENABLE PROMPT SUGGESTION=false. Prompt suggestions make extra AI calls and add suggested user lines to an unattended session. A bare launch keeps the Claude default. A value in the agent env replaces the adapter value. For a schema-v2 image with skills, the launch gate prepares agents/ /image-bridges/ / / before an image is promoted or an iteration row is created. The bridge contains copied skill bytes and generated adapter metadata; it never links back to the image or source tree. Publication is owner-only and atomic. The current adapter contract version is 2. A complete bridge is reused across iterations and daemon restarts, while an incomplete or modified cache is rebuilt. An OpenCode bridge stays valid with the @opencode-ai/plugin install entries that OpenCode adds at its root (node modules/, package.json, package-lock.json, bun.lock, .gitignore), so the install does not cause a rebuild. A preparation or harness-support failure leaves the previous image active and records the pending-image error. Because no iteration row exists yet, such a failure also halts the loop and records its cause in the agent's error reason, which the agent status surfaces as halt reason and the workspace header displays; the audit timeline records one iteration failed event with the image activation failed reason. Start or Restart clears it and resumes the loop. The adapters attach the bridge additively: | Harness | Projection | | --- | --- | | Claude Code | --plugin-dir | | Codex CLI | At-most-8,000-character prompt catalog with absolute /image/skills/ /SKILL.md paths | | OpenCode | OPENCODE CONFIG DIR= with an absolute skills.paths entry | | Cursor CLI | The same bounded prompt catalog as Codex, with the same image/skills paths | Claude Code requires version 2.1.227 or newer. OpenCode is capability-probed with opencode debug config; its effective configuration must report the generated absolute skill path. Codex needs no image-skill version probe and no plugin installation: Tariboy prepends escaped name, description, and path metadata to the shared prompt file, and Codex reads the selected skill on demand. The catalog names the active image's image/skills directory rather than the digest-keyed bridge, which holds the same files, so each path is about 90 characters shorter. Activation swaps image/ only before an iteration starts, so the files do not change while an iteration reads them. Tariboy does not change CWD, HOME, or CODEX HOME, and it does not disable normal global or CWD discovery. Schema-v1 images retain their legacy CWD-relative skill materialization. Harness adapters select their native execution mode from the persisted interactive setting. Batch Codex iterations use codex exec --json with stdin disconnected so the loop receives machine-readable output and cannot wait for terminal input. Interactive Codex iterations instead launch the top-level Codex TUI with the assembled prompt and an open terminal. Both modes consume the same catalog-prefixed prompt; Codex image skills do not appear in native /skills, $ completion, or plugin inventory. Claude similarly omits its print-mode flags. Model, effective environment, working directory, and AI-proxy routing still apply in both modes. Codex receives the agent's effort as -c model reasoning effort=" ", and opencode run receives the agent's model as --model; OpenCode has no effort setting. Both Codex modes take their approval flag from the daemon's codex approval mode (codex approval mode in daemon config), read when each iteration starts: yolo, the default, passes --yolo (no sandbox, no approval prompts), and approve-for-me passes --approve-for-me (the workspace-write sandbox, with approval requests reviewed automatically by Codex). Change it with tariboy harness codex-approval set MODE or Settings → Agent defaults → Codex ; a running iteration keeps the flag it started with. --approve-for-me needs a Codex CLI that has the flag; an older one fails the launch with an unknown argument error. See Security controls. The Cursor CLI runs its agent executable with the prompt as the last argument, --force, --endpoint , and --model when the agent names one. Batch iterations add -p --output-format stream-json --trust, and the loop reads token usage from the result event on harness stdout (see AI proxy). Interactive iterations launch the Cursor TUI.
