Like Codex, a prompt too large for one argument fails the launch. The agent's effort setting has no Cursor equivalent and is ignored. While a timed iteration is running, Agent Overview shows its deadline and can extend it by one configured soft-timeout period. Each extension is persisted before the watchdog is updated, so a daemon restart can adopt the running iteration with the same deadline and extension count. Extensions are unavailable after the timeout starts firing or for agents with no soft timeout. Agents signal completion with scripts/loop.sh done (surfaced as i-am-done). When a schema-v2 template declares runtime: workdir, preparation resolves the agent's managed agents/ /workdir to an absolute path and renders it separately from the effective CWD in runtime: identity. The two paths are the same for a default-CWD agent and differ when the operator configured an external repository CWD. Rendering the path grants no new filesystem access; the harness already runs with the daemon account's permissions. :::note Loop policy is set with the tariboy loop … subcommands — interval, schedule, timeout, hard-timeout, on-timeout, on-error, max-idle, ai-stall-timeout. See the command reference. ::: Stall probe An iteration is stalled when it made no AI-proxy request for ai stall timeout s. A harness often waits for a long agent command at that time, for example make check. The stall probe tells these two cases apart. It changes only the reported state. Restarts, on error, on timeout, timeout s and hard timeout s do not change. The daemon runs the probe only for a stalled iteration: 1. The daemon asks the iteration's shim for the harness pid with the status RPC. Without tmux, the shim starts the harness and knows its pid. With tmux, the pane supervisor starts the harness and reports its pid with the harness started RPC. 2. The daemon reads the process table once: /proc/ /stat and /proc/ /cmdline on Linux, the kern.proc.all and kern.procargs2 sysctls on macOS. 3. The rule proctree.AgentCommand decides from that snapshot. A process is a live agent command when all of these are true: - It is a direct child of the harness and is not a zombie. - Its name is a shell: bash, sh, zsh, dash or fish. Harnesses run tool commands through a shell. - No exclusion applies to it. The direct children decide, because a live shell is itself a child of the harness. When the shell exits, its children move to another parent. These processes are excluded: - A direct child that is not a shell. This covers MCP servers, such as node, npx, uvx, python or the tariboy binary, and harness plugins. - A shell whose -c script is an instant mail hook command that the daemon wrote for this harness. The script must be equal to the command, or start with the command and a space. The commands come from the same builder that writes hooks.json for claude and the -c hook arguments for codex. - The tmux server, the pane supervisor, the shim and the tariboy tool bridges. They are ancestors or siblings of the harness, so the rule never sees them. If the rule finds a live agent command, the state is running with the state reason waiting for agent command. In all other cases the state is error with the stall error reason. These cases include a probe error, a probe that runs longer than 1 second, and a shim that reports pid 0. An older shim or supervisor reports pid 0. The daemon keeps each result, failures included, for 15 seconds per iteration. Only one probe for an agent runs at a time. agent.ps probes all stalled agents at once with one process table read, so it waits 1 second at most for any number of agents. The probe has these limits: - The shell name is a heuristic. A harness that keeps one shell alive between commands shows running while that shell is alive. - An MCP server from the user's configuration (.mcp.json, /.claude.json) that the harness starts through a shell counts as an agent command. The daemon does not write or read that configuration. - The hook commands are in daemon memory. After a daemon restart, an adopted iteration has no hook commands, and a live hook shell counts as an agent command. A hook runs for 5 seconds at most. - The probe works only when the daemon and the harness run on the same host in the same pid namespace. Image capabilities Schema-v2 agents receive exactly the plugins declared by their image, including an empty list. No core union is implicit. The familiar built-in capabilities are: - whoami — identity: which agent, cwd, current iteration, and client/daemon versions. - loop — iteration control: signal done, start/stop the loop. - mail — read, send and answer letters with tmail (older images name it messages). On top of the core, an image opts into optional capabilities : - context — durable working memory, - status — a one-line "what I'm doing", - schedule, scripts, tasks, - image-creator and any validated, explicitly installed external plugin capability. The built-in workdir plugin is instruction-only. The goal capability adds only scripts/goal.sh set , allowing an agent that started without a Goal to select an active task assigned to itself and attribute subsequent AI requests. It cannot replace a different Goal already attached to that iteration. A schema-v2 image explicitly packages their skills and composes the matching runtime value. See built-in plugins. See Built-in plugins for the complete capability, command, prompt, and persistence reference. Capabilities gate routes and compatibility shims, but do not package skills or contribute prompt text automatically. Schema-v1 images retain the historical core union and render the matching skill instructions for compatibility. The plugin list of an agent can change between iterations with agent plugins. The engine reads the agent row again before each iteration, so tool access and the instant mail hooks use the new list. The launch gate writes the i-am-done and tasks shims from that list before every launch and removes the shim of a plugin that is no longer in it. It writes only the files that changed. The running iteration keeps its plugins. Before each iteration's prompt or message preparation, the launch gate first honors a pending image assignment. Without one, it checks whether the active ordinary mutable-build ref now resolves to a different digest and stages that digest as pending. It then validates the new artifact, prepares and verifies any native skill bridge, reconciles image-owned shims, atomically promotes the DB assignment, and records the iteration's image ref, source version, digest, and template hash. The runtime: identity value renders that immutable source version when present. A running iteration is never interrupted. Backup and staging markers make an interrupted swap recoverable without changing durable agent state. Recovery compares the pinned digest, not only the ref. For daemon-managed and ordinary mutable-build refs, both inspection and staging resolve the exact retained digest recorded on the agent, including assignments that were pending when the daemon was upgraded or the ordinary ref was rebuilt. The agent image read API projects the same selection order under the image store lock: explicit pending digest, ordinary mutable active ref, then current pinned image. Current version metadata always comes from pinned inspection. This read does not stage or promote an assignment; next is a preview at read time and can change before the launch gate runs. A changed digest triggers activation even if the source version stays the same. A failed inspection is returned explicitly, and the separate pending error preserves activation failures even without a pending ref. Manager internals and lock order The loop manager (internal/loop) keeps one engine per running agent. It is a facade over these parts: | Part | Owns | | --- | --- | | Agent runtimes (runtimes.go) | The in-memory registry: running engines, tools servers bound before an engine starts, iterations being adopted, a Restart pending after adoption, and stale-kill markers. It also holds each agent's lifecycle gate and handoff lock. | | Script supervisor (scripts.go) | Durable script runs: claim, start as the agent through the tariboy-shim script-run wrapper, cancel, time out, and record the result from the run's state file. At start it adopts the runs that a restart handed over (see Restart handoff). | | Tools facade (tools facade.go) | The per-agent tools socket API. It reaches the manager only through narrow interfaces, so the API does not depend on a loop engine. | | Image activation (image activation.go) | Pending image activation, the Reprovision swap, the skill bridge, and crash recovery of an interrupted swap. | | Iteration watcher (iteration watcher.go) | The one polling loop that waits for result.json. It resyncs the hard deadline, enforces the soft deadline and the done grace with at most one Kill, and, for adoption, probes the shim. For a shim the runner launched, it also ends the wait when the reaped shim process left no result.json, which the runner records as harness error. The runner and adoption both use it. | The manager takes its locks in one order: 1. The agent's lifecycle gate . It serializes the lifecycle of one agent: start, Stop, Remove, Reprovision, and a Restart launch after adoption from its decision until its iteration row exists. A wait for it ends when the daemon shuts down. 2. An image lock. Each image name has its own name lock ; a build or an image detail read takes the lock of the one name it touches, so builds of different names run in parallel. The store lock covers the whole image store: image activation, Run, Reprovision, agent image assignment, image removal, and migration take it for writing, and it excludes every name lock. A name lock holds the store lock for reading, so the store lock is always taken first, and neither lock is taken twice. 3. The registry lock. It guards only the registry maps. No database call, socket operation, or callback runs while it is held. A path that holds a later lock never waits for an earlier one. For example, Reprovision takes the agent's lifecycle gate before the image store lock, the same order as a Restart launch that activates an image. Run never starts an agent, so it never takes a lifecycle gate while it holds the image store lock. A normal iteration launch takes only the image store lock. The agent's handoff lock (see the shim) is taken while no gate is held. Image activation can take long: it unpacks the image, prepares the skill bridge, and probes the harness. While a Restart launch waits in it, only the lifecycle operations of that same agent wait for it: Start, Stop, Restart, Remove, Reprovision, and the agent's own loop start and loop stop`. Kill, state reads, wakes, other tools calls, and every other agent continue.
description: An agent runs a series of supervised iterations, driven by a timer or by mail, on top of a whoami / loop / mail core.
title: Agents & the iteration loop

content: Every message in Tariboy is a letter from one principal to another, stored in one SQLite table, mail (service in internal/mail, schema in internal/store/migrations/0072 mail.sql). An agent has an inbox; a letter in it wakes the agent's loop; the agent answers it. This page is the architectural summary; the mail reference covers tmail, tariboy mail, the routes and debugging. One table, three views A letter has a sender, a recipient, a subject, a body, a kind (message unless the producer names another, such as task.question or script.result), a JSON data object and its state. A send to several recipients writes one row per recipient , each with its own id and state, so a broadcast shows one row per recipient in the sender's Sent view. Every mailbox is a filter over that table: | View | Rows of principal P | | --- | --- | | Inbox | recipient = P, still open (answered at and dead at empty), oldest first | | Sent | sender = P, newest first | | Archive | recipient = P, closed or dead, newest first; dead letters are tagged | So an operator reads exactly what an agent saw, sent and answered, and nothing is stored beside the table "for the transport": per-recipient state lives on the letter row. Answering never deletes a letter. Principals | Principal | Who | As a recipient | | --- | --- | --- | | agent:<name | an agent | must exist; its inbox wakes its loop | | user:<login | the customer | must be the customer login; read in the Desktop or with tariboy mail | | plugin:<name | a plugin | must be installed, enabled and declare mail.receive (type mail-sink), because only such a plugin has a drainer; the plugin host delivers the letter to the plugin's /deliver | | system:<component | a daemon component | always accepted; stored closed, because nothing reads a system inbox | | queue:<prefix | a task queue | must exist; stored closed; exists for queue triggers | | group:<name | an alias | expands to every group member except the sender | Any other recipient is refused with unknown recipient, and a group whose only member is the sender with empty group. A sender must be an existing agent, the customer, an installed plugin or a system: component. The customer login is a fixed value rather than the account tariboyd runs as, so user:customer names the same person on every server. It defaults to customer and is overridable through the customer login key in daemon config. On the first start without a stored customer login, the daemon writes customer and moves earlier customer principals, in tasks, comments, waits and letters, to user:customer in one transaction. Changing the key later rewrites nothing. Requests and notices Every letter is a request or a notice , chosen by its sender: - A request needs an answer. It leaves the inbox when its recipient replies. - A notice needs no answer. It leaves an agent's inbox when the agent has read it, and the customer's inbox when the customer archives it. A reply goes to the original sender with subject Re: <subject and in reply to set, and closes the original in the same transaction. A reply is a notice unless the sender marks it as a request (tmail reply --ask). A subject is one line: send replaces line breaks and other control characters with spaces, and the prompt renders a subject the same way. Without this split every answer would be a new obligation: two agents would answer each other until the attempt limit, and every answer to the customer would wait in the customer's inbox. A reply to a closed letter is recorded and reopens nothing. A reply to a letter whose sender no longer exists (a deleted agent, an uninstalled or disabled plugin) is stored closed, like a letter to system: , and still closes the original, so the recipient can finish the request. A reply to a task.question letter is refused with answer on task: the answer belongs on the task, and the tasks service closes the letter. When a letter closes Closing sets answered at. A reply also sets answer id; any other close leaves it empty and records a close note. | Recipient | A request closes when | A notice closes when | | --- | --- | --- | | agent: | the agent replies | it was rendered into an iteration that finished successfully (close note = read) | | user: | the customer replies or archives it | the customer archives it; opening it or tariboy mail read only marks it read | | plugin: | the plugin's /deliver accepts it (delivered) | the same | | system: , queue: | at once: stored closed | at once | | any, task.question | the question is answered on the task (task-comment:<id ), a workflow outcome resolves it (task-outcome:<status ), or the customer dismisses it (task-wait-dismissed) | — | An operator can archive any letter without a reply (tariboy mail close, with an optional note). The agent tool has no archive: an agent answers. A notice rendered into an iteration that ends in an error, a timeout or a kill stays open and is rendered again next iteration, like a request. Attempts and dead letters - Rendering a letter into a prompt adds one to its attempts in the same transaction that reads it. A letter whose next render would be its sixth is marked dead with reason attempts instead of being rendered. - A letter to an agent whose open inbox already holds messages max queue letters (default 100) is stored dead with reason queue limit and wakes nothing. So the limit bounds runnable work, not mail storage. - A row whose data does not decode is marked dead with reason decode error; the other letters are still rendered. - A dead letter sits in the recipient's Archive. Requeue clears its dead state, attempts and close fields and puts it back in the inbox. Requeue is refused with 409 queue limit while the agent's inbox is at its cap; close letters first. A requeued request whose deadline is still ahead gets its deadline armed again; a passed deadline is cleared. - A send with an idempotency key that the recipient already holds returns the existing letter and writes nothing. Native Tasks' notification outbox, schedules, the Goal reconciler, script results and plugins use it. - Clear deletes every open letter of one agent (tariboy mail clear --as agent:NAME or POST /api/agents/{name}/mail/clear); closed and dead letters stay. Maintenance purges closed letters older than the more recent of the retention period and chat retention days (the field kept its name), and never a letter to a queue that the workflow ingress has not consumed yet. Wake path The loop starts a message-triggered iteration only for a started agent whose open inbox count is above zero; a positive interval s is not needed. A stopped agent keeps its letters open until it is started. At prepare time the runner reads the oldest open letters, requests first and notices after them, up to messages batch (default 10), and renders them into the ## Messages section of the prompt with the standing instruction that names tmail reply. Requests the agent sent with a deadline and no answer are listed under ### Awaiting replies. See the mail reference for the exact text. Instant delivery An instant letter has the flag instant. It reaches the running iteration of its recipient at the next end of a tool call, through a harness hook that runs tmail instant. Without a running iteration it wakes the agent like any letter. The flag uses the same Send path with these additions: - Only the customer, plugin:telegram, and an agent that the recipient allows may set it. The recipient setting mail instant senders lists the allowed agents. When it is not set, the lead of the recipient's group may send. Every recipient must be an agent. - Mail reads the loop state through the InstantRuntime seam, which the loop manager implements. A letter to an agent with a running iteration starts waiting, and the manager creates the flag file of that iteration. A letter to an agent that starts iterations on its own starts queued. Any other letter starts stopped. One function, agentIterates, decides whether an agent starts iterations on its own. - POST /tools/mail/instant takes the waiting letters once. It adds one attempt to each, with the same limit of five as the prompt render. The prompt render marks an instant letter read, and a dead one becomes not delivered. After loop.sh done it takes nothing and keeps the flag file, so a Stop hook cannot continue a finished iteration. - Claude Code 2.1.227 or newer runs tmail instant from the hooks PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure and Stop in both modes. tmail prints the hook JSON itself (--format claude-post-tool-use, claude-post-tool-use-failure, claude-stop). The letter text reaches the model only as hook output. A long tool call holds the letter, and model output without a tool call is not stopped. - Codex 0.141.0 or newer in the yolo approval mode runs tmail instant from the hooks PostToolUse and Stop in both modes (--format codex-post-tool-use, codex-stop). The runner passes the hooks as -c overrides with --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust, so no file goes into CODEX HOME, /.codex or the repository. - OpenCode 1.19.5 or newer runs tmail instant --format opencode-tool-after from a Tariboy plugin with the hook tool.execute.after, in both modes. The plugin adds the printed text to the result of each successful tool call. OpenCode does not call the hook after a failed tool call, and it has no hook at the end of a turn. In these cases the letter stays waiting for the next successful call or the next prompt. - An older Claude Code, an older codex, an older OpenCode and codex in approve-for-me read the letter in the next iteration. - At done, the runner closes the notices that a hook delivered in the iteration, as it closes the rendered notices. The web UI and Desktop render one mailbox. Its form sets the flag with the Deliver to the current iteration switch when the customer writes to an agent. The list tags an instant letter instant, and the letter card shows a Delivery field with the instant state of the letter. The Web UI mailbox section describes them. The mail reference gives the rules, the states, the hook command, the block format and the harness table. Producers Every producer writes through the one Send operation, so the Inbox and Sent views never miss a letter. | Producer | Sender → recipient | Kind | Request or notice | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Native Tasks notifications | the principal that caused it (the asker, the assigner, system:workflow; system:tasks when that principal can no longer send) → the agent or the customer | task.assigned, task.question, task.answered, task.triage | task.question is a request closed by the answer on the task; the others are notices | | Goal reconciler | system:goal → the agent | task.goal | request: the reply is the agent's report on its Goal | | Script results | system:scripts → the owning agent | script.result | request | | Schedules | system:schedule → the schedule's recipient (default the owning agent) | schedule.fire unless the template names another | request unless the template sets notice | | Request deadlines | system:schedule → the requester | deadline, data.request id | notice | | AI proxy budget | system:proxy → the agent | budget.warn | notice | | Operator or Desktop | the customer, or --as another principal → anyone | message unless given | request unless notice | | Agents | the calling agent → anyone, through tmail | sender's choice | sender's choice | | Telegram | plugin:telegram → the mapped agent | message | request | | Plugin workflow event | plugin:<name → queue:<prefix | plugin's choice | stored closed | A request with a deadline sent by an agent arms a one-shot schedule keyed on the request letter's id; the reply or archive that closes the request cancels it in the same transaction. When the deadline passes first, the requesting agent receives the deadline notice. A deadline on a request from any other principal is stored but arms nothing. Goal delivery The per-agent Goal reconciler sends task.goal with the selected task key and the selected or iteration completed reason. Its idempotency key includes the agent, task key, task revision and terminal iteration identity, so recovery and repeated scans do not duplicate a generation. An open Goal letter suppresses another one; a dead one does not, and a positive per-agent cooldown (60 seconds by default) still suppresses rapid repeats. The reconciler never starts an iteration directly: the letter wakes the agent. Disabled agents or disabled loops receive no new Goal letter. Task notifications Task notifications are letters, and the task stays the source of truth: mentions, waits and answers live on the task. A task.question letter is answered on the task (ttasks comment, or the task drawer in the Desktop); when the wait resolves, the tasks service closes the matching open question letters with close note = task-comment:<id , for an agent recipient and the customer alike. The asker is matched by data.from, so a question the outbox sent as system:tasks closes too. A notification whose recipient no longer exists is marked failed in the outbox with last error and is not retried. A workflow outcome that resolves the customer's open wait closes its question letters with task-outcome:<status . When the customer dismisses a question without an answer (tasks.waits.dismiss), its letters close with task-wait-dismissed, and each asker gets a task.answered letter that says no answer is needed. A task.question goes only to a principal that exists: a registered agent, or the customer login. A mention ends at the last letter or digit of the name, so punctuation after it is not part of the principal. A comment that mentions a missing principal sends no letter, and ttasks ask on a missing principal fails with principal not found. See Questions and notifications. A task letter names its task in the subject, the key and then the title, for example Question on DEV-1: Ship the release. Its data carries task key and task title. The title is the one the task had when the letter was sent. The body of a task.question or task.answered letter starts with one line, for example agent:dev asked for an answer on DEV-1, then an empty line, then the full text of the comment. The comment is Markdown, and the Mailbox shows it as Markdown. A task.question from a workflow customer status carries the workflow's comment. The task.assigned and task.triage bodies are one line with the key and the title. Stale task notices never wake an agent. When an iteration that ran with Goal task T ends, the tasks service closes the agent's open task.goal, task.assigned and task.answered letters about T created up to the end of the iteration, with close note = iteration-end:<iteration , and marks such notifications not sent yet as sent. The Goal reconciler then sends a fresh task.goal only when T still needs the agent. Before a wake counts open letters and before a prompt renders them, the daemon also closes those three kinds when their task is done or cancelled, is assigned to another principal, is paused, or is in a workflow status that no pool owns, with close note = task-not-assigned-work; a task.answered closes this way only when its recipient is the task's assignee. Neither rule closes a task.question. Groups Group membership is the data group:<name expands over; groups create no mailboxes of their own. tmail send --to group:dev-team writes one letter to each member except the sender, and a lead asks one member with tmail send --to agent:<member , with --deadline for a timed request. The group tools that are not sends (info, status, observe, loop) are unchanged. Queue triggers A plugin that wants a workflow event to create a task sends a letter to queue:<prefix . That letter is stored closed and exists for ingress. A trigger of queue <prefix fires for a letter whose recipient is queue:<prefix , whose sender matches the trigger's pattern (a principal glob such as plugin: or plugin:telegram), and whose data.correlation key equals the trigger's correlation key when one is set. The ingress reads the monotonic mail.seq. A letter to an agent never trips a trigger. See Task workflows. Plugins A plugin declares mail: {send, receive} in its manifest with the types mail-source and mail-sink. It sends letters as plugin:<name through POST /api/plugin/mail, which answers 409 inbox full when the recipient's inbox is at its cap. The plugin host drains the inbox of plugin:<name like a prompt drain, with the same attempt and dead-letter rules, calls the plugin's /deliver with each letter, and closes it as delivered on success. The drainer is woken after a committed send; a 5-second fallback timer retries failed deliveries. A plugin receives only the letters addressed to it. See Plugins. The bundled Telegram process stays outside the daemon. It authorizes forum updates and sends each one as a letter to the agent mapped to its topic. An agent answers with tmail reply, which addresses plugin:telegram, and the plugin's /deliver posts the reply to the topic of the sending agent. Live hints and the event hub GET /api/mail/ws streams one frame per written letter, {id, from, to, kind, ts}, and one frame per change of the instant state of a letter. A frame is only a refetch hint: the HTTP responses stay authoritative. Nothing is replayed, because a client refetches on connect and on every reconnect. GET /api/agent-states/ws uses the same hint loop for agent state. It sends {agent, type, ts} for every iteration and state event of any agent on the host, so the UI refetches the agents list and the agent status. The loop manager emits state when an agent is started or stopped, when its status line changes, and when its loop halts or stops for idleness. The route is not under /api/agents/ because an agent may be named ws. These sockets and the agent SSE stream GET /api/agents/{name}/events read from one in-memory event hub. The hub never blocks a publisher: each subscriber has a buffer of 64 events, and an event for a full buffer is dropped. The hub gives every event a rising sequence number seq and counts each drop in the OpenTelemetry counter tariboy.events.dropped. When a subscriber that lost events has room again, the hub first sends it a reset event with data.dropped set to the number of lost events. The SSE stream writes each event as id: <seq and event: <type , so it forwards event: reset. A hint socket closes with status 1013 (try again later) on a reset; the client reconnects and refetches, which recovers what it missed. The hub keeps no history, so neither stream replays the lost events. Audit Mail writes the audit events mail sent, mail answered, mail closed, mail dead, mail requeued and mail cleared to the agent's audit log. A hook delivery writes mail instant shown with the letter and the iteration to the audit log of the recipient agent.
description: Every message is a letter from one principal to another, stored as one row of the mail table; an agent's inbox wakes its loop until each letter is answered or read.
title: The mailbox

content: The metrics commands report how long tasks take, how many iterations, tokens and US dollars they use, how often they come back for rework, and how the assessments score them. The daemon computes every value when it receives a request. It stores no aggregate and adds no table. The code is in internal/metrics. The commands are in internal/commands/metrics.go. | Command | Route | Result type | | --- | --- | --- | | tariboy metrics task KEY | GET /api/metrics/tasks/{key} | TaskMetrics | | tariboy metrics server | GET /api/metrics | MetricsReport | Access is the same as for tariboy usage. The daemon socket and the loopback HTTP listener of the operator serve the commands. The tools socket of an agent does not serve them. See the command reference for the flags and examples. Units - A time is a whole number of seconds in JSON. Its field name ends in s. The text output of the CLI shows hours and minutes, for example 12h 05m. - A cost is in US dollars, rounded to 6 decimal places, as in tariboy usage. - Tokens are counted by kind: input, output, cache write, cache read. - A value that is not known is null, not zero. This applies to lead time s of a task that is not done, to the lead times of a slice without done tasks, and to quality without scores. Metrics of one task metrics task accepts the current key of a task or an old key. Old keys come from task key aliases. All metrics of the task use the current key and all old keys. | Field | Unit | Definition | Source | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | lead time s | seconds | From the first entry to in progress to completion. null if the task is not done or has no start. | tasks.started at and tasks.completed at. If started at is empty, the first task events row that sets status to in progress. | | status time s | seconds per status | The sum of the time in each status. An open interval counts up to the time of the request. done and cancelled do not count. | A workflow task: task status visits (left at − entered at). A task without a workflow: the task events rows that set status, with task.created or task.imported as open. | | usage.iterations | count | The number of distinct iterations of the task. A request without an iteration id adds tokens and cost, but no iteration. | COUNT(DISTINCT iteration) of ai requests with task id equal to a key of the task | | usage.tokens | tokens | Token sums by kind. | The same ai requests rows | | usage.cost usd | US dollars | The cost sum. | The same ai requests rows | | rework rounds | count | The number of visits that ended with changes requested, rework or conflict. | task status visits.outcome | | rework by outcome | count per outcome | The same count for each of the three outcomes. | task status visits.outcome | | rejected advances | count | The number of advance requests that a check rejected. | Sum of task status visits.rejected requests | | customer questions | count | The number of waits for an answer of the customer. | task waiting for rows with expected principal equal to tasks.customer | | quality | score from 0 to 100 | For each axis image process, role, task fit: avg, min and count of the scores. An axis without scores is null. Without any score, quality is null. | assessment axes with verdict = scored of the latest assessment of each iteration and task with the task's key | | agents[] | | For each agent: usage and images[], the image versions of that agent's iterations. | ai requests.agent | | images[] | | The iterations, tokens and cost on each image version: image, image ref, image version, image digest. | See Image version of an iteration | | workflows[] | | The workflow versions of the task's visits: name, version, digest. Empty for a task without a workflow. | task status visits.workflow digest → task workflow images | A task without a workflow has no visits. Its rework rounds and rejected advances are 0. Latest assessment An assessment is never changed. A reassessment adds a new record. quality uses only the latest record of each assessed object, so the scores of a replaced record do not count. tariboy assessment ls uses the same rule, see assessments. - The object of an iteration assessment is its iteration id. - The object of a task assessment, with an empty iteration id, is its task key. An assessment of an iteration and an assessment of its task are two objects. The task's quality counts both. The rule that selects the latest record is in State model. Questions to the customer ttasks ask and a question of the workflow engine create a task waiting for row. The row names the principal who must answer. customer questions counts the rows that wait for the customer of the task. Only one wait for each principal can be open on a task. A second question before the answer to the first one makes no new row, so it counts as one question. The table task workflow questions is not a source: no code writes it. Image version of an iteration The image version comes from the iteration, not from the current configuration of the agent. 1. The iterations row of ai requests.iteration gives image ref, image version and image digest. The image name is image ref without its tag. 2. If retention removed the iterations row, ai requests.image name and image tag give the reference and ai requests.image digest gives the digest. The version comes from another iterations row with the same digest. 3. If no row gives the version, the version is unknown. The iteration goes to the image slice with the version unknown. Workflow version of an iteration The workflow version of an iteration comes from the visit of its task that was open when the iteration started (entered at ≤ start < left at, or left at is empty). The start is iterations.started at. Without an iterations row, the start is the time of the first AI request of the iteration. The visit's workflow digest maps to task workflow images.name and version. - If no visit was open at the start, for example because the iteration started before the first visit, the current tasks.workflow digest of the task gives the version. - If task workflow images has no row for the digest, the workflow name is unknown and the version is empty. - An iteration without a task, or with a task without a workflow, goes to the workflow slice none. Server report metrics server reports one period. The default period is the 30 days before the request. --since is an inclusive bound and --until is an exclusive bound. The report has total, agents[], images[] and workflows[]. Each slice has three blocks: - usage: the iterations, tokens and cost of the AI requests with ts in the period. Each iteration goes to the exact agent, image version and workflow version of that iteration. - usage without task: the part of usage whose requests have no task. A request without a task has a task id that is NULL or empty. Such a request comes from an iteration without a selected Goal, or from an iteration before it ran scripts/goal.sh set. These requests go to the workflow slice none. The filters limit this block the same way as usage. A period without such requests gives zeros, not null. - tasks: the aggregates of the tasks with status = done and completed at in the period. The iterations, tokens and cost in this block are for the whole life of each task, not only for the period. In usage without task, the tokens and cost usd are an exact part of usage, and cost usd is never more than usage.cost usd. iterations counts the iterations with at least one request without a task. An iteration that selected its Goal after its first requests counts in both usage.iterations and usage without task.iterations. So you cannot subtract usage without task.iterations from usage.iterations to get the iterations with a task. The tasks block does not include requests without a task. tariboy metrics server shows usage without task.cost usd in the column NO TASK COST USD, after COST USD. | tasks field | Unit | Definition | | --- | --- | --- | | tasks done | count | The done tasks of the slice | | mixed tasks | count | Image and workflow slices only: done tasks that ran on more than one version and also on this version | | lead time median s, lead time avg s | seconds | Median and average of lead time s. null without a lead time. | | sum | | Sums of iterations, tokens, cost usd, rework rounds, rejected advances, customer questions | | avg | per task | The same values divided by tasks done, rounded to 2 decimal places. Not in the response when tasks done is 0. | | quality | score | Per axis: average, minimum and count of the scores of the slice's tasks, from the latest assessment of each object. null without scores. | Tasks with several agents or versions - Agent slices: a task counts in the slice of each agent that made an iteration for it. total counts each task once. - Image slices: a task counts in a version slice only if all its iterations ran on that one version. A task with iterations on more than one version adds 1 to mixed tasks of each of those versions. Its lead time, rework and questions go to no version slice. A task without iterations goes to no image slice. - Workflow slices: the same rule, with the workflow versions of the task's visits. A task without a workflow goes to the slice none. Filters --agent, --image NAME[:VERSION] and --workflow NAME[:VERSION] limit the report: - usage keeps only the iterations of that agent, on that image, under that workflow. - tasks keeps only the done tasks with an iteration of that agent, with an iteration on that image, and with a visit under that workflow. - The slice lists keep only the agent, the image versions and the workflow versions that the filter selects. A kept task adds nothing to the slices of other agents or versions. The version rule still uses all versions of the task, so a kept task with two versions adds to mixed tasks. An image name can include a registry port, as in --image localhost:5000/dev:1.0. The version follows the last colon after the last slash. --workflow none selects the iterations and tasks without a workflow. --image NAME:unknown selects the iterations without a known version. An input that is not NAME or NAME:VERSION fails with invalid param. A --since or --until that is not an RFC 3339 time fails with bad time. Retention Retention removes ai requests, iterations and assessments rows older than the retention period. It removes task events, task status visits and task waiting for rows only with their task. As a result: - the iterations, tokens and cost of an old task are smaller than the real values, or 0; - the image version of an old iteration can be unknown, which can make its task mixed; - quality can be null although an assessment existed. Performance The metrics read the database in one read-only transaction. ai requests has no index on task id, so each request scans that table a small number of times. On a copy of a database with 67,832 AI requests, metrics server for 30 days answered in less than 2 seconds.
description: Task, agent, image, workflow and server metrics that the daemon computes on request from tasks, workflow visits, AI requests, iterations and assessments.
title: Metrics

content: The shim (cmd/tariboy-shim, internal/shim) runs a single harness iteration under a watchdog . The daemon hands it: - the iteration directory, - the agent and iteration ids, - a hard timeout, - and a tmux session for interactive harnesses. Everything after -- is the harness command it supervises. The harness gets the environment of its iteration through the shim unchanged, including TARIBOY INSTANT MAIL FLAG. A harness hook uses it to run tmail instant after each tool call. Claude Code 2.1.227 or newer gets these hooks in both modes: PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure and Stop, in a plugin under <base-dir /agents/<name /harness-hooks/claude/. Codex 0.141.0 or newer in the yolo approval mode gets PostToolUse and Stop in both modes, as -c overrides with --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust in its argv. OpenCode 1.19.5 or newer gets one plugin in both modes, <base-dir /agents/<name /harness-hooks/opencode/tariboy-instant-mail.js, from the configuration overlay. Its hook tool.execute.after runs after each successful tool call. The hooks run inside the harness, so the shim does not change for them, and it never types a letter into the tmux session. An older Claude Code, an older codex, an older OpenCode and codex in approve-for-me get an instant letter in the next iteration. A long tool call holds the letter until the call ends, and the hooks do not stop model output that has no tool call. The shim binds its RPC socket before it starts the harness or creates the tmux session. A bind failure is fatal: the shim writes the error to shim.log and exits without result.json. The daemon reaps the shim process it launched; when the shim exits and no result.json exists, the daemon ends the iteration as harness error with the reason shim exited before writing result (see shim.log). A shim launched by a previous daemon is not watched this way. Until the harness process or harness window exists, a Kill RPC answers harness not started yet instead of reporting a stop that did not happen, so the caller can retry. For tmux-backed interactive iterations, the pane command is a hidden supervisor mode of the same shim binary. That supervisor starts one directly owned harness process group and places it in the pane terminal's foreground before exec, so stdin and terminal-generated signals go to the harness rather than the supervisor. A native observer reports only the direct leader's real exit: Linux uses waitid(P PID, pid, WEXITED|WNOWAIT) and macOS uses kqueue EVFILT PROC|NOTE EXIT. Stop, continue, unrelated, and forged SIGCHLD notifications do not end supervision. The observer does not reap the leader; the supervisor remains its sole reaper. This is a mode of the existing shim process: it does not poll tmux, start a helper process, or reap arbitrary descendants. The supervisor also catches the SIGHUP tmux sends when a pane is destroyed. On SIGHUP, it sends SIGTERM to the owned group and waits up to two seconds for confirmed leader exit, then escalates to SIGKILL and waits at most two more seconds. Once exit is confirmed, both natural and HUP teardown send a final SIGKILL to the still-pinned group before the sole blocking Wait4, so lingering descendants are removed without risking a reused process-group id. ESRCH means the group is already empty and is not an error. A cooperative leader keeps its exit status; forced termination records 137. Observer, signal, reap, and wait-deadline failures return promptly after a best-effort final group kill and leave the transient status absent, preserving the outer shim's fail-closed unknown result (-1). The supervisor never discovers a pane PID from tmux or signals a process after reaping its leader. It does not restore terminal foreground ownership because it performs no further terminal I/O and exits immediately after recording the result. After it starts the harness, the supervisor reports the harness pid to the outer shim with the harness started RPC on the same socket. The shim then reports that pid in status until the harness exited report, and pid 0 before and after. The daemon stall probe uses this pid. The supervisor keeps the harness unreaped until it exits, so the pid is not reused meanwhile. The report is best-effort and bounded to one second. A shim without the method answers with an unknown-method error, and the supervisor ignores it. After successful observation, group cleanup, and the exact leader reap, the supervisor captures the harness's real numeric status, writes it to an owner-private temporary file, and atomically renames it within the iteration's private logs directory. It then reports the exit to the outer shim with the harness exited RPC on the shim socket. The shim passes that socket path only to the harness window, and the supervisor removes it from the harness environment. The report is best-effort and bounded to one second. The socket path belongs to the agent, not to one iteration. A supervisor can outlive its shim: the shim writes result.json and exits, and the daemon starts the next iteration on the same socket. The old supervisor then reports to the new shim. For this reason, each shim run creates a random token of 16 bytes and gives it to its own harness window in TARIBOY SHIM SUPERVISOR TOKEN, next to the socket path. The supervisor removes the token from the harness environment and sends it with harness started and harness exited. The shim accepts a report only with its own token. It rejects any other report with an error and writes WARN ignore harness exited from another supervisor (or harness started) to shim.log. A supervisor from an older shim build sends no token, so the new shim rejects its reports. The shim then ends its wait with the has-session fallback. The outer shim waits for the first of three events: the supervisor's exit report, its own cancellation, or a fallback tmux has-session check every ten seconds that finds the session gone. The fallback covers a session killed from outside before the supervisor could report, and a supervisor from an older shim build that does not send the report; a newer supervisor that reaches an older shim gets an unknown-method error and ignores it. SIGTERM, SIGINT, and the hard-deadline watchdog cancel the wait. After a report, the shim lets tmux close the pane on its own for up to one second, which keeps the end of the pane log, and then removes the exact session if it is still there. After a cancellation it removes the session at once. The session never outlives result.json. A cancelled shim writes no termination reason other than the existing hard timeout; without a recorded status the exit code is -1. The outer shim then validates and removes the transient status file before writing result.json. A non-zero harness status is preserved; a missing, malformed, or unreadable status becomes unknown failure (-1), never success. Timeout and explicit termination reasons still take precedence. The status file is not in the support-bundle allowlist. A second hidden mode, tariboy-shim script-run -- ARGV, owns one script run. The daemon starts it as the leader of a new process group, with the run log as stdout and stderr and the locked run state file as fd 3. The wrapper sets close-on-exec on fd 3, so the script cannot hold the lock. It catches SIGTERM, SIGINT, and SIGHUP and does not act on them. A signal to the group ends the script, and the wrapper still records how the script ended. It runs ARGV with stdin from /dev/null, waits for it, and writes exit code, signal, or start error as JSON to the state file. Then it exits and the lock is released. The wrapper does not depend on the daemon, so a run outlives a daemon restart. See Restart handoff. The tmux session wraps the harness's native interactive command, not its batch renderer. In particular, interactive Codex agents run the top-level Codex TUI with stdin attached, while non-interactive Codex iterations continue to use codex exec --json outside tmux. The Desktop only attaches another tmux client; disconnecting it does not replace or terminate the harness TUI. All agent tmux targets match the full session name exactly: session commands use =name, and window or pane commands use =name:. tmux otherwise accepts prefix and pattern matches, so a missing image-creator could resolve to image-creator-sam. Existence checks, terminal attach, screen capture, input, exit waiting, and cleanup therefore cannot select another agent by prefix. When Tariboy creates an interactive tmux session, it disables tmux mouse capture for that exact managed session. This leaves browser and OS text selection available in the agent Terminal tab without changing global tmux options, user tmux configuration, or unrelated sessions. Separating the watchdog from the daemon means a runaway or hung iteration can be killed (tariboy agent kill) without touching the daemon or other agents. The outer shim matches the managed session's full name before using tmux's exact session target. An absent server or session is already stopped; other tmux operational errors remain visible to the caller. The shim isn't a subcommand CLI — it has exactly one job. It also makes daemon upgrades non-destructive. tariboyd cancellation does not signal the shim or its harness. The old loop observer detaches while the iteration row stays running; the new daemon probes the same per-agent shim socket, restores the absolute hard deadline, and waits for the existing result.json. Harness calls may see a brief local AI-proxy outage during the restart, but supported harnesses retry the stable proxy URL and carried token. While that wait is active, the replacement daemon keeps the adopted iteration as a current shim target: terminal clients and operator control RPCs reach the same socket, and Start or Exec cannot create a second engine or tmux session. An i-am-done call also survives the handoff: after the same two-second grace used by the original runner, adoption sends at most one cooperative Kill if no result.json has appeared, then finalizes the original row from that result. Each control request connects while the agent's handoff lock is held for reading, and adoption takes it for writing before it ends. Later reuse of the stable per-agent socket pathname therefore cannot redirect a request to a replacement iteration. The connection attempt has a finite timeout, so a wedged Unix accept queue cannot hold the end of adoption indefinitely; other agents and other lifecycle operations do not wait for it. When adoption finishes, the daemon reloads the current Enabled value before starting the normal loop engine. Restart also carries one explicit interactive-run intent across the handoff. The launch uses the agent's lifecycle gate, which Stop also takes. The launch acquires it only after tmux collision checks, holds it through image activation and the durable launch or manual-collision outcome, and releases it before runner preparation. See Manager internals and lock order. If Stop races the final detached process creation after winning stale-shim recovery, the runner briefly retries the shim socket and requests cooperative Kill so the shim terminates its owned harness process group or tmux session. If no shim becomes reachable, it kills the interactive tmux session explicitly. Its final managed fallback sends SIGTERM to the spawned shim group; a non-interactive shim handles that signal by force-killing its separately owned harness group, even when the harness ignores SIGTERM. The launcher SIGKILLs the outer group after a short bounded cleanup window. Daemon handoff continues to preserve a shim whose durable iteration remains running. For an interactive iteration, each Desktop terminal connection asks the shim to start a separate tmux attach-session client inside a PTY. The shim checks tmux has-session first and keeps the attach client's own stderr outside the PTY, so an iteration that already ended — including one that disappears during attach startup — cannot leak tmux's no sessions diagnostic into xterm. The browser side is always xterm.js, so only this attach client receives the fixed outer terminal type TERM=xterm-256color. The shim invokes that client as tmux -u attach-session: tmux therefore preserves Unicode output even when a GUI launcher supplied no UTF-8 locale. Tariboy does not synthesize or replace LANG, LC ALL, or LC CTYPE; the daemon, harness, agent, and tmux session environments are unchanged. A failed attach writes only a stable failure category and session identifier to shim.log; tmux stderr and environment values remain excluded. Closing a browser connection tears down only that attach client; it never kills the tmux session or harness. The daemon distinguishes terminal lifecycle from transport lifecycle. A PTY EOF is closed as WebSocket 1000/eof. Desktop stops reconnecting immediately and shows the stopped-session panel. WebSocket 4404 means no current iteration exists or the shim does not support an interactive terminal. Start can return before the loop publishes its current iteration, so Desktop retries 4404 for at most five seconds with capped exponential delay. After that grace, it shows the same panel. A shim connection failure or a non-EOF stream failure closes with 1011, not 4404 or 1000/eof. These failures and other abnormal WebSocket closes reconnect indefinitely with capped delay. A live terminal can thus recover across a brief daemon or network interruption without reporting that the session ended.
description: tariboy-shim runs a single harness iteration under a watchdog, so a runaway iteration can be killed without touching the daemon.
title: The shim

content: The SQLite DB is the single source of configuration. There is no config.json per agent and no stored state column; an agent's live state (running / idle / stopped / error) is computed from the DB config plus what is actually running, not persisted. A running iteration also has persisted AI-proxy liveness evidence. Its started at time is the initial activity point, and every authenticated request for that exact agent and iteration updates last ai request at before upstream work begins. When the newest point is at least the agent's positive ai stall timeout s old (1800 seconds, 30 minutes, by default), live state is derived as error with an informational error reason; the loop and iteration continue. The next attributed request updates the timestamp and live state derives as running again. Stale requests for older or completed iterations are ignored. Before the daemon reports such a stall, it runs the stall probe. The probe looks for a live agent command under the harness process, such as a long make check. If it finds one, live state is running and the agent readers (agent.inspect, agent.ps, agent.status.show) report state reason: "waiting for agent command" with no error reason. The state reason key is absent when the state has no reason. See the stall probe. Reconciliation and reaping are therefore flag-independent: the daemon derives what should be running from the DB and converges to it. The loop schedule is the agents.schedule rrule column: the normalized DTSTART and RRULE lines, empty when unset (migration 0065 agent schedule.sql). Only loop schedule writes it. The next start is computed from it on demand and is not stored, so the daemon does not replay occurrences missed while it was off. Stored times Every time in the database uses one text format: UTC with exactly nine fractional digits, for example 2026-10-19T06:33:58.123000000Z. This is store.TimeLayout in internal/store/timefmt.go. All values have the same width and the same zone, so SQLite sorts the text in time order. Queries compare time columns directly (ts = ?), and the indexes on those columns serve range filters such as the Usage since and until bounds. Only the store package knows the format: - store.FormatTime writes a time. - store.ParseTime reads a stored time and rejects every other format. - store.ParseInputTime reads a time from outside the database, such as an API or CLI parameter, a worker report or a manifest. It accepts any RFC 3339 value with any offset and converts it to UTC. - store.SQLNow is the SQL expression for the current time. SQL column defaults use it. SQLite has millisecond precision, so the last six digits of a default value are zero. Migration 0067 canonical timestamps.sql rewrites every registered time column to this format and changes the old millisecond SQL defaults. A value that is not a time stays as it is, and the migration logs its table and column. The registry of time columns is timeColumns in internal/store/timefmt.go; a test fails when a new time column is missing from it. Backup restore also converts old-format values in those columns, so an old backup does not bring old formats back. The Store service database has the same format and its own migration. API responses return stored times as they are, so they have nine fractional digits. Examples are the Usage request ts and the task usage first ts/last ts, which earlier had three digits or a variable number. These are valid RFC 3339 values. Mail table, indexes and letter ids Every letter is one row of mail (migration 0072 mail.sql), one row per recipient. A letter is open while answered at and dead at are empty; a closed letter keeps its row. idx mail inbox on (recipient, answered at, created at) serves the inbox, the open count that wakes the loop and the queue-depth gauge; idx mail sent on (sender, created at) serves Sent; idx mail thread on in reply to finds the reply of a letter; and the partial unique index idx mail idempotency on (idempotency key, recipient) makes a producer retry return the existing letter. A letter id is m-<yyyymmddThhmmssZ -<seq , where seq is the row's INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, zero-padded to six digits. seq is also the monotonic ingress number that queue triggers read. The migration dropped the channel bus and chat tables without moving their rows: mail started empty. Schema migrations The daemon database and the Store service database use one migration runner, internal/migrate. It applies each .sql file once, in name order, in its own transaction, and records the file name in schema migrations. A file sets flags with header lines at its very top: - -- tariboy: foreign keys=off turns off foreign key enforcement for the migration, for example to rebuild a referenced table. The runner checks pragma foreign key check before commit and rolls back on a violation. - -- tariboy: skip if column=TABLE.COLUMN skips the body when the column exists and still records the file as applied. - -- tariboy: step=NAME runs the named Go step after the body, in the same transaction, such as canonical timestamps for the stored-time migration. An unknown key or step name stops the migration with an error. Background operations The operations table (migration 0073 operations.sql) has one row for each image or workflow build that the daemon runs in the background: - kind is image.build or workflow.build; - status is running, succeeded, failed or interrupted; - title, initiator (ui, cli, compose, auto or empty) and params, a JSON object of the request arguments; - result, the JSON build result of a succeeded operation; - error code and error message of a failed or interrupted operation; - created at and finished at. The full log of an operation is the owner-only file <base-dir /operations/<id .log, not a table. The log of one operation stops at 10 MiB with one line about the truncation. At start, the daemon sets every running row to interrupted: a build does not survive the daemon process that ran it. Agent-owned tables The tables whose rows belong to one agent are listed once, in store.AgentTables in internal/store/agent tables.go. Each row gives the table's scoping condition, the removal step that deletes it, and its place in an agent backup. KeepOnRemove marks the agent history: iterations and ai requests. Agent backup and restore use the rows with a backup position. Iteration retention deletes the tables in store.IterationTables. store.RemoveMode selects what Manager.Remove deletes: | Mode | Caller | Rows | Agent directory | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | remove | agent rm NAME, compose rm | agent.Store.Remove deletes every registry row without KeepOnRemove, in one transaction | deletes image/, bin/, workdir/ | | keep | compose down | keeps all rows, sets enabled=false on the agent row | deletes image/, bin/, workdir/ | | purge | agent rm NAME --purge, the UI, compose down --volumes | agent.Store.Delete deletes the core rows, then PurgeAgentData deletes the side-table rows | deletes the whole directory | iteration tags and script runs go with their parent rows by ON DELETE CASCADE. store.CascadeParent names them. assessments reference the agent by value, and no mode deletes them. The mail row deletes only the letters to the agent, so the letters that the agent sent stay with their recipients. store.RemovalReport builds the deleted and kept lists of the agent rm answer from the same registry. A purge remove also works without an agent row. It then deletes what an earlier remove kept: the registry rows and the agent directory. A valid agent name is required, because the name becomes a path. Iteration retention reads only the agents in the agents table. It does not prune the kept iterations of a removed agent. After a remove, iteration ls still reads the iterations, but iteration tag commands answer not found, because they need the agent row. task agent pool members references agents with ON DELETE RESTRICT. The tasks service owns pool membership, and agent removal does not change it. A remove or purge of an agent that is in a task queue agent pool fails before the daemon stops the agent. The error names each queue and pool. Remove the agent from the pool in the queue settings, then delete the agent. Mode keep does not check pools, because it keeps the agent row. A new table with an agent, agent name or produced by agent column, or a foreign key to a registry table without ON DELETE CASCADE, needs a registry row or an exemption with a reason in agentKeyedExempt. Otherwise the schema test in internal/store fails. Filesystem-backed shell scripts The global pre-iteration script at <base-dir /global-agent-shell.sh and an agent script at <base-dir /agents/<name /agent-shell.sh are intentionally not SQLite fields. The daemon validates a complete submitted value with bash -n before atomically replacing an owner-only file. A rejected value leaves the previous file unchanged; a missing or empty file is a no-op at launch. Pricing and Usage snapshots Model-price state has three layers with distinct ownership. Operator-managed and LiteLLM-managed rows live in ai pricing; built-in prices are runtime fallbacks rather than persisted manual overrides. The resolved in-memory map is derived with manual rows first, then litellm rows, then the built-in fallback. model-prices-litellm.json is a rebuildable cache of the external source, not a second editable configuration store. A valid cache is reconciled into the managed database rows during startup before its complete generation is published to the proxy. Each ai requests row is historical evidence, not a projection of current configuration. The proxy calculates cost usd once from one complete price generation and persists that value with mutually exclusive input, output, cache-write, and cache-read token buckets. Later price refreshes do not recalculate Usage or budget history. The same row stores nullable request-time group id and group name snapshots. Moving an agent, renaming or deleting a group, or changing current membership does not rewrite those columns. Rows created before snapshots existed remain null and appear as Ungrouped; reindexing an old transcript does not guess a group from current state. See AI proxy and audit for the recording and filtering flow and Images and groups for the operator-visible consequences. Recorded halt reasons The loop can be turned off automatically as well as by hand: a stop policy (on error or on timeout set to stop) halts it after a failed or timed-out iteration, and the idle limit halts it after enough consecutive self-declared idle iterations. An agent has one on/off column, enabled; migration 0064 agent drop loop enabled.sql removed the former loop enabled column and turned off every agent that was enabled with that loop flag off, unless it was halted or used bare:latest. A policy halt leaves enabled set: the non-empty error reason alone keeps the engine from launching iterations, and Start clears it. An idle stop clears enabled. The reason is already persisted in two existing columns — a policy halt in error reason, an idle stop as a status message carrying the shared idle limit prefix — so no new column and no migration stand behind it. A derived accessor computes a halt kind and reason from those two fields, because both can be populated at once; an error halt wins over an idle stop, being the more urgent explanation. All three agent read surfaces — agent inspect, the agent ps rows, and the agent status endpoint — report it as halt kind (error or idle limit) and halt reason, and only when there is a reason: with none, both keys are omitted entirely rather than emitted empty. An agent-authored status line is never reported as a halt reason, since only the idle prefix qualifies. Iteration tags An iteration row is immutable evidence of an execution, so tags are not a column on it. They are rows in iteration tags, keyed by (iteration id, tag), with an ON DELETE CASCADE reference to iterations. Retention pruning and agent deletion therefore retire an iteration's tags with the iteration itself, and no tag write can touch the iteration row. A batch of tag changes over several iterations of one agent commits in one transaction, and an id belonging to another agent fails the whole batch rather than writing part of it. Tags are a property of the iteration, not of the agent that applied them: who tagged an iteration is not recorded. Assessments An assessment is a record of how well an agent did the work of one iteration or one task. Another agent, the assessor, writes it. Later reports use assessments to compare image versions and workflow versions. Migration 0075 assessments.sql adds three tables: - assessments: one row for each assessment. The id is as-<yyyymmddThhmmssZ -<seq , where seq is the row's INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, zero-padded to six digits. The row holds created at, the assessor (assessor agent, assessor image ref, assessor image version, assessor image digest), rubric version, the subject (iteration id, task key, or both), the snapshots and summary. - assessment axes: exactly three rows for each assessment, one for each axis. The axes are image process (the agent followed the process of its image), role (the agent followed ROLE.md) and task fit (the result fits the task and what the customer expected). The verdict is scored, with a score from 0 to 100, or not applicable, without a score. An image without an approved ROLE.md gets not applicable on role. - assessment violations: zero or more rows for each assessment. Each row has an axis, a description, a quote and its evidence. The evidence kind is transcript (an iteration id and a locator in its transcript), task event (a task key and a task events.sequence) or script run (a srun-... run id). The daemon does not make sure that the evidence still exists, because retention deletes transcripts, events and runs. The daemon writes the assessor and the snapshots. The request cannot set them. The assessor is the agent of the tools socket, and its image fields come from the iterations row of its current iteration. Without a running iteration, the write fails with 409 no iteration. The subject snapshots are subject agent, image ref, image version and image digest from the iterations row of the subject iteration. For a task that follows a workflow, the snapshots also include workflow digest and workflow version, the tag of the workflow image. The daemon takes them when it writes the assessment. The write fails with 400 invalid assessment in these cases: - The request has no iteration id and no task key. - The iteration or the task does not exist. - The request has both, and they are not linked. - rubric version or summary is empty. - The axes are not exactly the three axes, each one time. - A scored axis has no score or a score outside 0..100, or a not applicable axis has a score. - A violation has no description, no quote, an unknown axis or evidence that does not match its kind. An iteration and a task are linked when the agent of the iteration is the assignee of the task, or when task events of the task has an event with actor = agent:<agent of the iteration . The second condition is necessary for a task that follows a workflow. After the agent leaves its status, the task goes to the customer or to another pool, but the events of the agent stay. An assessment is immutable. No command changes or deletes one. A second assessment of the same iteration or task is a new row with a new id. The row, its axes and its violations are written in one transaction, so a failed write leaves no part of an assessment. Metrics and assessment.ls without history read only the latest row of each assessed object. The object of a row with an iteration id is that iteration. The object of a row with an empty iteration id is its task key. The latest row of an object is the first row in this order: 1. created at, newest first. 2. At an equal created at, rubric version, latest first. 3. At an equal rubric version, seq, highest first. A rubric version of the form name/N has a name and a number. N is one or more digits at the end, after a /, and name is not empty. The daemon compares the names as strings, then the numbers as numbers. Thus iteration-review/10 is later than iteration-review/2, and iteration-review/1 is later than iteration-review. A value of another form is a name without a number. The choice happens at read time and changes no row. The SQL condition is assessment.IsLatest. It checks each row against the other rows of its object. An iteration row uses idx assessments iteration created (iteration id, created at). A task row uses idx assessments task iteration created (task key, iteration id, created at). The check reads only the rows of the object from the created at of the row on, and it skips the row itself. The same two indexes serve the --iteration and --task filters of assessment ls and the task filter of the metrics report. On a test database with 10,000 assessments, assessment ls takes about 4 to 9 ms. A metrics report over 1,000 tasks takes about 155 ms. The axes and the violations reference assessments(seq) with ON DELETE CASCADE. The tables have no foreign key to iterations, tasks or agents. An assessment stays after iteration retention deletes its iteration and after the operator removes its agents. For this reason the three tables are in agentKeyedExempt, and the snapshots keep the image and the workflow of the subject. The nightly VACUUM INTO backup copies the tables with the rest of the database. Retention deletes old assessments, see the next section. Nightly backup and data retention Maintenance settings are one JSON value under maintenance in daemon config; a missing value means the defaults: enabled, 03:00 daemon-host local time, 7 backups, 90 days of retention, 7 days of mail history (chat retention days, which kept its name), compaction on at 10% free pages. A field missing from a stored value takes its default. The last run's result (times, trigger, backup path, rows deleted per category, logical size before and after, compaction, error) is stored under maintenance last run. Operators change both with Settings → Agent defaults → Backup & data retention , tariboy maintenance get|set|run, or /api/maintenance. A run, scheduled or manual, is serialized and always starts with a backup: VACUUM INTO on its own short-lived connection writes a consistent copy while the daemon keeps serving and writing, to <base-dir /backups/db/tariboyd-<UTC time .db, and only the newest configured number of those exact names are kept; other files in the directory are never rotated. If the backup fails, nothing is deleted. The run then prunes agent iterations (see Iteration retention) and removes data older than the retention period, each category in its own transaction. Mail uses the mail history period instead when it is shorter, and is deleted even when retention is 0: - Native Tasks — only whole trees whose every task is done or cancelled with completed at before the cutoff, with their comments, waits, events, notifications, relations, and outbox rows. A tree related to a task that stays is kept. After the deletion commits, each deleted task's <base-dir /tasks/<KEY / directory is removed; a key that is not a single path element is skipped. - AI proxy Usage — ai requests rows. Retention is 0 (keep everything) or at least 31 days, so the calendar-month budget window never loses rows, and rows inside the longest rolling budgets period are kept even when it exceeds the retention period. tariboy daemon reindex can restore deleted rows from retained transcripts; the next run deletes them again. - Mail — closed letters: answered, archived, read or dead. Open letters, and letters to a queue that queue-trigger ingress has not consumed yet, are never deleted. The cutoff is the more recent of the retention period and chat retention days (any value = 0; 0 leaves mail to the retention period), which covers every mailbox at once. Old mail therefore ends at that cutoff and stays only in the database backups. - Operations — operations rows of builds that finished before the cutoff. A running operation is never deleted. After the deletion commits, the log file <base-dir /operations/<id .log of each deleted operation is removed. - Daemon events (events) and task mutation idempotency records. - Assessments — assessments rows created before the cutoff, with their axes and violations by cascade. The run counts them as assessments. The category uses the general retention period and has no separate setting. When retention is 0, every assessment stays. When compaction is on and at least the threshold share of pages is free, a full VACUUM plus wal checkpoint(TRUNCATE) returns the space to the file system. VACUUM holds the daemon's single writer connection, so every write waits for the few seconds this takes; the read-only pool that serves the polled API reads continues. The disk needs free space about the size of the database. A failed VACUUM is rolled back by SQLite and recorded in the run result. The scheduler checks the wall clock every minute, so the slot holds across system sleep; a slot noticed more than 15 minutes late — the daemon was down or the machine asleep — is skipped, not caught up. To restore, stop the daemon, replace tariboyd.db with a backup file (and remove any tariboyd.db-wal and tariboyd.db-shm), then start it again. Iteration retention The nightly run prunes every agent's iterations after the backup and records the count as iterations in the run's deleted counts; tariboy prune <agent|all and Prune now in an agent's settings run the same pruning on demand. The limits are keep iterations, keep days and max bytes. The server-wide default is one JSON value under retention default in daemon config, where 0 means unlimited. A row in retention policies overrides it per agent field by field: each non-zero field replaces the default's, and 0 inherits it, so an agent cannot be unlimited where the default sets a limit. Operators set the default with Settings → Agent defaults → Backup & data retention or tariboy retention set default, and an agent's override in its settings or with tariboy retention set <agent . The newest iteration and any running one are never pruned. Every pruned iteration is backed up first to <agents-dir /<agent /archive/<iteration .tar.gz (mode 0600): the iteration directory plus db-rows.json, which holds its iterations row and its ai requests rows as column-to-value objects. Only after the archive is written and synced are those rows and the directory deleted; an iteration whose archive fails stays untouched. Archives are not rotated. The legacy archive column of retention policies is ignored. Customer identity and read state customer login in daemon config is the fixed customer login, defaulted to customer and adopted once — with existing tasks, comments, waits and the senders and recipients of existing letters carried over in the same transaction — instead of following whichever account runs tariboyd. Read state is the letter's own read at: opening a letter in the Desktop or tariboy mail read sets it. A read notice to an agent closes; a read notice to the customer stays in the inbox until the customer archives it. Inbox state Inbox saturation is derived rather than persisted. The agent status endpoint counts the agent's open letters and returns messages pending, the configured messages max queue, and messages queue full. The flag is true when the open count is at or above the limit. The send-time cap, status, the loop wake and inbox clearing use the same open-letter predicate, so the UI never maintains a second estimate. Native task state Each agent row persists goal enabled (default true), a positive goal wait customer timeout s (default 300), a positive goal delivery cooldown s (default 60), daemon-owned last goal delivery at, and its read-only current goal task key. Disabling Goal clears the selected key; re-enabling it selects from current task state rather than restoring an old choice. The goal reconciler normally owns selection; an agent may explicitly select an active task assigned to itself during a live iteration. Manually blocked tasks and tasks with an active incoming blocks relation are not eligible; a selected task is released if it becomes blocked. Only the reconciler writes the delivery timestamp. Task queues, the unlimited parent tree, comments, waits, relations, events, notification outbox, customer notification state, and mutation idempotency records are normalized tables in the same tariboyd.db. A task key is its queue prefix plus four random characters (TEST-fkt3), minted against the task key UNIQUE constraint rather than a counter, and it never changes when a task moves between parents or between daemons. task key aliases holds the numeric keys retired by that migration so they keep resolving; the daemon rewrites any remaining numeric key on its first start after the upgrade, in one transaction that also rewrites agents.current goal task key and records the rewrite in task legacy keys migrated.
