Later starts skip it, because a random suffix can be all digits too and must not be mistaken for a legacy key. task queues.next number is left in the schema but is no longer read or advanced. After that migration the daemon inserts the default TASK queue when no queue has that prefix. Recursive CTEs derive descendants, inherited access, blocking cycles, and active descendants without a configured depth limit. visibleCTE in internal/tasks/repo.go is the one visibility rule for an agent. A parent can have a child in another queue. The recursive step that gives write access to descendants follows only a child with the same queue prefix as its parent. The read-only ancestor chain also stops at a parent in another queue. The author of a child in another queue gets rank 0 (context) for that child only. Authorship gives write access only to a child in its parent's queue. Priority is persisted as a constrained P0 through P3 value and defaults to P2. Every root or nested sibling set has canonical order (priority, position, task key). Positions are kept per (queue prefix, parent id, priority), so the children of one parent that are in different queues have separate orders. Manual positions are normalized within a priority bucket, so reparenting preserves priority without disturbing other buckets. started at records the first time a task's status became in progress and never moves afterward: a task paused in wait customer, reopened, or started again keeps it. The tasks started at trigger stamps it on every status write path — update, claim, and a resolved customer wait — with that write's updated at. Migration 0049 backfilled existing tasks from the earliest task.updated event with status in progress, or task.claimed still in task events; a task with no such event keeps an empty value until its next real move into in progress, rather than taking the time of an unrelated edit. Export and import carry the field. Every task mutation, its event, and any notification intent commit in one SQLite transaction. The notification publisher sends the letters afterward from the durable outbox with a stable idempotency key. The WebSocket is only a delivery optimization: task events.sequence is the resume authority and HTTP queries remain authoritative. See Native Tasks. Queues also own agent pools and queue triggers, and the daemon keeps a persisted mail-ingress cursor over mail.seq that startup reconciles so a trigger never creates a task twice. The earlier task workflow engine tables were dropped by migration 0054; tasks that had been managed became ordinary tasks and keep a workflow.removed event that records what they ran on. The unused tasks.workflow version id and workflow revision columns and the empty task workflow versions table stay in place, always NULL or empty, because SQLite cannot drop a column with a foreign key without rebuilding tasks. Migration 0055 adds the workflow image engine. tasks.workflow digest pins the image a task follows, set in the transaction that creates the task from the queue's binding; the task is never migrated to another version, and the image row (task workflow images) cannot be removed while a queue binds it or an unfinished task pins it. tasks.workflow status holds the workflow status (and tasks.workflow paused reason, the pause reason, empty unless the task is paused), while tasks.status keeps holding the category for every task. Migration 0069 stores two values that every task read used to compute per row: tasks.workflow owner kind, the owner kind of the current status read from the pinned manifest, and tasks.open blockers, the number of open tasks that block the task. Triggers keep both current on every write path: the owner kind when workflow status, workflow digest, or the image manifest changes, and the blocker count when a blocks relation is added or removed or a blocker moves into or out of done or cancelled. Task visibility is a recursive CTE that queries join, so no query binds a variable per visible task. Task JSON shows the workflow status as status and the stored value as category; for a task without a workflow both are the stored status. New tables: task queue workflows (one binding per queue, with a revision and an ON DELETE RESTRICT reference to the image; migration 0068 adds workflow tag, the tag the binding follows, empty for a pinned binding and for every binding made before it), task workflow holders (the last holder per task and pool), task status visits, task transition requests (at most one pending per task), and task artifacts. Workflow mutations append workflow.transitioned, workflow.transition requested, workflow.moved, workflow.cancelled, and artifact.set task events, and queue bindings append queue.workflow bound and queue.workflow cleared, in the same transaction as the change. See Task workflows. Migration 0056 adds task queue secrets: per-queue secret values for workflow scripts, in plaintext like agent secrets, deleted with their queue. No read route returns a value; setting and removing a key append queue.secret set and queue.secret removed with the key only. Migration 0066 adds its secret column: a row with secret = 0 is a plain queue env var whose value the env routes return, with queue.env set and queue.env removed events; every earlier row stays a secret. Migration 0057 adds task script runs, the durable record of every check and watch run (kind, script, mode, state, verdict, exit code, message, process id, times, and log path), with a unique partial index that allows one pending or running run per task, and task status visits.next watch at, when the open visit of a script status runs its watch next. Migration 0058 adds task script runs.holder, the agent a run as: agent check ran as, which decides who may read its log. Migration 0059 adds only indexes: runs by task, visit, and request, the pending and running runs, and the open visits with a scheduled watch. A check moves its transition request to applied, rejected, or failed in the transaction that records the run; rejections and failures increment the visit's rejected requests and script failures counters. Script runs append workflow.script run, workflow.transition rejected, workflow.transition failed, and workflow.script failed events; a quiet watch run appends none, and only the newest 20 quiet runs of a visit are kept. Closing a visit by any route cancels its pending transition request. When the worker starts, before it starts any run, it terminates a script a crashed daemon left running when /proc proves the recorded PID is that run's script, then records every run still running as interrupted. Run files live under <base-dir /tasks/<KEY / (state/ and runs/<run-id /), owner-only; only the newest 20 quiet watch runs of a task keep their run directories, counted by the running worker, and nightly retention removes the directory of every task it deletes. Migration 0060 adds task workflow holders.released (default 0): the customer's release decision sets it on the holder's row, which makes that agent neither the previous holder nor free for the task in that pool, with either value of sticky holder, until another agent replaces the row or an operator move deletes it. Migration 0061 adds task workflow holders.unavailable since (default empty): when the holder was first seen unable to work, cleared by every dispatch, which the daemon compares with the unavailable grace limit. tasks.workflow paused reason is now set: a pause writes one of idle iterations, rejected requests, script failures, or holder unavailable, together with category wait customer, an open customer wait authored by system:workflow, and a workflow.paused event; a resume decision, an operator move, or a cancel clears it, and a decision or move appends workflow.resumed. Both are written in the transaction that changes the task. Migration 0062 adds an index on task transition requests(visit id, created at), which the idle-iteration count reads, and task status visits.resumed at (default empty): a resume decision writes the time on the open visit, and an iteration that started before it does not count as idle. See Task workflows. Migration 0071 adds task status visits.workflow digest (default empty), the digest the task was pinned to when it entered the status, filled for existing visits from tasks.workflow digest. An operator upgrade changes tasks.workflow digest to the queue's current binding and enters the new version's initial status in one transaction, with a workflow.upgraded event; the visits of the earlier version stay as history. See Task workflows. Migration 0074 adds task status visits.owner pool (default empty): the pool that owns a customer status in the customer's place, copied from the queue env var CUSTOMER AGENT POOL when the task enters the status. It replaces the owner kind triggers so that tasks.workflow owner kind is pool while such a visit is open. See Task workflows. Migration 0063 adds task queue source runs, the durable record of every run of a workflow source (queue, source, script, image digest, state, verdict, exit code, message, number of tasks created, process id, times, and log path), with a unique partial index that allows one running run per queue and source, and task queue source items, every item key a source turned into a task, keyed by queue, source, and key. A source run creates its tasks, their artifacts, and their keys in the transaction that records it, so a crash never repeats a task; keys are never deleted, so a removed task is not created again. A quiet run leaves no event and only the newest 20 quiet runs of a source are kept; a failed run appends the queue event queue.source failed. At startup the worker terminates a proven orphan of a source run as for a task run, then records every running source run as interrupted. See Task workflows. Image assignment state User Store registrations belong to each daemon's SQLite database and persist their unique name and source. The image stores row also holds the automatic build policy (auto interval minutes, auto images, auto last run at) and, since migration 0078, auto results: a JSON array with the last automatic build attempt of each selected image (image, selector, at, image version, error). A cycle replaces the entry of the image it built, and store auto drops the entries of deselected images. Since migration 0080, the row also holds ref: the branch, tag or commit of a Git Store ('' is the default branch of the remote). The checked-out commit is read from the clone, not stored. Git clones live under <base-dir /stores/<name /; local absolute sources stay in place. Image names, versions, and diagnostics are read from images/ on disk for every view, never stored as a second inventory. Store refresh and build preparation are serialized so a pull cannot race source freezing. Store builds then use the ordinary image snapshot and publication path below. Workflow images live on disk under <base-dir /workflows/<name /. Content is addressed by SHA-256 digest in refs/<digest /, and tags are pointer files in tags/ that hold a digest. The task workflow images table records the manifest of each published digest, so a manifest can be read from SQLite without touching the filesystem; a unique index on name and version keeps one digest per published version. The daemon reconciles the table with the stored content at startup: it inserts missing rows and deletes rows whose content is gone. See Workflow images. The sticky holder setting of a workflow and of its pool statuses lives only in that manifest JSON, in the parsed definition. No migration adds a column for it. A manifest without the field, such as one built before the setting existed, reads as false. Dispatch reads the value from the manifest of the digest that the task pins. See Dispatch. Directories left under <base-dir /store/versions/ by an older release are untouched legacy data. Current daemons neither read nor refresh them. Each agent row owns an active image ref/digest and a separate pending ref/digest/error. Selecting another image changes only the pending fields. The iteration launch gate validates and stages that artifact, reconciles image capabilities, and promotes active plus pending state in one guarded transaction. Every new iteration snapshots its image ref, source image version when present, digest, and prompt-template hash, so later switches cannot rewrite historical execution identity. Historical iterations and legacy images keep an empty version instead of inheriting the ref's current value. The agent row remains authoritative during crash recovery. An incomplete local image swap is either rolled back to the DB-active backup or completed when the already-promoted image digest matches the row. Each unpacked image records the ref it was materialized for and a daemon-owned id marker, so two generations of one ref cannot be confused. Provisioning unpacks an image atomically: it writes a staging directory next to the agent's image/, syncs it, and renames it into place, so a failed unpack leaves no partial image/ and a repeated provision keeps no stale files. A crash while the staging directory is written, or between the two renames, can leave .unpack- staging or backup directories under the agent root; the next provisioning of that agent removes them. Generations are kept by id under images/<name /refs/, so active and pending assignments survive a moved tag. Harness, model, effort, environment, CWD, context, workdir, mail, history, and group are not image assignment fields. Image content is addressed by ref id, the digest of its content (see "Refs, tags and identity" in Images). A tag is a pointer file naming that id. Archives from earlier releases keep their id: either sha256(name + "\n" + image version) or the archive file digest. One build publishes one ref and moves every requested tag onto it, so a versioned tag and latest always agree. Content stored under an id is never rewritten. A build of an image version that is already stored with other content fails with image version conflict unless it is forced. The build records where those tags pointed, then commits every source snapshot and provenance row in one SQLite transaction. A failure restores the tags and deletes only content the build introduced, never a generation an agent may be pinned to. There is no publication journal. A store written before this model is migrated once at daemon startup, keeping each archive's digest as its ref id so pinned digests keep resolving. Image locks keep every reader off an uncommitted generation. Ordinary, editable-source, agent-authored, compose, and import publication take the lock of the one image name they write, so publications of different names run in parallel and publications of one name run one at a time. Assignment, activation, provisioning, reprovisioning, removal, and migration read or change several names, so they take the store-wide lock, which excludes every name lock. The locks are in-process: tariboyd is the one process that writes the image store. Compose publishes through the daemon rather than writing its image store from the client process. Restart handoff A running iteration is owned by tariboy-shim, not by the lifetime of the daemon process. During a graceful daemon restart, cancellation detaches the old engine observer without changing the durable iteration row from running. Before any of that, the replacement daemon reconciles each stored agent's bin shims against its active image (see Agent bin shims), so adopted work continues with the launchers pinned by that image. The replacement daemon enumerates live shim sockets before starting loop engines, adopts each matching iteration, and finalizes the existing row when result.json appears. It never launches a duplicate shim while adoption is in progress. Pending adoptions are also registered as current live iterations inside the replacement manager. Terminal attach, resize, input, screen, and Kill RPCs therefore continue to reach the original shim before the normal loop engine is created. Start remains idempotent during this window, direct Exec cannot bypass the adoption barrier, and post-adoption startup reloads the current persisted Enabled value instead of using a pre-restart snapshot. Restart records one replacement interactive-run intent until handoff completes, even for an agent that runs no autonomous iterations; the engine consumes that intent through a launch gate shared with Stop, so a later Stop can cancel work that has not started. The gate is acquired after external tmux checks and covers the durable launch or manual-collision outcome. If Stop then races detached process creation, the runner uses bounded cooperative shim Kill so the shim stops its owned harness process group or tmux session. An unreachable interactive shim receives an explicit tmux kill. The final managed fallback signals the spawned shim to force-kill its separately owned non-interactive harness group, then escalates against the outer shim group after a short bound. This cleanup is skipped when the row is still running for daemon handoff. Shim connections are acquired under the handoff lock with a finite dial timeout, preventing a pending control operation from crossing into a replacement iteration when the stable socket pathname is reused without allowing a wedged listener to block lifecycle operations indefinitely. The durable completion flag follows the same lifecycle on both sides of a restart. Once an adopted iteration calls i-am-done, the replacement manager allows the harness a two-second grace period to exit naturally, then sends the shim exactly one cooperative Kill request if no result.json has appeared. The shim writes the result and adoption finalizes the original row, preserving the productive or --idle declaration recorded with the completion flag. The AI-proxy endpoint and active per-iteration leases are carried through the same restart, so harness retries reconnect after the short listener outage. If the old shim is no longer reachable, adoption is the component that terminally classifies the stale row as harness error. Script runs follow the same handoff. The daemon starts each run as tariboy-shim script-run -- ARGV. This wrapper leads the run's process group, and its pid is script runs.pid. The daemon creates the state file agents/NAME/scripts/RUN.state next to the run log, takes an exclusive flock on it, and passes it to the wrapper as fd 3. The lock stays with the wrapper until it exits. When the script ends, the wrapper writes its result to the file as JSON: exit code, signal, or start error. The supervisor decides how a run ended from this file, not from wait. A held lock means the run is alive. A free lock with a result means the run ended with that result. A free lock without a result, or no file, means the process is lost. The pid takes no part, so a reused pid never looks like a live run. Later daemon versions read this file, so its fields are added but never renamed. daemonctl.Restart creates the marker file daemon-handoff in the runtime directory before it stops the daemon, and removes it when the stop fails. tariboy update and tariboy daemon restart use daemonctl.Restart. tariboy daemon stop creates no marker. A daemon that stops with the marker leaves its script runs running. Without the marker, the stop sends SIGTERM to each run's group, SIGKILL after two seconds, and records interrupted. The next daemon removes the marker at start. Before it recovers stale runs, it adopts each running run whose wrapper is alive or has written a result. Its timeout counts from started at, and a pending cancellation request is applied again. Recovery records every other running run as interrupted, or as cancelled after a cancellation request. :::danger[This is why test daemons must be isolated] Two daemons pointed at the same base dir share the same DB and loop managers and will double-run each other's agents — double-executed iterations and reaped sessions. Always isolate a test daemon with its own base dir, runtime dir, and the web UI disabled. See Development → Test isolation. :::
description: The SQLite DB is the single source of configuration; live state is computed, not stored, which is why test daemons must be isolated.
title: State model — the DB is the source of truth

content: The main UI is a React single-page application under ui/src, loaded by the Tauri host in desktop/src-tauri. It talks to a selected local or remote tariboyd over HTTP and WebSocket. Daemons expose API/WS only and do not embed or serve the Desktop UI. npm run build:desktop writes the SPA to ignored desktop/dist. make desktop always rebuilds it before Tauri packaging, so this output must never be staged. The separate store UI builds from ui/store into committed internal/storeui/dist and is served only by tariboy-store. npm run build:android builds the same SPA for the Android app with VITE TARIBOY SHELL=android. In that mode isDesktop() is false, so servers use the browser registry (localStorage metadata, sessionStorage tokens) and no native command is called. The implicit same-origin "This daemon (local)" host is absent, the router is HashRouter, the daemon banner is hidden, an empty start screen offers Add server , and the server dialog accepts https:// or plain http:// to a loopback port only. A web link navigates the WebView, and the Android host's navigation guard cancels that without waiting for the system browser. A background task opens the browser, so the navigation callback does not block the Android UI thread. If the browser cannot open the link, the current screen stays in place and the host logs a fixed message without the URL or error details. The app shows no failure message for this native attempt (see Security and controls). See Remote hosts. Linux native UI verification uses make desktop-e2e: Playwright specs speak a small W3C WebDriver client through tauri-driver to a real debug Tauri/WebKit executable. The harness uses fresh owner-only daemon and Desktop state, rejects the live listener, and owns all driver/display cleanup. This complements the fast browser fixtures; it does not replace them and does not build Linux package artifacts. Tauri creates one visible main window and opens the SPA directly. Daemon adoption/start and saved-host reconnect continue independently in the background, so their existing status banners may be visible during startup. Dock reopen and the menu-bar Open action raise the same main window. Application settings live at /app-settings and remain available without a daemon connection; Settings → Application opens them. Desktop update checks use the native application host and never target the selected local or remote daemon. The settings screen, update status, and ready banner use English labels. Automatic download is enabled by default, persists in WebView localStorage, runs on startup and then every six hours while enabled, and never installs automatically. A verified package stays only in Rust process memory, so quitting Desktop discards it. When one is ready, the route-independent banner below the titlebar requires an explicit install action and reports installation failures for retry. There is no interface mode. Every user gets the same agent workspace, and it uses progressive disclosure: the everyday views are tabs, and the rarer views are one step away. The agent header's ⋯ → Diagnostics opens the existing diagnostic views, including Mailbox . Settings → Advanced → Other views keeps its links to the same routes. The terminal hotkeys are behind Keys , and the header's rarer actions are in its ⋯ menu. A value that an older release stored under app:ui-mode:v1 is ignored. The New agent dialog shows five fields in this order: Run on (only when the workspace has more than one host), Folder , Image , Coding tool , and Name . One Advanced disclosure holds every other field. The dialog and the first-run card on the home screen (see First run) are one component, ui/src/pages/terminals/create-agent/NewAgentForm.tsx, driven by useCreateAgentForm. Ordinary creation starts with the documented defaults and submits one complete create request; the daemon writes one complete stopped agent row. A new agent opens on its Terminal tab. - Folder is the agent's working directory on the selected host, with path autocomplete. It is required. Advanced → Folder → Use a managed folder clears it and sends an empty cwd, so the daemon makes a managed workdir. - Image lists one row per image name, with the newest built tag selected. Each row shows the name, the newest image version, and the source when the daemon knows it. Typing filters by name. basic is first and selected by default, the other names follow in A–Z order, and bare is last as Plain terminal (bare) . Advanced → Image → version picks another tag. When the host has no built image except bare, the host's checklist rows are shown above the field. When the list is closed and the selected image has a ROLE.md, a fragment of it is shown under the field. The fragment is the first paragraph that is not a heading, else the first list item, as plain text in two lines at most. The field's aria-describedby names it. If the file has more blocks or the fragment does not fit, Show role opens the full text as Markdown in a box of 240px at most, with its own scroll, and Hide role closes it. A new image closes it. The fragment comes from the manifest that the form already loads, so it adds no request. The form shows nothing for bare, for an image without ROLE.md, while the manifest loads, and when the manifest fails. - Coding tool is a radio group from the host's harness detection (GET /api/onboarding), labeled with the harness ID, for example Claude Code · claude . stub is never offered. The form selects the image's default harness when it is found on the host, else the first found tool in the order Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor. When the image declares no harness, the request carries that detected harness instead of an empty value. A tool that is not found stays selectable, shows its install hint, and blocks Start agent . A daemon without the onboarding route shows all four tools without found marks and blocks nothing. The field is hidden for a bare image. - Name is suggested as <folder basename -<image name , or <image name for a managed folder, made unique against the host's agents with -2, -3, and so on. The suggestion follows the folder and the image until you type a name. Advanced has these groups: Identity (alias, team, color, notes), Image (version, plugins), Folder (managed folder, environment), Coding tool ( Headless (no terminal) , off by default), Autopilot (interval, soft and hard timeouts, timeout and error policies, idle limit, AI inactivity timeout, message batch and queue limits, standing prompt), and Tasks (the Goal settings), then Create without starting . Environment is a string-valued JSON object, schema-v1 plugins remain editable, and schema-v2 plugins are image-owned and read-only. Bare images are always interactive. There is no separate loop switch: Create without starting decides whether the new agent starts, and the footer button reads Start agent or Create agent . Interactive starts on for every new agent and selecting an image does not change it; the manifest's harness.interactive is not applied. Clone mode copies the source agent's value. Ordinary creation defaults the soft iteration timeout to 7,200 seconds (2 hours) and the hard timeout to 10,800 seconds (3 hours). Clone mode continues to copy both timeout values from the source agent. Agent creation, clone, and the agent's Settings carry the per-agent Goal settings: an enabled-by-default switch, a positive whole-second customer-wait timeout (300 by default), and a positive Goal delivery cooldown (60 seconds by default). Settings shows the daemon-selected goal key read-only. While the agent works, the header sentence names that key. A question-mark action in the Settings Advanced → Goal section explains the sticky selection and release rules. The former server-global policy screen is not part of Settings. Right-clicking any grouped or individual sidebar agent exposes Clone . Clone loads the source inspect projection from that agent's explicit host, suggests a free name, and prefills every persisted agent-row configuration field, including raw configured CWD and message limits. Clone mode uses the same layout with Advanced open, so every copied field is visible. It does not copy secrets, history, runtime evidence, messages, subscriptions, scripts, workdir contents, retention, or budgets. The target host and image remain editable, and every follow-up request stays pinned to that explicit target. Older daemons that do not expose the complete clone projection must be updated. Starting the agent remains a separate retryable lifecycle request after creation. The daemon rejects a folder that does not exist with bad cwd, so a typo never creates a stray directory. 300 ms after you stop typing, the form lists the parent folder on the selected host with GET /api/fs/list. If the last part of the path is not in that listing, the field shows This folder does not exist. Create it . The link makes the create request send create cwd: true, and the daemon makes the directory and its parents (mode 0755, owned by the daemon user) before it validates the path. A path that exists as a file still fails. If the parent cannot be listed, the form shows no link. A clone always starts without create cwd. While Start agent is disabled, the footer names the first unmet condition next to it: the source configuration, the target host's image list, an unselected or unbuilt image, the starter image that the daemon still makes, the image manifest still loading, an empty folder, or a coding tool that is not installed on the host. A failed manifest load stays visible until the host or image changes, and Retry image loads it again. While the daemon still connects the catalog or builds basic, only basic waits: the image list shows it with the waiting reason, and Plain terminal (bare) starts at once. Model and effort are shown as one line under the coding tool, for example Model: opus · Effort: medium . change opens the two fields. They are editable preset fields: they start from explicit runtime defaults for schema-v2 images and accept arbitrary values. Their suggestions come in two labeled groups. From harness holds the catalog the selected host returns from GET /api/harnesses/{type}/models (see Harness model catalog); it shows a loading note, the host's error, or a note that an older daemon does not list models instead of failing. When the chosen model carries its own efforts (Codex), the effort field offers those, otherwise the harness-wide list. Saved holds the values the operator entered earlier for that harness, the current value, and the image default, minus anything already listed under the harness. Schema-v1 image defaults remain readable for compatibility. Successful creates and successful Settings Model saves remember the model and effort in the Desktop WebView by harness; failed ones do not add values. Neither group validates a value: an unsupported model still fails at the harness. Shell and sidebar The titlebar has the sidebar toggle, the product name, one search field, the ? (Help) menu, and the theme toggle. It has no settings gear, no workspace dropdown, and no view switch. The content island shows only the open object's own tabs: there is no server bar above it. The search field filters the agent list in the sidebar as you type. It also opens a result list with matching agents and matching tasks of every host in the workspace. Tasks match by key or title, open or closed: the lookup sends GET /api/tasks?text=…&status view=all&limit=8 to each host 250 ms after the last key. A host that fails adds no results and shows no error. Enter opens the first result. ⌘K or Ctrl+K focuses the field. On a compact screen the field is at the top of the navigation drawer instead. The sidebar has seven items: | Item | Opens | | --- | --- | | Home | / (see Home) | | Tasks | /tasks | | Inbox | /inbox | | Agents | nothing: it opens and closes the agent list in place | | Library | /library/images, with Images , Workflows , and Sources tabs | | Metrics | /metrics (see Metrics) | | Settings | /settings/hosts, the first of the Settings pages | Home, Tasks, and Inbox stay above Agents in visual and keyboard order. Only the agent list scrolls. Library, Metrics, Settings, and the hosts line stay at the bottom. Metrics has no count. Settings has one flat list of seven pages. There is no index page: | Page | Route | Content | | --- | --- | --- | | Hosts | /settings/hosts | the local and SSH hosts: Add host , Edit , Remove , Update , Update all (N) when hosts are behind, and the host workspaces | | Teams | /settings/teams | create, edit, import, and export teams; ?team=<name opens one team | | Usage & budgets | /settings/usage | the AI usage of the host and its budgets, as two sections | | Agent defaults | /settings/agent-defaults | the Global Agent Shell Script, the Codex card, and Backup & data retention | | Integrations | /settings/integrations/:plugin? | an Installed plugins tab and one tab for each plugin with settings, such as Telegram | | Maintenance | /settings/maintenance | Backup and restore , the Operations log , and the Support bundle ; an operation opens at /settings/maintenance/operations/:id | | Application | /app-settings | the application settings; the list shows this page last, as a link | Hosts reads the host registry of the app, so it opens when the selected host does not answer. Every other page reads one host. The route host boundary wraps its body, not the Settings list, so the list and Hosts stay usable when a host is unreachable. The Library has these routes: | Route | Page | | --- | --- | | /library | redirects to /library/images | | /library/images | the Images tab | | /library/images/:name | the newest tag of the image, with its Versions | | /library/images/:name/:tag/ | that tag: Overview, template, skills, files | | /library/workflows | the Workflows tab | | /library/workflows/:name/:tag | one workflow image, with its Versions | | /library/sources | the Sources tab: one card per Store | | /library/sources/:name | the card of one Store | Tasks shows the number of tasks that need you, and Inbox shows the number of your open letters. A task needs you when its waiting on is customer and it is not in its workflow's initial status (workflow initial), or when its waiting on is pause (needsYouTask in ui/src/lib/needsYou.ts). A task that waits on a script, or that is in the initial customer status (for example backlog), never counts. The Tasks count is the number of distinct task keys on the hosts that answered: a task counts when needsYouTask selects it or when it has an open task.question letter, and it counts once. One read serves the two counts, Home, Inbox, and the agent states below: it reads each workspace host's active task list, GET /api/mail/unread, and the Inbox box at the sidebar's poll interval (3 seconds, or 15 seconds while the agent state socket is live). A host that does not answer adds nothing. When no host answers, the counts are hidden. The agent list under Agents is open by default; the WebView remembers it in terminals:sidebar-agents:v1. It starts with a New agent button and the pinned agents. A row's context menu pins and unpins it, and the WebView remembers the pinned set in terminals:sidebar-pinned:v1. A pinned agent shows only in the pinned block. Then each host lists its expandable Teams and its Individual agents . With one host in the workspace the list has no host heading. With two or more, each host has a heading with its reachability, an Update action when it runs an older daemon, and a ⋯ menu. The menu has Host settings , which opens /settings/agent-defaults?host=<id , and Maintenance , which opens /settings/maintenance?host=<id with backups and the operations log. A registered host also has Edit host and Remove host ; the local daemon has none. A host heading opens /tasks?host=<id . An agent row shows the agent's derived state (see Agent state). The dot has the color of the state. On the right, the row shows one pill: needs you · n in the accent color, working · 12 min with a clock that moves each minute (or working · waiting for agent command when the state has that reason), error in the danger color with the reason in its tooltip, or a muted off. An idle row shows no pill. The row has no other state, budget, or unread-letter badge; an open question is in Inbox and its task is in Tasks . The foot of the sidebar is one line about the workspace's hosts: Local · ready , 2 hosts · ready , or 2 hosts · 1 unreachable , with a dot when a host can be updated. The line opens Settings → Hosts, which holds Add host , Update all (N) , and the host workspaces. Update all asks you to confirm the named hosts first. Then it runs the same host update on each of them in turn. If a host fails, the page error line names it, and the other hosts are still updated. Host headings, team headings, and agent rows are themselves pointer- and keyboard-accessible drag surfaces; no separate drag handle is rendered. A drop reorders only like siblings, so it never changes team membership. The daemon stores each host's team and agent order in the versioned sidebar order v1 value under daemon config; missing or newly created names retain their current stable order. The Desktop WebView stores the cross-host order, including the implicit local host, in terminals:server-order:v1. Failed daemon writes restore the previous order and report the failure. Settings → Teams owns team creation and editing: arbitrary custom members, per-member runtime fields, rename/lead and membership controls, compose clipboard transfer, and portable archive import/export. All requests retain the active explicit host, including raw archive uploads and downloads. Routes and host scope /tasks, /inbox, /activity, /metrics, /metrics/compare, the Library pages, and the Settings pages other than Hosts show one host. They take an optional ?host=<id (local is the local daemon). Without it, the page shows the remembered active host. A ?host= that names another host selects it through the route host boundary, which shows Connecting to host… or Host unavailable. while it does. With two or more hosts in the workspace, the page has a host selector, and a pick replaces ?host=. In Tasks and Library, the selector comes first in the top content row, before filters or tabs. Both use HostScopeSelect, labeled Host , with a 28 px height, 16 px left padding, and 6 px between controls. Settings → Hosts and Settings → Application have no selector. With one host nothing about hosts is shown, and links that the UI builds carry ?host= only with two or more hosts. A desktop notification always names its host. The old URLs redirect, and keep the rest of their query: | Old URL | New URL | | --- | --- | | /servers/:hostId/mail | /inbox?host=:hostId | | /servers/:hostId/tasks | /tasks?host=:hostId | | /servers/:hostId/activity | /activity?host=:hostId | | /servers/:hostId/images/ | /library/images/ ?host=:hostId | | /servers/:hostId/workflows/ | /library/workflows/ ?host=:hostId | | /servers/:hostId/stores/ | /library/sources/ ?host=:hostId | | /servers/:hostId/settings/ | the /settings/ page in the next table, with ?host=:hostId | | / or /agents/… with ?view=all | /tasks | legacyServerRedirect in ui/src/lib/navRoutes.ts computes each target. A Library redirect copies the rest of the path unchanged, so an old tag list (/servers/:hostId/images/:name) opens the image page with its Versions. /images/ redirects to /library/images/ . legacySettingsPath maps an old Settings path to its page. It serves both /servers/:hostId/settings/ and the older bare /settings/ paths, which add no ?host=: | Old Settings path | Page | | --- | --- | | (none), the old General page | /settings/agent-defaults | | hosts, advanced/daemons, cli, appearance, advanced | /settings/hosts | | advanced/groups | /settings/teams | | advanced/usage, advanced/budgets | /settings/usage | | operations, advanced/ops | /settings/maintenance | | operations/:id | /settings/maintenance/operations/:id | | advanced/plugins | /settings/integrations | | integrations/:plugin | /settings/integrations/:plugin | | any other path | /settings/hosts | /hosts and /daemons open /settings/hosts, /groups opens /settings/teams, /usage and /budgets open /settings/usage, /plugins opens /settings/integrations, and /ops opens /settings/maintenance. Links inside the Library carry no ?host=, because the route host is the active host while a Library page is open. The image links of an agent's Settings carry ?host= when two or more hosts are registered. Home Home is the first screen of a workspace that has agents. It shows what needs the operator now and whether the agents are in order. The user is the operator who runs AI agents on one or more hosts. The task is to open the application, find the task or the letter that waits for an answer, see which agents run now and how the day goes, then go to the right place. Success: the operator understands in 5 seconds where an action is needed. At 1280 px all four sections (Needs you, Running now, Today, Recent) are visible on the first screen, and Needs you shows the most urgent items first, not every item. The goal is also recorded in ui/src/mockups/home/Home.stories.tsx. / is Home when the workspace has at least one agent (ui/src/pages/home/HomePage.tsx, loaded on first open). It has a New agent button and four sections: - Needs you (N) : the tasks that need you on every workspace host, newest first, then your open letters. Home shows the 7 most urgent rows, with Show all (N) under them. The link opens Inbox when every row is a letter and Tasks otherwise. Letters from one sender about one task are one row of the newest letter, and its meta starts with N letters. The inbox read returns at most 100 letters, so when a host returned that many, N is a lower bound and reads 100+. A question letter about a listed task is not shown again. The prefix Answer on KEY: or Question on KEY: of a letter subject moves to the meta line, so the subject starts the title. The meta of a task says waiting for you (or paused), and the age reads 12 min ago or 2 h ago for the last 24 hours and a date (Nov 4) before that. The rows are formatted in ui/src/pages/home/needsYouModel.ts. A task row opens the task drawer on its host, and a letter row opens /inbox?letter=<id . The chevron button Answer in place before a task row expands the row into its Needs you card, so you can answer without the drawer. With nothing to show it says Nothing needs you. When no host could be read, it shows the error and Retry . - Running now (N) : the agents in state running, with the time since current iteration started at. Each row opens the agent's Terminal. Home shows 8 rows. With more, Show all (N) shows the rest in place and Show less folds them again. - Today : the Activity totals of the page host for the last 24 hours, with History , which opens the Activity table at /activity. The number of a tile sits at the bottom of the tile, so a label that wraps does not move it. - Recent : eight agents, newest last iteration at first; agents that never ran follow in sidebar order. The meta is the time of the last iteration (2 h ago), or not run yet. First run While every host of the workspace has zero agents, / shows the first-run home (ui/src/pages/terminals/FirstRunHome.tsx) instead of Home. It has a welcome line, the Getting ready checklist, the inline Run your first agent card, and the line Later: connect another computer over SSH in Settings. As soon as any host has an agent, / shows Home. A dead agent route, an empty workspace other than the default one, and a workspace with no host keep their own empty states. The checklist shows the host selected in the card's Run on , which is the first host by default. It reads GET /api/onboarding through useOnboardingStatus and has three rows: - the Tariboy catalog: connected, connecting, could not connect, or removed (add it again in Library → Sources); - the starter image basic: ready (also when an image named basic already existed), building, or could not build; - the coding tool: which harnesses the host found and which it did not, with their install hints. When no tool is found, the row is a warning. The hook polls every 5 seconds while a row can still change by itself (the catalog is pending, or the starter image is pending or building) and stops when every row is final. A failed row shows one sentence, a Details disclosure with the raw daemon error, and Retry , which calls POST /api/onboarding/retry and starts polling again. A daemon without the onboarding route (older than this release) gives no status, so the checklist is hidden. The rules are pure functions in ui/src/lib/onboarding/firstRun.ts. A missing coding tool is never a red banner. The daemon still counts "at least one agent harness" among its missing tools, but the daemon banner removes that entry: when it is the only missing tool there is no banner, and when other tools are missing the banner names only those. A host added later shows its checklist inside the New agent dialog, when it has no built image except bare, and on its Stores page. After create, the agent opens on Terminal . Above the terminal, one banner line always says what the screen shows (see Agent terminal), for example Starting Claude Code in /code/my-app… while the coding tool starts, or Claude Code did not start: and the reason, with Retry (start the agent and reconnect the terminal) and Open settings . Without a session, the terminal says No terminal session. Start the agent, or turn on Interactive terminal in Settings → Autopilot. Below 1200 px, the agent header puts its buttons on their own row under the sentence. Onboarding The onboarding tour explains the work process on the screen itself. Each step dims the window, puts a ring around one element, and shows a card with a short English text, a counter such as 4 of 12 , and Skip tour , Back , and Next ( Done on the last step). The arrow keys move between steps, and Esc closes the tour. While the tour is open, clicks on the dimmed interface do not pass. The tour shows where an action is, but it does not open dialogs or create objects. The steps go through the screen in this order: Welcome, Agents , the agent workspace, the agent's Settings tab, the sidebar's Tasks item, the sidebar's Library item (images), the Library's Sources tab, the hosts line at the foot of the sidebar, Add host on Settings → Hosts, the Filters menu of Tasks (queues), the Library's Workflows tab, and the ? (Help) button. The Agents step goes to / and highlights the New agent button of Home, or Start agent on the first-run card; it never highlights the sidebar's New agent button. A step with a route opens that page through navPath in ui/src/lib/navRoutes.ts: tasks and inbox open /tasks and /inbox, and the Library items open /library/images, /library/sources, and /library/workflows on the active host, and settings opens /settings/hosts. The agent steps open the first agent of the sidebar. If the sidebar has no agent row when the tour starts, the tour leaves out the agent steps, and the counter counts only the steps it shows ( 1 of 10 ). Done, Skip tour , and Esc go back to the route where the tour started. If the sidebar is hidden on a wide window, a sidebar step shows it. On a phone width, the sidebar is a modal drawer that takes focus from the card, so the tour closes the drawer, and the sidebar steps show their card in the center. A step whose element is not on the screen, or has no size, also shows the card in the center without a ring. The tour checks for the element every 100 ms, so the ring follows the element after a route change, a resize, or a scroll. The agent workspace step says "Work, Terminal, Activity and Settings of one agent: …". The agent settings step says "Settings sets the coding tool, model, working folder, Autopilot and spending limit. Everything else is under Advanced." Its ring is on the Settings tab link. ui/src/lib/onboarding/tour.ts holds the steps and TOUR ANCHORS, the data-tour values. A component marks an element with data-tour={TOUR ANCHORS.name}, and a step names the same constant, so a step cannot name an anchor that does not exist. tour.test.ts also checks that a component uses each anchor that a step names. The steps whose element moved to the sidebar shell carry since: "0.101.0" and updated: true, so What's new shows them after that release. The version of the UI comes from scripts/release-version.txt, which scripts/set-version.sh writes at release time. onboarding:state:v1 stores the version whose tour the user finished or skipped. The full tour never starts by itself. API layer ui/src/lib/api/ is the only HTTP client of the Desktop UI. @/lib/api resolves to its index.ts, which assembles the client and re-exports the modules; it holds no requests of its own. - client.ts owns the transport: JSON requests that unwrap the {ok, result} / {ok, error} envelope, raw requests for archives, uploads and text exports, and the single ApiError class (status, code, message, details). Every request uses cache: "no-store", sends the host's bearer token, and passes the caller's AbortSignal. A JSON GET that gets no complete response in 30 seconds fails with network error and the message request timed out, so a connection that never answers cannot stop a refresh loop. Writes and raw requests have no time limit. - lib/resume.ts calls its listeners when the page becomes visible again or the browser comes back online. On that event the tasks, mail and agent state WebSockets and the agent event stream close and open again at once, and the shared query client rereads its active queries. A WebView can keep a socket open after its connection stopped, for example after an Android port forward dropped. - hosts.ts owns server selection: the active host that the host switcher sets, the local daemon origin that Desktop sets at boot, and the ApiTarget type (undefined = the active host, null = the local daemon, a Daemon = that host). - One module per domain: agents, iterations, usage, daemon, harnesses, plugins, scripts, files, images, imageSources, groups, stores, mail, audit, tasks, workflows, and metrics. Each module re-exports the types of its responses (see API types) and exports a factory that receives a transport bound to one host. Domain methods never take a target. lib/tasks.ts and lib/audit.ts keep only presentation helpers. - mail.ts is the mailbox client: list, show, send, reply, close, read, requeue, unread, and clear (an agent's inbox). Each call takes an optional as, the principal it acts as; without it the daemon acts as the customer. lib/letters.ts holds letterTaskKey(letter), the string data.task key of a letter or "", apart from the client so the shell's eager modules can read a letter without loading it. createApi(target) returns an ApiClient: the bound transport plus one section per domain, such as api.tasks.getTask(key) or api.images.listImages(). The target is fixed when the client is created: undefined resolves to the active host once, and a later host switch never redirects an existing client. A registered host without an endpoint (an SSH tunnel that is reconnecting) yields a client whose ready is false; its requests fail with host not ready and never fall back to the local daemon. React code reads the client from context: tsx const api = useApi() const detail = await api.tasks.getTask(taskKey, signal) ApiProvider fixes the server for the tree below it. DaemonProvider provides the active host, RouteHostBoundary provides the route host, and an agent workspace, a server pane, or a dialog with its own host picker mounts a provider for that host. Components do not pass a target down to children. useApi() outside a provider throws, and component tests render through @/test/queryRender or the apiWrapper / fakeApi helpers in @/test/api.tsx. An equal target keeps the same client across renders, so effects and subscriptions that depend on api do not restart. A new endpoint or token for the same host gives a new client without changing any tree key: loaded data and unsaved drafts survive a reconnect, while requests and subscriptions move to the new connection. A response from the previous client never replaces data of the current one. Code that works with several hosts at once creates one client per host with createApi(daemon): the all-hosts agent list, the all-servers task view, and customer question notifications. A transfer between hosts (a task, an image, a workflow image) holds one source client and one destination client for the whole operation. The native host registry, SSH tunnels, and Keychain tokens stay in lib/daemons.ts and lib/desktop.ts. Do not edit it; see Go control plane and plugins for the workflow after an API change. Each schema is a top-level type with the Go type's name, such as AgentRow or TaskDetail. The directory ui/src/types/ holds the types. It has one file for each domain, such as agents.ts and tasks.ts. A domain file re-exports the types of that domain from the generated file and holds the hand-written types listed below. ui/src/types/index.ts re-exports every domain file with export type from "./<domain ". Components, stories, fixtures and new code import types from @/types, or from @/types/<domain . A file in ui/src/types/ has types only and no runtime code, so a story can import a response type without loading the API client. ui/src/test/typesOnly.test.ts fails when a file there compiles to JavaScript. A domain module in ui/src/lib/api/ re-exports the types of its domain from @/types/<domain , so older imports from @/lib/api still work. The API client types (ApiError, ApiClient, ApiTarget, Transport) and the narrowing functions stay in ui/src/lib/api/. Comment and Event would shadow DOM globals, so types/tasks.ts re-exports them as TaskComment and TaskEvent. Where the spec has a plain string and the UI needs a union, the module narrows it at one place, such as taskPriority(task). The types follow the spec exactly. A list that Go can return as null is T[] | null, and an optional field is optional, so the code handles both. Test data is a complete response, not a partial literal; the factories in ui/src/test/fixtures/apiFixtures.ts fill the fields a test does not check. These types stay hand-written. Each response type among them has a comment that says why the spec does not cover it: - Responses that internal/api/server.go serves outside the command registry: the agent event stream (AgentEvent), the tasks WebSocket frame (TaskEventHint), the mail WebSocket frame (MailHint), the operations WebSocket frame (OperationHint), and the image, team, and workflow image archive imports. - The transcript calls of audit.ts, which the spec describes only as objects. - Request bodies and filters, such as CreateAgentSpec and TaskFilters, and types that the UI derives, such as AgentPromptLayer. Code splitting The first download contains only the shell: the titlebar with the search field, the sidebar navigation and agent list, the hosts line, the "needs you" context, the providers, host selection, and the agent workspace frame. Everything else loads with React.lazy when it first renders: - the pages in TerminalsRoutes (Home, Tasks, Inbox, Activity, Metrics, the version comparison, Images, Workflows, Sources, and Settings), the host selector, and the nested image and settings routes of routes.tsx; - NeedsYouLive, which reads the counts and rows of "needs you", the task lookup of the search field, and the workspace manager dialog; - every agent workspace tab and the Goal task drawer in AgentWorkspace; - the Needs you card (tasks/NeedsYouCard.tsx) in the Work tab and the Home and Inbox lists, because it brings the Markdown renderer; - the TipTap editor (tasks/TaskMarkdownEditor.tsx): MarkdownEditor in TaskMarkdown.tsx is a lazy wrapper, so MarkdownContent never loads TipTap; - the full role text of the New agent form (role/RoleMarkdown.tsx), so the form loads the Markdown renderer only after Show role ; - the file viewer of FileBrowser, with CodeMirror, its languages, and the highlighted preview; - the onboarding tour overlay and the Changelog window with CHANGELOG.md. The shell keeps only the ? menu, the steps, and the version check. components/LazyBoundary wraps each place that renders a lazy component. It sits inside the layout that stays mounted, so the titlebar, the sidebar, and the settings navigation stay visible. While a chunk downloads, the content area shows a role="status" text, Loading… . A later open uses the loaded module. A navigation inside the router is a transition, so the previous screen stays until the next one is ready. If a chunk fails to load, for example after an update or when the server is unreachable, the boundary shows This screen failed to load. and Reloading discards unsaved input. with a Reload button. It never retries by itself. A new route path, tab, or file clears the error. vite.desktop.config.ts puts vendor libraries in named chunks with build.rolldownOptions.output.codeSplitting.groups, the Vite 8 replacement for manualChunks: react (React, React DOM, and the router), codemirror, tiptap (TipTap and ProseMirror), xterm, and markdown (react-markdown, remark, rehype, and highlight.js). One more group, api, holds the app's own HTTP client (src/lib/api/, lib/daemons.ts, and lib/storage.ts): the shell and most lazy screens share it, and without the group the bundler folds it into the entry chunk once enough screens share it. Only react and api are part of the first download; each other group loads with the first screen that needs it. Keep a group narrow: if the shell imports one module of a group, the whole group becomes part of the first download. npm run bundle:budget, a step of make frontend-check, has three limits in bytes before compression. The entry chunk is limited to 351,000 bytes. The entry chunk plus its static imports is limited to 723,000 bytes. All JavaScript chunks, lazily loaded ones included, are limited to 3,383,000 bytes. The step fails when a size is over its limit. The budget does not measure CSS or the start time on a device. Component boundaries The public screen components keep their existing imports and properties. Their internal modules separate form state, requests, and presentation: - terminals/create-agent owns the single creation draft, source and image loading, request validation, and the Target, Identity, Runtime, Loop, and Lifecycle sections. Submission keeps creation separate from a retry of Start. - terminals/server-dialog separates HTTPS and SSH forms from host-operation events and progress. The operation result remains separate from connectivity. - components/file-browser separates the tree, toolbar, viewer, dialogs, and file actions. FileBrowser keeps the public API and source reset boundary. - agents/configuration owns the configuration blocks. The existing draft and commit modules still own the single Save operation for the page. - mailbox is one two-pane mailbox for Inbox and the agent's Mailbox: Mailbox holds the box switch and the panes, MailboxList, MailboxLetter and MailboxCompose render them, MailboxTaskAnswer is the answer form of a task question, mailboxModel holds the pure readings, and mailQueries the query keys and the live refetch. - Tasks separates local view state, panel sizing, query composition, and write actions. TaskDetail keeps one draft with its original revision. Its fields, relations, history, and dialogs render that state without another server cache. - components/tui-screen separates the xterm lifecycle and sizing hook and the tmux scrollback hook from the toolbar, compose, and help markup. The input handler stays stable, so a render does not recreate the terminal. - lib/audit.ts and lib/auditCodex.ts read an audit record through handler tables keyed by event kind, harness message type, and Codex item type. components/audit renders each row kind in its own small component and keeps the full log's filter and paging state in hooks. - pages/audit-log separates the URL query and the polled iteration list from the list and tag editor markup. Shared helpers and styles Helpers that more than one screen needs live in ui/src/lib/, and each name is declared once: - lib/errors.ts exports errorText(error). It returns the message of any Error, ApiError included, and String(error) for other values. A plain error therefore shows Failed to fetch, without the class name. - lib/ids.ts exports idempotencyKey(prefix). It returns crypto.randomUUID(), or prefix-<time -<random when the WebView has no randomUUID. - lib/statusTone.ts exports flexibleStatusLabel(status) for a flexible task status. lib/tasks.ts alone exports taskStatusLabel(task), the label of any task. Styles are Tailwind utilities on the element. The @theme block of ui/src/index.css names the dense text sizes and the radii between the --radius steps: | Utility | Value | | --- | --- | | text-nano, text-micro, text-tiny, text-caption, text-meta | 9, 10, 10.5, 11, 11.5 px | | text-ui, text-body-sm, text-body, text-body-lg, text-title | 12, 12.5, 13, 14, 15 px | | rounded-hair, rounded-xs, rounded-chip, rounded-sm, rounded-control | 1.5, 2, 5, 6, 7 px | | rounded-md, rounded-panel, rounded-lg, rounded-card, rounded-xl | 8, 9, 10, 12, 14 px | The text sizes set only font-size, so the element keeps its line height. Sizes, spacing, and ring widths use the 4 px spacing scale: h-6.5 is 26 px. cn() in lib/utils.ts tells tailwind-merge about the new names. Without that, tailwind-merge reads text-ui as a color and drops the color class next to it. When you add a text size or a radius to @theme, add it to cn() too. ui/src/lib/utils.test.ts fails when the two lists differ. ui/src/test/arbitraryPxPolicy.test.ts fails when production code under ui/src or ui/store uses a class of the form utility-[Npx]. Composite values, such as grid-cols-[76px minmax(0,1fr)], are allowed. The shadcn primitives under ui/src/components/ui/ are not checked, so they stay the same as upstream. Story files are not checked: a story sizes its demo frame in pixels. An inline style is only for a value that the code calculates at run time, such as a column width or a CSS variable. Text fields use the shared controls: Input, Textarea and CommandInput under ui/src/components/ui/, SearchInput for a search field with an icon, and TaskMarkdownEditor for task Markdown. These controls turn off spell checking, autocorrection and autocapitalization in the browser, in Desktop and in the Android shell, so WebKit does not change names, paths or identifiers. The defaults are in components/ui/input-assistance.ts. To turn one on for a single field, pass the prop, for example <Input autoCorrect="on" / . ui/src/test/textInputPolicy.test.ts fails when production code outside components/ui renders a <textarea , an <input of a type other than checkbox, radio or file, or a contentEditable element. A CSS file is only for a rule that utilities cannot express clearly: pseudo-elements, a media query for one widget, or a rule that must override another component. ui/src/pages/tasks/tasks.css lists the rules it keeps and gives the reason for each at its top. Designer workflow in Storybook A designer sees and changes the UI in Storybook, not in the app. The stories live next to the components (ui/src/components/ / .stories.tsx, ui/src/pages/ / .stories.tsx) and in the mockups (ui/src/mockups/ / .stories.tsx). Shared values are in ui/src/fixtures/ (agents.ts, tasks.ts, images.ts, operations.ts, metrics.ts, activity.ts, and the fixed clock time.ts). The decorators are in ui/src/storybook/decorators.tsx. npx tsc -b compiles the stories with the app, so a change of the props of a view component breaks the stories that use it until they compile. Development tells how to run Storybook and why it never reaches a daemon. Style rules - Character. Tariboy UI is shadcn/ui on Tailwind v4, with achromatic metal neutrals (hue 250, chroma at most .008), one blue accent, and Geist Variable. A design reads as a control surface for dense operator tooling (agent consoles, task trees, image and host tables), not as a marketing page. - Colors are always semantic tokens, never hex and never a Tailwind color scale. So light and dark both work. viewLintPolicy.test.ts enforces it. - Surfaces: bg-background, bg-card, bg-popover, bg-muted, bg-accent, bg-secondary. - Text: text-foreground, text-muted-foreground, text-card-foreground, text-primary-foreground. - Emphasis: bg-primary with text-primary-foreground. - Danger: text-destructive, bg-destructive/10. - Lines: border border-border, border-t, border-b, border-input. - Focus: ring-ring/50, focus-visible:border-ring. - CSS custom properties are for inline styles and for what utilities do not cover: --background, --foreground, --card, --popover, --primary, --secondary, --muted, --accent, --destructive, --border, --input, --ring, --radius, each with a -foreground partner where it carries text, plus --sidebar and --chart-1 to --chart-5. - --background is a window-wide gradient. background-color and color-mix() drop a gradient value. In an inline background-color and in color-mix(…, var(--background-base)), use --background-base. bg-background resolves to it. Only the window itself paints --background. - Status is a system, not a color choice. --status-running is in progress. --status-failed is failed or out of budget. --primary is waiting on the customer. --status-queued, --status-done and --status-stopped are quiet text. A fill is only for what is alive and what needs a person: text-status-running with bg-status-running/13, text-status-failed with bg-status-failed/12, text-primary with bg-primary/12. Open, done and cancelled get text-muted-foreground and no fill. - Elevation has two levels, never three. --raise is for a selected row and the active segment of a segmented control. --lift is for the content island and menus. The island is bg-card, rounded-[var(--panel-radius)] and shadow-[var(--lift)], and it sits on a --background chrome without borders. - Typography. Body is text-sm. Secondary meta is text-xs. Headings are text-base or text-lg with font-medium or font-semibold. Task keys, image refs, digests, paths and terminal output are font-mono. Identifiers, durations and timestamps are font-mono with tabular-nums, so they line up down a column. - Controls, spacing and radius. Buttons are h-8 (h-7 for sm, h-6 for xs). Inputs are h-8. Spacing is gap-1, gap-2, gap-3, p-3 and p-4. Radius comes from --radius: 0.625rem through rounded-md, rounded-lg and rounded-xl. Console surfaces are denser: rows 30px, buttons 24, 26 and 28px, pills 17, 19 and 20px, radii 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 12 and 14px. - Icons are lucide-react: 16px at the default control size, 14px at sm. Never use emoji. - Dark mode is the class .dark on an ancestor (<html in the app). ThemeProvider sets it, and ThemeToggle is the titlebar control. Storybook has a theme switch in its toolbar. - Content is realistic product content: agents builder, reviewer, packager, docs-bot; images worker:v1, bare:latest; hosts This daemon (local) and build-01; task keys such as TB-142. - Where the truth is. The tokens are in ui/src/index.css. The API of a component is its props type in its source file. - Storybook compiles src/index.css with Tailwind over the same src sources, so every utility works in a story. An inline style with var(--token) is only for what utilities do not cover. The other designer paths have no data access to forbid. - Take types from @/types. A view takes the narrowest type it needs: Pick<… or its own XProps. - A component without a view file: copy its markup into a local view part ui/src/mockups/<page /<Name .view.tsx (or ui/src/mockups/<component /<Name .view.tsx), change it there, show it in the mockup story, and ask in handoff.md to split the component. Do not edit the container. - A change of a token or a primitive variant lists every affected story in ## Tokens and styles of the handoff. Check those stories in both themes. - See a story. Run cd ui && npm run story:shot -- <story-id <light|dark <width . The command builds storybook-static when there is no build, when a file the build reads is newer than it, or with --rebuild (it prints the reason on stderr), serves it on a loopback port, and writes a PNG of iframe.html?id=<story-id &viewMode=story&globals=theme:<theme . It prints the path of the PNG, ui/.story-shots/<story-id .<theme .<width .png. Check each changed story in light and dark, at the smallest supported width (360 px) and at 1024 px. The story id is the title and the story name in kebab case, joined by --: mockups-home--width-360 (Storybook puts a hyphen before the digits of the export name Width360). All ids are in storybook-static/index.json. - Build stories from the fixture factories: agentRow({ name: "builder", state: "running" }). A mockup story uses parameters: { layout: "fullscreen" } and one story for each supported width (Width360, Width390, Width820, Width1024, Width1180) with withWidth(width). - Put handoff.md next to its mockup. A change of one component without a page mockup has ui/src/mockups/<component /handoff.md next to <Component .stories.tsx (title: "Mockups/<Component "). - Hand off a change: 1. Work in a branch designer/<task -<topic of your own worktree. 2. Before you hand off, run make designer-check. After scripts/npm-ci-locked.sh ui (about 30 seconds in a new worktree), it takes the host check slot and runs six steps: the type check, oxlint on the files changed against origin/main (uncommitted files included), ui-fmt-check (oxfmt), one Vitest run of viewLintPolicy.test.ts, storybookSafety.test.ts, storyNetwork.test.tsx, arbitraryPxPolicy.test.ts and textInputPolicy.test.ts, Knip (ui-dead-code) and build-storybook. It fails if one step failed. It does not run ui-api-types, ui-lint, the rest of ui-test, ui-branding, ui-bundle-budget and docs: the developer's pull request runs them. 3. Run git rebase origin/main and git push origin <branch . Report the branch on your own TARIDESIGN task in a comment that mentions the PM. The developer opens the pull request. 4. When make frontend-check fails in the developer's pull request on a designer file, the developer fixes a mechanical error (the format) in that pull request and says so on the developer's own task. For any other error, the developer reports it to the PM on the developer's own task, and the PM orders the fix from the designer. - Propose a new prop in handoff.md. Do not add it to a container. A developer change that breaks a story fixes the story in the same commit. | Paths | Designer | Developer | | --- | --- | --- | | ui/src/index.css, ui/src/components/ui/ .tsx | Owns colors, radii, density, shadows and the cva() variants | Changes only accessibility and behavior, after agreement with the designer | | ui/src/ / .view.tsx | Owns markup and styles. The developer follows these rules: - Own the props type of every view file. A change of a props type changes the stories in the same commit, and npx tsc -b fails until they compile. - Keep data hooks, @/lib/api, react-query, router hooks, state and handlers in containers and pages. A view takes props and callbacks and returns JSX. - Import types from @/types in new code. - Move a component to the view layer one component at a time. Split data and markup, rename the markup file to .view.tsx, and add or move its story. - Change the primitives in ui/src/components/ui/ only for accessibility and behavior, and tell the designer. - To implement a handoff, open the pull request from the designer's branch. Write the answer to each open question under it in handoff.md, add the first line Implemented in #<PR , and keep the final type in the view file. If the handoff asks to split a component, split it and move the local view part of the mockup into the new view file. - When a props change breaks a story, fix the story in the same commit and tell the designer on the task of the change. - Keep the Storybook setup and its checks (ui-storybook, make designer-check) green. Fixtures - A fixture file ui/src/fixtures/<domain .ts is typed with @/types and is a complete response value, as the rule in API types says. - Each file exports a factory <entity (over: Partial<T = {}): T with complete defaults, such as agentRow, taskItem, imageSummary, operation and metricsReport. A story writes only the fields that matter. - Each domain also exports a set of edge states: empty, one, many (50 items) and longText (long names and texts, for truncation and wrapping), such as agentRows.many and taskItems.longText. The exception is activity.ts: it exports one factory of totals, taskActivityTotals, not a list, so it has no set. - A fixture of a shape that only the UI uses takes the type of the prop of its view, as agents.ts does with HomeAgentLink. - All dates come from NOW in ui/src/fixtures/time.ts, or from minutesAgo() and hoursAgo(), which count back from it. A story passes NOW as now to a component that takes one, so "5 min ago" is the same on each run and in each screenshot. - A value that only one story uses stays in that story file. - ui/src/test/fixtures/apiFixtures.ts re-exports the factories that stories use, so tests keep their imports. A fixture never imports that file, because it is test code. Handoff format A handoff.md has these sections, in this order. It is in the language of the designer's request, and the interface texts in it are in English. 1. # Handoff: <page or component , then one line with the date, the key of the design task and the story ids, such as mockups-home--width-1024. 2. ## What changed: each visible change with the story that shows it. 3. ## New props: a table with the columns Component, Prop, Type, Meaning and Source of data. The type uses @/types names or a narrow type such as Pick<AgentRow, "name" | "state" . The source names the API call or the state, or says "unknown". The designer only proposes a prop. The developer owns the final type. 4. ## Changed and removed props: the same table for a prop whose type or meaning changes, and for a removed prop. 5. ## States: each state with its story id (empty, loading, error, long text, many items). 6. ## Behavior: what happens on click, keyboard, hover and focus. Name a change of behavior as a change. 7. ## Texts: every interface text that the stories do not show, such as API errors, toasts, aria-label values and tooltips. 8. ## Accessibility: labels, focus order, focus return after a dialog closes, how an error is announced, and the contrast of new token pairs. 9. ## Layout at widths: the layout at each supported width, at least at 360 px, each with the story or the story:shot width that shows it. 10. ## Screenshots: a table of the shots that show the change, with the columns Story id, Theme and Width. The PNG files are not in git. The developer repeats each shot with npm run story:shot. 11. ## Tokens and styles: new or changed tokens in ui/src/index.css and changed cva() variants. List every affected story. 12. ## Acceptance criteria: numbered criteria that the developer and the reviewer check one by one. 13. ## Open questions: questions for the developer. WebView storage ui/src/lib/storage.ts owns all access to localStorage and sessionStorage in the Desktop UI and the Store UI. It declares every key in one registry with its area, name, version, parser, and fallback value. Other modules call readKey, writeKey, and removeKey with a key from that registry. The unit test ui/src/test/webStoragePolicy.test.ts fails when production code under ui/src or ui/store uses localStorage, sessionStorage, or window.dispatchEvent directly. It scans the sources because the lint policy has no rule for it. Tests and fixtures still seed raw values, so they detect a change of a stored format. Storage access is best effort. A missing value, a value the parser rejects, broken JSON, and storage that throws (blocked, private mode) all read as the fallback value. A failed write returns false and does not throw, so the interface keeps its state in memory until a reload. A read that finds a bad value does not delete it; the next write replaces it. Values are never logged, because some of them are tokens. Key names did not change when the registry was added, so saved state survives upgrades. A new key uses the form <area :<purpose :v<N , and the registry test requires a versioned name to end with its version. When a format changes incompatibly, the key gets a new name with the next version. The old name stays in the registry only so it can be read once, like terminals:workspace:v1. Initial host discovery and recovery both establish a silent baseline: current questions populate the in-app indicators, but do not replay native notifications. Observed letter IDs and per-host snapshots exist only in React memory for the current Desktop session. They are not written to Web Storage or persisted by the daemon, and current-session ID tracking deduplicates repeated hints and snapshots. For a newly observed unread agent question after the baseline, the coordinator asks the native bridge to show one notification with only host id, notification id (the letter id), and task key in its activation payload. Native permission denial, unsupported notification delivery, and send failures are fallbacks: they do not alter the authoritative HTTP snapshot or remove in-app attention. Activation uses the original explicit host, marks the exact letter read, refreshes that host, and navigates to /tasks?host=<hostId &task=<key (the packaged hash route is #/tasks?host=<hostId &task=<key ), where the task detail is selected. A failed read does not block that navigation, and an unresolved remote host is never replaced with local authority. Task changes arrive over the resumable /api/tasks/ws?after=<sequence socket. Hints trigger typed HTTP refetches; they never replace authoritative task responses. A surface opens the socket only once it knows the host's current sequence, read from the authoritative HTTP snapshot it already loads, so it never asks the daemon to replay the whole task log. Remote targets map HTTP(S) to WS(S) and put the existing bearer token in the WebSocket query because browser sockets cannot set an Authorization header. Queue settings expose explicit pool membership, edited with the revisioned pool route, the workflow binding with the statuses of the image, and queue secrets. The UI does not edit a workflow definition, and it does not infer phases from title prefixes or assignee. Operator history remains available after completion. See Task workflows. The first state that matches wins: | State | When | | --- | --- | | error | the agent state is error or failed, it has a halt reason whose halt kind is not idle limit, it has an error reason, or a budget is exhausted. The state carries the reason. | | needs you · n | n is more than 0 (see below) | | working | the agent state is running; the elapsed time starts at current iteration started at.
