Host workspaces A workspace is a named, independent list of registered hosts in one app window. Settings → Hosts has a Manage workspaces… button. When there are two or more workspaces, it also has a selector that lists them with a check on the current one, followed by New workspace… and Manage workspaces… . Choosing a workspace narrows the agent list, the hosts line, the search, the Tasks and Inbox counts, and Home to that workspace's hosts, so an empty workspace shows no agents. Settings → Hosts stays open after the pick. Home of an empty workspace shows <name has no agents yet with a Manage workspaces button. Polling continues for every host, so the manager can show each host as ready or offline, and agents on hosts outside the current workspace keep running: a workspace filters the window, it does not isolate hosts. Agents and tasks live on their daemon, so a host in two workspaces shows the same agents and tasks in both. Default is built in and cannot be renamed or deleted. A host may belong to several workspaces. A host that no workspace lists, such as the local daemon or a host registered before workspaces existed, is in Default. Add host puts the new host in the current workspace only, for SSH and HTTPS alike; adding the same alias or URL again makes a second host entry. The manager dialog creates a workspace (Enter or Create workspace ; blank names are ignored) and selects it, and renames a custom workspace as its name is typed without ever saving a blank one. Add to… and a click on a target workspace add a host there and keep it in the current one. Remove takes a host out of the selected workspace only; a host left in no workspace returns to Default, so the manager offers no Remove for a host that only Default holds. Delete workspace asks inline; its hosts in no other workspace return to Default, and deleting the current workspace switches to Default. Remove host in a host's menu removes the host from the app and so from every workspace. The state is the WebView localStorage record app:workspaces:v2: {version: 2, workspaces: [{id, name, hosts: [hostId]}], active}, where the first entry is Default. When it is missing, the version 1 record app:workspaces:v1 ({version: 1, workspaces: [{id, name}], hostWorkspace: {hostId: workspaceId}, active}) is read once: each host keeps its one workspace, and a host without an entry stays in Default. The version 1 record is left in place. The state is local to one app installation and is not stored by any daemon, because hosts are the set of daemons rather than something one daemon owns. Malformed or unavailable storage falls back to Default only; unavailable storage keeps changes until the window closes. Switching agents and reconnects The former All tasks view, one task table across every host, is removed. /tasks shows one host at a time, with a host selector when the workspace has two or more hosts, and an old ?view=all URL opens /tasks. Selecting another agent in the sidebar while an agent workspace is open keeps the tab that is currently open and shows the new agent in it, so the same view answers the same question about the next agent. An unknown tab still falls back to Work, and a selected task in the ?task= query is dropped because it belongs to the agent being left. A sidebar agent selected from any other page opens on Work. A freshly created agent opens on Terminal. Start and Stop are in the agent header. The empty Terminal panel also has a Start button. When a known explicit server route temporarily loses its tunnel or its authoritative aggregate refresh fails, the Desktop retains its last successful server and agent snapshot in React memory rather than flashing the whole pane to an error. The live host badge and a local status message identify the unavailable/reconnecting state; that host's agent controls and cached sidebar agent rows are read-only until a successful refresh for the same host replaces the snapshot atomically. Cached data is never persisted or used as an API target, other server navigation remains available, and a missing host still fails closed rather than falling back to local authority. A reconnect never remounts a server page. An SSH host loses its endpoint while its tunnel reconnects and comes back on a new local port. Neither change is part of a page's identity: Tasks, Workflows, Stores, the Settings pages and an agent's Settings tab keep their loaded data, the open task, filters, scroll position and every unsaved draft. The route boundary keeps one tree shape and only dims the page and makes it inert under a single status line. A host object keeps its identity until one of its fields changes, so the sidebar poll does not restart page loads. While the host has no endpoint, background loads are skipped rather than failed. When the new endpoint arrives, each page re-reads once in place: the task list, the open task, the agent header, the agent's Settings and Mailbox. A background read that cannot reach the host (host not ready, network error) keeps the last data and shows no toast, because the host header in the left panel already reports the host as offline with its error. An explicit action such as Save , Create or Send still reports its failure. Its draft stays in the form, ready to send again once the host is back. Drafts live in tab memory only and are not queued for later delivery. The agent's Settings tab has four groups in order: - Model : coding tool, model, and effort. - Working folder : the current path and Change… , available while the agent is stopped. The editor includes Create directory if missing . - Autopilot : Only when given tasks or messages , or Also every with an interval in minutes. Stop a run after sets the soft timeout in minutes, with 0 for no limit. Interactive terminal is here too. - Spending limit : Day , Week , and Month USD limits, with the daemon's current spend beside each. 0 means no limit. Advanced starts collapsed. It contains Image , Schedule and timeouts , Goal , Mail , Hour budget (USD) , Environment , Retention and cleanup , and Other views . Schedule and timeouts holds the schedule builder, hard timeout in seconds, timeout and error policies, idle limit, and AI inactivity timeout. Its next scheduled start comes from the daemon and follows Save changes. A saved schedule can start runs even when Autopilot has no timer interval. Below Advanced, About names the image and host. The image links to the Library. Danger contains Delete agent . Start, Stop, and Restart stay in the agent header and apply immediately. Field values, including secrets, never enter the search. Matching Advanced sections and the working folder editor open temporarily. Clearing the query restores the full form and the previous disclosure state. Whitespace alone does not filter. No matches shows a message and Clear search . Schedule is a builder for the agent's RRULE (see Schedule). You select a mode and fill in its fields: None (no schedule), Every N minutes / hours , Daily (one time), Weekly (days and one time), Monthly (a day of the month or the last day, and one time), Once (a date and a time), or Custom RRULE (a text field for any rule). The builder shows a one-line summary and the rule it sends. Times are in the time zone of the daemon host, not of the browser. When the page loads a saved rule, the builder selects the mode that builds exactly that rule. If no mode does, for example a rule with two times or with UNTIL, it selects Custom RRULE and shows the rule unchanged. A rule you do not edit is not marked Changed . When you select another mode, the builder drops the saved DTSTART, and the daemon starts the new rule at the current minute. Every editable field belongs to one page-wide draft. A field is dirty when its normalized draft differs from the value last loaded. The field shows Changed . A sticky header at the top lists the unsaved count and groups, with Reset and Save changes while edits exist. The Advanced disclosure also counts its unsaved edits. Closing it keeps those drafts. Reset drops every draft. Save changes first validates every changed field in the browser and sends nothing while any is invalid. It opens Advanced or the folder editor when needed, clears a blocking search, and focuses the field. Then it sends only changed fields through the existing per-field endpoints. Requests run serially in the existing order, with harness before model and effort. The four budget limits and the two retention limits each save as one request. It stops at the first failure without sending the fields after it: acknowledged fields adopt the daemon's canonical values after a reload, while the failed field (with the server's reason beside it) and the ones never attempted stay dirty drafts, so the next Save sends only them. There is no batch endpoint, so a Save is not atomic. Harness and Interactive are saved with the page like every other field; they take effect the next time the agent starts and never restart it. Create directory if missing is saved with the working directory as one request: when it is on, Save sends the path with create: true, and the daemon makes a missing directory before it validates the path. After a successful Save the switch is off again. For a stopped agent, the working directory is edited with the selected host's directory autocomplete. Saving changes the CWD used by the next launch; it does not move files or start, stop, or restart the agent. Active agents show the current CWD read-only until they are stopped. Remote agent reads, directory suggestions, and saves all use the host identified by the agent route rather than whichever daemon was previously active. Refreshing live agent, image or host status does not replace an unsaved draft; the draft is discarded only when the agent or the host changes. The agent image is a draft field too; Copy digest , Cancel pending and Retry of a failed pending assignment stay immediate actions in an actions row that says they are not part of Save. Model and effort use the same grouped suggestions as agent creation, for the agent's host and the selected harness. Advanced → Schedule and timeouts exposes the positive AI inactivity timeout in seconds, defaulting to 1800 (30 minutes) per agent. When a running iteration exceeds it without an attributed AI-proxy request, the daemon reports state=error, which the agent header shows. The controls remain enabled because this signal does not stop the loop or iteration; the next request restores state=running. Ordinary creation starts at 1800 seconds, while Clone preserves the source agent's configured value. The Advanced → Mail section uses that same draft contract for the positive whole-number messages batch and messages max queue fields. New-agent drafts use a maximum queue of 100, while Clone keeps the source agent's configured value. Settings also renders the daemon-authoritative per-agent USD budget projection. The browser never recomputes spend. Older daemons simply omit the additive projection. The workspace header also consumes daemon-authoritative message status. The normal status refresh removes the indicator after processing or clearing lowers the queue. Without a halt, an error reason from the daemon is the error reason. It sends tmux's own copy-mode entry sequence (prefix C-b, then `) over the existing byte socket, and the toolbar then shows a persistent Viewing scrollback status, Page back / Page forward controls, and an Exit scrollback button. Live keystrokes are paused while tmux is in copy-mode; press q in the focused terminal or use Exit scrollback to return to live output. Every control is a labelled button reachable by keyboard. Because the browser has no authoritative tmux mode event, the status describes the state Tariboy requested , not a verified tmux mode, and it is cleared whenever q is typed in the terminal, Exit scrollback is used, the socket closes, the terminal identity changes, the session becomes absent, or the tile unmounts — leaving copy-mode any other way still strands the status, notably via Escape, which cancels under tmux's default emacs table (including from the toolbar's own Esc hotkey) but only clears the selection under copy-mode-vi, so the browser cannot infer it. Entering and leaving scrollback are both announced through a status region that stays in the DOM either way — a live region that unmounts announces nothing — and leaving via Exit scrollback returns keyboard focus to the Scrollback control, while leaving with q keeps focus in the terminal. tmux mouse reporting stays off, so wheel and drag input continue to belong to the inner harness TUI. What Scrollback browses is the tmux pane history , not xterm scrollback, and it is bounded: the shim sets each managed session's history-limit to 10,000 lines (tmux's own default is 2,000), so older output is discarded by tmux and cannot be recovered from the browser. Nothing about the history is persisted by the UI. The agent header's ⋯ menu has Run once… , only while the agent is enabled and not bare:latest, for interactive and non-interactive agents alike. It opens the Run once dialog, whose optional, memory-only one-shot text is sent to the route-selected host and affects only the newly requested iteration. Run once does not start the agent or persist the draft. A successful request closes the dialog and, when the Terminal tab shows an interactive terminal, reconnects its startup handling; a rejected request keeps the dialog and the draft for retry. Settings → Danger → Delete agent opens an in-app confirmation dialog. It names the agent and warns that its durable data is also removed. Confirm sends the existing force=true and purge=true request. While that request is pending, the dialog cannot be dismissed or submitted again. The workspace returns home only after success; on failure it keeps the dialog open, restores its controls, and reports the error so the operator can retry. Force-stop current run in the ⋯ menu is a separate action. It asks for confirmation in an in-app dialog, stops only the current iteration or session, and does not delete the agent or its durable data. An agent's Advanced → Retention and cleanup section edits its override of the server-wide iteration defaults with the page Save: each field shows 0 = server default (N), and the block lists the effective limits and that pruned iterations are archived with their database rows first. Secrets in Advanced → Environment are write-only. The section lists key names only. Removing a key and adding a key and value are page drafts applied by Save: a removal is shown as Will be removed until then, and a new value lives only in tab memory, is sent in a POST body and never in a URL, is never rendered, and is cleared once the daemon acknowledges it. Preview cleanup and Prune now stay immediate actions outside Save. The in-app retention prune is guarded by a confirmation dialog that names the operation as permanently destructive and bounds it to the current retention policy. Confirming dismisses the dialog and issues the real, non-dry-run prune; while it is in flight the destructive action is disabled and cannot be issued twice. A failure is reported beside that action inside the bounded destructive section, not in the dialog, so the operator can read it and retry. Previewing what the policy would remove stays a separate, unconfirmed action. Terminal connection outcomes are intentionally distinct: - 4404 is retried for a five-second startup grace because the agent engine and shim socket can become ready shortly after Start returns; - 1000/eof means the attached PTY ended and stops immediately; - abnormal transport closes retry with capped exponential delay while the view remains mounted. The Desktop SSH host dialog also keeps transport connectivity separate from the result of the current provision or update operation. It maps native phases into six ordered user-facing steps and retains a failed update result even if rollback restores a healthy old tunnel. Native stdout and stderr events are bounded diagnostic output, not lifecycle results; only an explicit error event or a failed host runtime state terminates the operation. Raw process output is collapsed under Technical details , while the main flow renders one actionable error and one primary next action. DaemonProvider also exposes daemon status.app version` to both host-list surfaces. Their compact Update action is derived only from a confirmed mismatch between that bundle version and the non-empty persisted/runtime remote daemon version. Unknown versions fail closed without an update indicator; the host editor retains its explicit manual update action. See [Development for source and generated-artifact verification.
description: React and xterm.js provide the Desktop control surface while host-local daemons remain API and WebSocket services.
title: Desktop web UI

content: Autopilot is the daemon-controlled iteration loop of a started agent. An agent has one on/off switch: Start turns the whole agent on (iterations, messages, Goal, and the interactive Terminal), and Stop turns all of it off. There is no separate Autopilot switch. Agents from the terminal-only bare:latest image never run autonomous iterations. To keep a non-bare agent from iterating on a timer, set its interval to 0. In Settings → Autopilot , select Only when given tasks or messages and click Save changes . A separate schedule under Advanced → Schedule and timeouts can still start runs. Set Schedule to None there to run only for messages, including Goal tasks. Trigger model While the agent is started, an iteration can start from: - a configured timer interval or schedule; or - an open letter in the agent's inbox, including a task.goal letter. Letters are durable. Sending a letter to the agent stores it in its inbox and nudges the loop. The runner includes the open letters in the next prompt. A request stays open until the agent replies to it; a notice closes when the iteration finishes normally. Harness errors, timeouts, and kills leave both open for bounded redelivery. Stopping the agent prevents new scheduled and message-triggered iterations. It does not delete open letters. A stop policy (on timeout=stop or on error=stop) halts the loop with an error reason. The agent stays started and shows the error state. Start it again to clear the reason and resume the loop. Configure conservatively Start with: - an image prompt that defines one coherent unit of work; - a long enough interval to inspect outcomes; - a soft timeout that fits normal work; - a hard timeout that bounds the worst case; - a low cost budget; - no external plugins sending mail until the timer path is understood. Set the interval and soft timeout in minutes under Settings → Autopilot . Also every sets a timer interval. Stop a run after sets the soft timeout, with 0 for no limit. Open Advanced → Schedule and timeouts for the schedule, hard timeout in seconds, and timeout and error policies. Set daily and monthly USD limits under Spending limit . Hourly and weekly limits are under Advanced → Hour and week budgets (USD) . Click Save changes at the top to apply the draft. During agent creation, the interval and timeouts are under Advanced → Autopilot . Activity shows trigger, iteration state, result, deadlines, audit, usage, and cost. For Claude and Codex harnesses, the audit is presented as a readable timeline of messages, reasoning, commands, skills, tool calls, and results; model and token metadata remains available on each AI call. A running soft deadline may be extended only before timeout enforcement starts. Controls - Start / Stop (agent header) — turn the agent on or off. From the CLI use tariboy agent start NAME and tariboy agent stop NAME. - Run once… (the ⋯ menu of the agent header, shown while the agent is enabled) — start one manual iteration immediately. It is available for both interactive and non-interactive agents; optional one-shot text, entered in its dialog, is appended only to that iteration's assembled prompt. - Force-stop current run (the ⋯ menu of the agent header) — after you confirm, immediately stop the current iteration or session; use when work is unsafe or stuck. - Budget — reject AI calls once the configured spend limit is reached. - Audit (Activity → Runs log ) — inspect each proxied AI request and tool timeline. Copy readable Markdown or export a ZIP for the selected iteration or all retained iterations. Exports contain sensitive agent data; review the warning before downloading them. After a force-stop, verify the Activity outcome and the agent's open letters before starting the agent again. A killed or failed iteration leaves its letters open for redelivery. Event-driven progression Mail is the layer behind message triggers. It lets agents, plugins, schedules and scripts wake work without polling. Begin with one sender writing to one agent, then add groups after the single-agent letter lifecycle is understood. Read an agent's inbox, sent letters and archive, with its dead letters, with tariboy mail inbox --as agent:NAME, sent and archive. See Mailbox architecture and the Mail reference for the complete contract.
description: Run bounded, observable iterations on timers and durable message triggers.
title: Autopilot

content: make build builds eight real binaries: | Binary | Role | | --- | --- | | tariboyd | The daemon — long-running, owns all durable state. | | tariboy | The operator CLI — human/CI client over the socket. | | tariboy-tasks | The Native Tasks client; installers also provide its ttasks alias. | | tariboy-mail | The mail client; installers also provide its tmail alias. | | tariboy-scripts | The agent client of the scripts plugin; installers also provide its tscripts alias. | | tariboy-shim | Runs one harness iteration under a watchdog. | | tariboy-store | A standalone image registry server. | | tariboy-plugin-telegram | The bundled Telegram mail and operator-surface plugin. | The daemon installs or refreshes the Telegram plugin from its sibling binary at startup. Optional external plugins are built and distributed independently. make build does not embed agent image sources or skills. Register a Store such as the tariboy Store ( Add tariboy Store on the Stores page, or tariboy store add tariboy https://github.com/alekzonder/tariboy-store.git) and build the desired image on each daemon that needs it. The daemon synthesizes only the reserved empty bare:latest image. Client/daemon version drift tariboy and the agent tool scripts read the X-Tariboy-Version header the daemon stamps on every response. When that version differs from the client's own build, the client prints a warning naming both versions and its own path, strictly on stderr . It does not change stdout or the exit code, so output parsing is unaffected. A daemon old enough to send no header produces no warning. This matters because packaged skill scripts and the agent tasks / i-am-done compatibility shims execute from the active image's image/skills directory: without the warning, a script too old to know a newer flag looks like it simply did nothing. scripts/whoami.sh prints both client version and daemon version for exactly this reason — it is the first command to run when the tools behave strangely. The authoritative operator command list is generated from the binary (tariboy --help-json) and documented in the command reference. Queue agent pools and triggers are configured with the operator ttasks client or operator REST, and pools also through tariboy compose. Workflow images are built and stored with tariboy workflow; see Workflow images and Task workflows. The three command surfaces tariboy <group <command — run by a human or CI against the daemon. Packaged skill-local scripts — run inside an agent over its per-agent socket. ttasks <verb — Native Tasks for operators and identity-bound agents.
description: Core binaries and the Telegram plugin built by make build.
title: Binaries & commands

content: Run inside an agent from the applicable packaged skill directory. Each scripts/ .sh launcher executes the skill's Python 3 standard-library client. Only the legacy tasks and i-am-done also have PATH compatibility shims. The scripts talk to the identity-bound per-agent socket selected by $TARIBOY TOOLS SOCKET; the daemon derives the agent identity server-side. For non-bare iterations, python3 is resolved to an absolute path from the final agent environment before the harness starts. An explicit agent PATH must therefore include it. | Tool | Purpose | | --- | --- | | scripts/whoami.sh | agent, cwd, current iteration | | scripts/status.sh [set …] | read / set the one-line status | | scripts/loop.sh done | finish this iteration (i-am-done) | | scripts/context.sh get / set <text | read / overwrite durable working memory | | scripts/goal.sh set <TASK-KEY | select an assigned active Goal for this iteration | | tmail inbox/sent/archive/show | read the mailbox | | tmail send --to P … / tmail reply ID TEXT | send a letter, answer one; --instant sends an instant letter | | tmail instant [--format text\|json] | for a harness hook: print the instant letters that wait for this iteration (POST /tools/mail/instant) | | scripts/schedule.sh add/ls/cancel | agent-owned scheduled wake-ups | | tscripts run/schedule/rerun/ls/runs/logs/cancel/rm | local asynchronous commands and run history | | tariboy assessment add --file PATH / ls [--history] / show ID | record an assessment (needs assessments); read assessments (open to every agent). ls returns the latest assessment of each iteration and task; --history returns every assessment | | GET /tools/group/info, status, observe/{member}, POST /tools/group/loop | group coordination; group sends are tmail send --to group:<g or agent:<member | tariboy-tasks is installed globally with the ttasks alias. Packaged daemons also expose it through a shared runtime bin/ttasks symlink on their baseline PATH, so fresh Desktop agents can use it before optional CLI installation. An explicit agent PATH override must retain that directory or another installed ttasks. A non-empty TARIBOY TOOLS SOCKET selects its identity-bound agent mode and a missing or unreachable socket fails closed; without the variable it uses the host Unix daemon socket as the customer actor. Images that enable plugins: [{name: tasks}] also get the bare tasks legacy compatibility shim. See Native Tasks for the command flow. tariboy-scripts is installed globally with the tscripts alias, and the daemon links it as runtime bin/tscripts in the same way as ttasks and tmail. It replaces scripts.py of the scripts skill and prints the same output, errors and exit codes. It works only in agent mode: without TARIBOY TOOLS SOCKET it exits 2. The skill launcher scripts/scripts.sh stays a thin launcher, exec tscripts "$@", like tasks.sh and mail.sh. --json, or TARIBOY TOOLS JSON=1, prints the result as compact JSON. tscripts --version prints the client build. Exit codes: - 0: the command succeeded. - 1: the daemon refused the request. The client prints the message of the daemon. - 2: the command line is wrong, TARIBOY TOOLS SOCKET is not set, or the socket is not reachable. On a task that follows a queue's workflow the daemon assigns the work, and ttasks done, ttasks update --status, and ttasks ready --claim do not apply. The agent reads ttasks workflow get KEY, sets declared artifacts with ttasks artifacts set|ls|show, and leaves its status with ttasks advance KEY --outcome NAME --from STATUS, where --from makes a retried advance fail with status changed instead of applying twice. advance waits for the transition's check scripts and exits non-zero on a rejection or failure, naming the next command; --no-wait returns the pending request at once. ttasks workflow runs KEY and ttasks workflow log KEY RUN show what the scripts did. ttasks workflow move, ttasks cancel, ttasks requeue, and the ttasks queue commands are operator-only. Workflow scripts themselves never receive the tools socket. tariboyd normally selects and persists one sticky assigned task per enabled agent, then stamps its key and top-level root onto the AI-proxy lease before the harness starts. If an iteration starts without a task, the agent may create or claim one through ttasks and run scripts/goal.sh set <TASK-KEY . The task must be active and assigned to that agent. Subsequent requests use the new task/root attribution; earlier requests remain unattributed. A second call with a different key is rejected. Task priority is one of P0 (Critical), P1 (High), P2 (Normal), or P3 (Low). New tasks default to P2; set or change it explicitly with: ttasks show, list commands, and --json output include priority. Roots and nested siblings are returned in priority order (P0 through P3), then by their manual position within the same priority bucket. Unknown flags are rejected A flag that no command branch reads is a hard error: the script prints unknown flag … and exits 2. The check runs after the request is built but before it is sent, so nothing reaches the daemon. Older builds dropped an unread flag silently and exited 0, which is how ttasks update --priority could look like it worked while changing nothing. tscripts run and tscripts schedule have a -- separator: flags are parsed up to it, and everything after it is taken verbatim for the local command — that is why -- curl --silent URL hands --silent to curl. No other command has one, so elsewhere an argument that starts with -- cannot be passed through: it is always read as a flag, and the token after it as its value. Use the --flag=--value form there, which keeps the value inside a single token. Durable scripts Scripts run shell commands in the agent's workdir without blocking its current iteration. Like an iteration, each run first sources the global and agent shell scripts, so their exports, such as tokens, reach the command. Queue one run, or create a fixed-delay recurring definition: Each run's combined stdout and stderr is kept in its own agent scripts log. Exit 0 records success; every other exit, including 2, records failure. Both send a script.result letter from system:scripts so the next iteration can act. The letter carries script/run IDs, name, mode, status, optional exit code, and the absolute log path, without embedding stdout or stderr. Read that file when the result details are needed. The one exception is the quiet exit code 111, available to the script as TARIBOY QUIET EXIT: a recurring run that exits with it publishes nothing and keeps its schedule. The run and log remain visible. Recurring runs start once immediately, wait the configured delay after completion, and never overlap. The --quiet-exit CODE flag is deprecated; see scripts.
description: Run packaged skill-local scripts inside an agent for identity, status, loop control, context, messaging, schedules, and durable work.
title: Agent capability scripts

content: tariboy compose (internal/compose) brings up a whole set of Stores, workflows, images, task queues, agents, and groups declaratively from a Tariboycompose.yaml. compose up starts the daemon if it is down. The Compose reference gives a complete file, every field, the phase order and every verb. The Compose decisions page gives the behavior in special cases: a partial failure, a Store that is not available, a version conflict, an entity in use, an entity removed from the file, a second up, secrets, --dry-run, versions and migration. Verbs: up, down, build, ps, status, start/stop/restart/kill, rm, exec, logs, validate, pack, unpack, and the deprecated aliases archive and import. Flags include -f/--file, -v/--volumes, --no-start, --dry-run, --tail, --daemon, -o/--output, --no-build, --archive, --yes. See Moving a project with pack and unpack. compose down then up preserves data by default; --volumes is the purge path. A plain down removes each agent in mode keep: the stopped agent row stays, so up re-provisions it. compose rm removes a stopped agent in mode remove: the agent is gone, and its history stays. See Removing an agent. down, stop and kill skip a member that is absent on the daemon, so a partly present project still cleans up; any other error still fails the command. start and restart of an absent member fail. Compose owns agent runtime choices: harness, model, effort, interactive and loop settings, CWD, and environment. An agent is interactive only when its harness.interactive is true; compose always sends the value explicitly, so the create endpoint's interactive default does not apply. loop.enabled (default true) is the agent's on/off switch: compose up starts an agent whose value is true and stops one whose value is false. Schema-v2 image manifests supply none of those defaults; they contain only plugins and the ordered prompt template. Compose may build an image from an original relative context, but portable runnable image artifacts do not replace that source directory for later rebuilds. An agent may optionally override its per-agent Goal settings; omitted values keep the daemon default or current value: wait customer timeout must be a positive whole-second duration. The compose file File name If you do not give -f FILE, a verb looks for the file in the current directory, in this order: 1. Tariboycompose.yaml. 2. tariboy-compose.yaml, the earlier default name. If the directory has both files, the verb stops with an error that names both. Remove one file, or give -f. If the directory has neither file, the error also names both. With -f, the verb reads that file and does not look for another one. The rule applies to every verb that reads the file, including validate and pack. A compose archive stores the file as compose.yaml and keeps its original name in the archive metadata. Version 1 and version 2 The version key selects the schema. The values 1 and 2 are valid. - Version 1 has the sections images (with context), groups, agents, and task queues. A version 1 file works as before. - Version 2 also has the tariboy key and the stores and workflows sections, and new source fields for images. If a version 1 file uses a version 2 key (tariboy, stores, a non-empty workflows, or an image path, store, source, tag or version), the error tells you to declare version: 2. An empty workflows: {}, as written by older team exports, is accepted in version 1 and ignored. The parser is strict in both versions: an unknown field in any section is an error. The version 2 sections are: | Section | Fields | Rules | | --- | --- | --- | | stores | git and ref, or path | Exactly one of git and path. git is an https://HOST/PATH URL without a user name, a password, a query or a fragment. ref is a branch, a tag or a commit, and is valid only with git. | | workflows | path, or store and source, and optional tag and version | Exactly one of path and store. source names the entry in the Store; it defaults to the entry name. tag is latest (the default) or a SemVer version. version is a SemVer version. | | images | path, or store and source, and optional tag and version | The same rules as workflows, but tag is any image tag except . and ... context is version 1 syntax: in version 2, use path. | | task queues, agents, groups | The same fields as in version 1 | See Task queues and pools, Agent settings and Group settings. In version 2, the references must name entries of the file, as listed below. | A relative path is resolved from the directory of the compose file. In version 2, these references must name an entry of the same file: - The image of an agent (the name without the tag) must be in images. - The group of an agent must be in groups. This rule also applies in version 1. - Each agent of a pool must be in agents. This rule also applies in version 1. - The responsible agent of a queue must be in agents. This rule also applies in version 1. - The workflow of a queue must be in workflows. If the value has a STORE/ prefix, that Store must be in stores, and it must be the store of the workflow entry. - The store of a workflow or an image must be in stores. In version 1, an agent image and a queue workflow can name objects outside the file, as before. Stores, workflows and images compose up applies the stores, workflows and images sections in its first three phases. compose build applies only these three phases. A team import (team.import.yaml and the archive import) does not apply them: it refuses a file with stores, workflows or an image with store, and the error tells you to apply the file with compose up. Stores For each Store of the file, the stores phase does one of these steps: | Daemon state | up | | --- | --- | | No Store with this name | Registers it with POST /api/stores. A path is sent as an absolute path. A relative path is resolved from the directory of the compose file. | | The Store has another source | Fails the Store and changes nothing. To change the source, run tariboy store rm NAME, then up. | | A git Store at another ref | Checks the Store out at the file's ref (POST /api/stores/{name}/ref), then refreshes it. An empty ref means the default branch. | | A git Store | Refreshes it (POST /api/stores/{name}/refresh) on every up. The Store is changed when the commit moved, else ok. | | A path Store | Reads it with GET /api/stores/{name}. The daemon reads the directory again. The Store is ok when the read succeeds. | up never refreshes a path Store. A refresh of a local Store that is a git checkout runs git pull --ff-only in your directory. Update that directory yourself. The source is compared as text: the git URL without surrounding spaces, or the clean absolute path. Thus https://example.com/a.git and https://example.com/a are different sources. up registers only an https git URL, so a Store that you registered with ssh gives a source conflict. Builds and versions A workflow entry builds with POST /api/workflow-images/build, from STORE/SOURCE or from the absolute path. The workflow builds on every up. A build of a version that the daemon already has, with the same content, publishes nothing and is ok. The name in Workflowfile.yaml must equal the entry key, else the entry fails before the build. For a Store source, up reads the name through POST /api/workflow-images/validate, which changes nothing. After the build, up makes sure that the entry's tag NAME:TAG exists. A workflow build publishes only the tags latest and its version, so tag is one of these. A version tag without version works as version: the source must give that version. An image entry from a path builds as a version 1 image with context does, but with the entry's tag. It builds on every up, and it is ok when NAME:TAG keeps its digest. An image entry from a Store builds with POST /api/images/build with name, tag and source: STORE/SOURCE. It builds only when NAME:TAG was built from another image version than the Store gives now. This is the rule of the automatic Store builds. A change in the Store without a new image version does not reach the image. version selects the version that the source must give. up reads the version before the build: - For a Store source, up reads the version that the daemon reads from the Store after the refresh. - For a path source, up reads image version from Tariboyfile.yaml or workflow version from Workflowfile.yaml. If the version differs from the file, the entry fails before the build, and its tag stays on the build it had: up compares the version again after the build. If the source changes between the first read and the build, the tag already moved to the new build, and the entry still fails with the same error. A source without a version gives the source gives no version. Updates To update an image or a workflow, change the source: commit a new version to the Store, or change the ref. The next up refreshes the Store, builds the new version and moves the tag to it. An agent on that tag gets the new image as its pending image and adopts it on its next iteration. A queue that follows the tag moves to the new build. A queue pinned with STORE/NAME is bound to the new digest in the queue bindings phase. A Store that is not available A Store fails when the daemon cannot reach it: no network, a wrong URL, a ref that does not exist, a path that does not exist, or another source under the same name. Every workflow and image from this Store is then skipped, and so are the agents on those images and the queue bindings of those workflows. Entries from a path and from other Stores still apply. up exits non-zero: A second up A second up on unchanged sources refreshes each git Store, builds each path image and each workflow again, and builds no Store image. The path builds and the workflow builds give the digests that the daemon already has, so no tag moves. up makes no change to agents and queues, and it reports every resource ok. The tariboy version range The top-level tariboy key of a version 2 file gives the tariboy versions that the file works with: Both bounds are optional and inclusive. A bound has the form MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH with an optional prerelease label, such as 0.111.0-rc.1. If min is greater than max, the file is invalid. Versions compare by the SemVer 2.0.0 rules. A prerelease is lower than its release, so 0.111.0-rc.1 is lower than 0.111.0. Thus min: 0.111.0 refuses a daemon at 0.111.0-rc.1. A bound can have a label itself: min: 0.111.0-rc.1 accepts 0.111.0-rc.1, 0.111.0-rc.2, and 0.111.0. If the file has a tariboy key, every verb that calls the daemon (up, down, build, ps, status, start, stop, restart, kill, rm, exec, logs) first reads the daemon version from GET /api/daemon/status. If the version is outside the range, the verb stops before any change. The error names the daemon version, the range, and the file: compose up reads the version after it starts the daemon. compose pack and compose unpack make the same check before any change (see Moving a project with pack and unpack), and compose validate makes it as Checking a file with validate describes. A file without the tariboy key makes no extra call. Checking a file with validate To check a compose archive instead of a file, see Checking an archive with validate --archive. compose validate checks the file and changes nothing: 1. The schema. If the YAML has unknown fields, it lists each one. A YAML syntax error stops the check. 2. The references between entries, as listed above: each store of a workflow or an image is in stores, and the STORE/ prefix of a queue workflow is the store of its entry. 3. The fields of the version 2 sections: a git URL is https only, a tag and a version have a valid form. 4. The existence of each local path in stores, workflows, and images, and of each version 1 image context. 5. The tariboy range against the version of the CLI. 6. With --daemon, the tariboy range against the version of the running daemon. This is one read of GET /api/daemon/status. If the file has no tariboy key, there is nothing to compare and it makes no call. Without --daemon, validate does not call the daemon and does not start it. If the file has no problems, validate prints PATH: valid and exits with 0. Otherwise it prints each problem on its own line to standard error, then compose validate: N problem(s) in PATH, and exits with 1: Moving a project with pack and unpack pack writes one compose archive with the file and every image and workflow image it needs. unpack applies that archive on another daemon without network access and without a build. Both verbs need a running daemon. They do not start it. pack compose pack does these steps: 1. It reads and checks the file, as up does. If the file has a tariboy range, the daemon version must be inside it. 2. It applies the stores, workflows and images phases, as compose build does. With --no-build, it builds nothing and takes the images and workflow images that the daemon has. A missing image or workflow image stops pack with an error that names it. 3. It exports the image of each agent and each workflow image of the file from the daemon. The workflow images are each workflows entry and the workflow of each task queue. It makes sure that each export has the digest that the daemon reports. 4. It writes the archive to FILE. If FILE exists, pack stops. If a step fails, pack removes the incomplete file. The archive is a tariboy-portable archive of kind compose. It holds these files: | File | Content | | --- | --- | | compose.yaml | The compose file, without changes | | images/NAME/TAG.tar.gz | The exported image of each agent (kind image-artifact), with its installed skills | | workflows/NAME/VERSION.tar.gz | The exported workflow image (kind workflow-image) | The manifest metadata gives the schema version (schema: 1), the version of the daemon that packed the archive (producer version), the name of the compose file, and the digest of each image and workflow image. The archive holds one workflow image for each workflow name. An archive does not hold Stores or secret values. The compose file holds only the name of each secret and its from env variable. pack does not read these variables. | Limit | Value | Reason | | --- | --- | --- | | Whole archive, compressed | 1 GiB | 16 images of 64 MiB | | Whole archive, expanded | 1 GiB | The members are gzip files already, so they do not get larger | | Files | 512 | The compose file, the images and the workflow images | | One image or workflow image | 64 MiB | The limit of the image and workflow import routes of the daemon | If one export is larger than 64 MiB, pack stops before it writes the archive. unpack compose unpack FILE does these steps: 1. It unpacks the archive into a temporary directory. It makes sure that the sha256 and size of each file match the manifest. 2. It checks the whole archive before any change. It recomputes the content digest of each image and each workflow image. It checks the compose file and makes sure that the archive has an image for each agent and a workflow image for each workflow of the file. 3. It reads the daemon version. The daemon must be inside the tariboy range of the file, and it must not be older than producer version. If either check fails, unpack stops before any change. 4. It prints the plan by phase, as up --dry-run does. With --dry-run, it stops here. Without --yes, it asks Apply this archive? [y/N]. 5. It applies the file by phase, as up does, with these differences: - The stores phase does not call the daemon. Each Store gets the outcome skipped (archive). - The workflows phase imports each workflow image of the archive. Import tags it with its version and latest. - The images phase imports each image of the archive. - If a ref already has the digest of the archive, unpack does not import it again. The outcome is ok. unpack does not build, does not run npx or git, and does not use the network. The temporary directory is removed when unpack ends, also after an error. The project directory of an unpacked file is the directory of the archive. An agent without cwd gets this directory. To use another directory, set cwd in the file before pack. Secret values do not move. After unpack, an agent or a queue gets its secret only if the from env variable is set in the environment of unpack. Otherwise the rule of up applies: a secret that is missing fails the agent or the queue. If an import or an action fails after the checks, for example on an image version conflict, unpack does not undo the actions that it already applied. As in up, the resource fails, the resources that depend on it get skipped, and the other resources are applied. Run unpack again after you correct the cause. It does not import again the images that already have the digest of the archive. After unpack, the target daemon has no Store for the images and the workflows. It cannot build them again until you register the Store, for example with compose up and the same file. Checking an archive with validate --archive compose validate --archive FILE checks an archive and does not call the daemon. It checks the sha256 of each file in the manifest, the content digest of each image and workflow image, the schema version, the compose file and its references, and that the archive has every image and workflow image that the file needs. It does not check local paths, because they are paths on the machine that packed the archive. It compares the tariboy range of the file with the version of the CLI, and the producer version with the version of the CLI. With --daemon, it also reads the daemon: the daemon version against the range and against producer version, and the plugins of the daemon. Each external plugin that an image needs must be installed. It never writes to the daemon. The full contract check of each image runs at import time. It prints problems in the same form as validate of a file. Older archives and the archive and import verbs compose archive and compose import stay for one release as deprecated aliases. Each one prints a warning to standard error: - compose archive runs compose pack. Its behavior changed: it wrote a team archive without a daemon, and now it writes a compose archive and needs a running daemon. - compose import --archive FILE runs compose unpack FILE. compose unpack also accepts a team archive version 1 that an older compose archive wrote. It sends that archive to the team import of the daemon (POST /api/team-imports), prints the preview and applies it after --yes or a y answer, as compose import did. The CLI does not write team archives any more. To move such a team with its images, apply the old archive, then run compose pack with the compose file of the team. How up converges compose up reads the live state once: the groups, agents, budgets, task queues with their pools, env, secret names and triggers, and the pending image of each running agent whose image differs from the file. It then plans the actions that move the daemon toward the file and applies them phase by phase: | Phase | What it applies | | --- | --- | | stores | Registers each Store of the file, sets the ref of a git Store and refreshes it, and reads a path Store. See Stores. | | workflows | Version 2: builds each entry of workflows after its Store. Version 1: builds each Store workflow a task queue names, once per source. | | images | Builds each declared image as NAME:TAG (latest by default), one action per image, after its Store. | | queues | Creates each task queue, restores a changed name, description and owners, and sets the plain env and the secrets of each queue. | | agents | Creates each new agent without a group , converges the settings of an existing one, stops one whose file sets loop.enabled: false, and sets the agent budget. | | groups | Creates each group without a lead, assigns the file's agents to it, sets the lead, and sets the group budget. | | queue bindings | Binds the agent pools of each queue, then sets its CUSTOMER AGENT POOL and its responsible agent, binds its workflow, and creates its triggers. | | start | Starts each new agent and each stopped loop the file enables, and restarts an agent whose harness changed. | The order follows what each step needs. A pool can only name agents that exist, and a workflow binding needs the pools it names, so the queue bindings come after the agents. A group's lead must already be a member, so the groups phase assigns the members first and then sets the lead with PATCH /api/groups/{name}/lead. A group without lead in the file keeps the lead it has. A new agent starts only after it joined its group. Agents start last, so their first iteration already has its group, its pools and its queue's workflow. A setting that already matches makes no call. Running up again on a converged file reports every resource ok. The only exception is the builds and the refresh of each git Store: compose cannot tell whether the local sources changed, so every up builds each path image and each workflow again. A build of unchanged sources publishes the digest the daemon already has and is reported ok; an image whose NAME:TAG digest changed, or a workflow version that was not published before, is reported changed. An image from a Store builds only when the Store gives a new image version (see A second up). An existing agent converges in place: - Image. A different image is set as the agent's pending image (POST /api/agents/{name}/image). The agent keeps running and adopts the image on its next iteration; there is no restart. A bare name means NAME:latest. - Harness. A different harness.type is stored (POST /api/agents/{name}/harness) in the agents phase. A running agent is then stopped and started in the start phase, after the agent's other changes and its group and pools, so the restarted iteration also uses the new image, CWD, loop, and Goal settings. The restart interrupts the current iteration, as a manual restart does. A stopped agent is not restarted: a re-provision or the start phase starts it with the new harness (see below). An agent whose file sets loop.enabled: false is not restarted; its next start uses the new harness. - Stopped agent. A data-preserving down removes the image tree of each agent and keeps the stopped agent. agent ps then shows the agent with image removed: true. up re-provisions only such an agent: in place, with the file's image, keeping its context, iterations, and audit log. Then the agent converges as above. The daemon starts a re-provisioned agent at once, in the agents phase, so its first iteration may run before the groups and queue bindings phases have set its new group or pool. A re-provision always starts the loop. Thus the first up after down starts an agent whose file sets loop.enabled: false, and then stops it in the same run. The agent can start an iteration between these two calls. - Agent that is stopped and has its image. up does not re-provision an agent that is stopped and still has its image tree, for example an agent whose file sets loop.enabled: false. It converges the settings of the agent in place. If the file enables the loop, the start phase starts the agent, and a changed harness applies at this start. Thus a second up on a file with a stopped agent reports the agent ok. - Group. An agent in another group, or a new agent, is assigned to the file's group in the groups phase (POST /api/groups/{name}/assign). An agent the file leaves without a group keeps the group it has. - CWD, timeout, loop settings, and the Goal settings the file sets converge to the file's values. - Environment and interactive mode. When a key in the file's env is missing from the agent or has another value, up sets the agent env. With env mode: merge, the default, up sends the current env merged with the file's keys. Keys the file does not declare, such as env from the image manifest, stay. With env mode: replace, up sends only the file's env, and the daemon removes every other key, the image manifest env included. When the file has a harness block, up sets the interactive mode to harness.interactive. Without a harness block, up keeps the agent's mode. - Other agent settings. Model, effort, plugins, the timeouts, the schedule, the user prompt, the mail settings, alias, notes, color, retention and secrets converge as Agent settings describes. The stores phase changes the ref of a Git Store as tariboy store ref does (see Images). Entities that are in use up changes a running project without waiting for it to be idle: - A new image is only pending: the agent finishes its current iteration on the old image and adopts the new one on the next. - A harness change restarts a running agent in the start phase and ends its current iteration. - Every other agent setting applies from the next iteration of the agent, as Agent settings describes. The current iteration keeps the old values. - Rebinding a queue to a new workflow version leaves the tasks that already started on the version they pinned; new tasks follow the new binding. Preview with --dry-run compose up --dry-run prints the plan by phase and applies nothing. It reads the live state with GET requests only: it does not start the daemon, build an image or a workflow, or make any other change. A phase with nothing to do is not printed. Each line shows the verb and the fields an action sets, with the live value before - when there is one: Env and secret values are never printed, only the names of the env keys. Without a build, the digest of a Store workflow is not known, so the dry run lists each build and each workflow binding as planned even when up would find it unchanged. It also lists the refresh of each git Store. It does not refresh a Store, so it does not know the version that a Store source will give. A version from a Store shows as (checked at apply time): When the daemon is not running, --dry-run fails with tariboyd is not running instead of starting it. When an action fails A failed action does not stop the run. The actions that depend on it are skipped in every later phase, and independent actions, including the other agents, still run. For example, a failed create of agent writer skips its budget, its group membership, the group's lead when writer is the lead, the pools that name it, the workflow binding that needs those pools, and its start. A failed image build skips only the agents on that image, and a failed harness change skips the restart. When the run ends, up prints one line per resource, in phase order: | Outcome | Meaning | | --- | --- | | ok | Already matched the file; nothing was done. | | changed | Every planned action succeeded. | | failed | An action failed; the line shows the first error. | | skipped | An action it depends on failed, so it was not attempted. | An agent's line covers its create or settings, its group membership and its start; a group's line covers the group and its lead; a queue's line covers the queue, its env, secrets, pools, workflow binding and triggers. If any resource failed, up exits non-zero and prints a one-line summary such as compose up: 1 resource failed to standard error; the report above already shows each error. The resources that succeeded stay applied, so the daemon can be partly converged; fix the cause and run up again to converge the rest. An error while reading the live state or planning stops up and --dry-run before any change. Removing an entity from the file up never deletes. An agent, group or task queue removed from the file stays on the daemon, unchanged. To remove it, run compose down before you edit the file, or remove it directly with tariboy agent rm NAME or tariboy group rm NAME. The daemon does not record which file created an entity, so compose status and compose up --dry-run find the leftovers by their ties to the file and list them as not declared: - an agent the file does not declare that is in one of the file's groups or in a pool of one of its task queues; - a group the file does not declare that has one of the file's agents as a member; - a task queue the file does not declare with a pool that names one of the file's agents; - a pool, env key, secret or trigger of a declared task queue that the file does not declare. An entity with no tie to the file, such as an agent outside the file's groups and pools, is not listed. not declared lines do not count as drift. compose status compose status reads the same plan without applying it. It prints one line per task queue and pool, agent, budget, and group, then the not declared entities, then drift: N. An agent's line lists each setting up would change, its group, model, effort and plugins included, in the form FIELD drift: have=X want=Y. An image that is already pending shows as image pending until the agent adopts it, and the file's plugins show as plugins pending until then. Environment drift lists the key names only, never their values. user prompt drift and notes drift do not print the text. Each agent secret has a line of its own. For a version 2 file, status also prints one line for each Store, workflow and image. A Store line shows the drift of its ref. A workflow or image line compares the version that NAME:TAG was built from with the version that its source gives now. Status does not refresh a Store: it reads the version from the current copy of the Store, and the version of a path source from the local file. Every line except ok counts as drift: Agent settings An agent can declare every setting that the CLI and the API have for an agent: If the file omits a field, up does not change the live value. The table gives the rules of each field and the daemon call that converges it on an existing agent. A new agent gets the field in the create request (POST /api/agents) or in an action right after the create. | Field | Rules | Call on an existing agent | | --- | --- | --- | | image | Required. A bare name means NAME:latest. | POST /api/agents/{name}/image, pending until the next iteration | | group | Must be in groups. | POST /api/groups/{group}/assign, groups phase | | harness.type | claude, codex, opencode or cursor. | POST /api/agents/{name}/harness, then a restart | | harness.model, harness.effort | An empty value keeps the live value. Compose cannot clear them, because the daemon reads an empty value as a read. | POST /api/agents/{name}/model, .../effort | | harness.interactive | Default false. Set only when the file has a harness block. | POST /api/agents/{name}/interactive | | plugins | The exact list of the agent. [] sets an empty list. Compared as a set. A new agent on a schema-v2 image starts with the plugins of the image, so up sets the list in an action after the create. | POST /api/agents/{name}/plugins; see Plugins and a new image | | env | Keys and values. | POST /api/agents/{name}/env | | env mode | merge (default) or replace. | Changes what env sends | | secrets | KEY: {from env: VAR}. The key rules of queue secrets apply. A key cannot be in env too. | POST /api/agents/{name}/secrets; see Agent secrets | | cwd | Default: the directory of the compose file. $CWD and $HOME expand. | POST /api/agents/{name}/cwd | | create cwd | true lets the daemon create cwd. The daemon does not store it, so it shows no drift. | Adds create: true to the cwd call | | user prompt | The standing user prompt. Compared exactly. | POST /api/agents/{name}/user-prompt | | alias, notes | An empty string clears the value. | POST /api/agents/{name}/alias, .../notes | | color | #rrggbb. Compared without case. An empty string clears it. | POST /api/agents/{name}/color | | messages batch, messages max queue | Whole numbers, at least 1. | POST /api/agents/{name}/messages/batch, .../max-queue | | mail instant senders | Agent names. [] refuses every agent. A sender can be outside the file. | POST /api/agents/{name}/messages/instant-senders, groups phase | | retention | keep iterations, keep days, max bytes, each at least 0. 0 means the daemon default. | POST /api/agents/{name}/retention with the fields of the file | | budget | limit usd, period, mode. | POST /api/budgets | | goal | enabled, wait customer timeout, delivery cooldown. | POST /api/agents/{name}/goal- | | loop.enabled | Default true. false stops the agent. | POST /api/agents/{name}/start or .../stop | | loop.interval, loop.timeout | Durations such as 30s or 60m. | POST /api/agents/{name}/loop/interval, .../timeout | | timeout | The older form of loop.timeout. If both are set, loop.timeout is used. | As loop.timeout | | loop.hard timeout | A duration of at least 0s. | POST /api/agents/{name}/loop/hard-timeout | | loop.ai stall timeout | A whole number of seconds, at least 1s, written as a duration. | POST /api/agents/{name}/loop/ai-stall-timeout | | loop.on timeout, loop.on error | restart or stop. | POST /api/agents/{name}/loop/on-timeout, .../on-error | | loop.max idle iterations | At least 0. 0 turns the idle stop off. | POST /api/agents/{name}/loop/max-idle | | loop.schedule | An RFC 5545 RRULE, with an optional DTSTART before it. An empty string clears the schedule. | POST /api/agents/{name}/loop/schedule | compose validate checks these rules. It does not check that a from env variable is set or that a sender of mail instant senders exists. The daemon accepts a sender of mail instant senders only when that agent exists. For this reason, up sets the senders in the groups phase, after the create of each sender that the file declares. A failed create of a sender skips the action. Compose cannot return the list to "not set", where the lead of the agent's group can send instant letters. For that, run tariboy agent messages instant-senders NAME --reset. The daemon stores a schedule as a DTSTART line and an RRULE line. If the file has no DTSTART, the daemon uses the time of the write, and compose compares the RRULE only. If the file has a DTSTART, compose compares both lines. When the settings apply up does not wait for an iteration to end. Every setting in the table applies from the next iteration of the agent, without a restart. The current iteration keeps the old values. These are the exceptions: - A change of harness.type restarts the agent in the start phase and ends its current iteration. - A new image is pending until the next iteration, and the plugins of the file follow one up later. See Plugins and a new image. - The daemon calculates loop.schedule again at once. The time of the next scheduled start changes. - loop.enabled: false stops the agent at once. Plugins and a new image The daemon checks a plugin list against the active image of the agent. When the agent adopts a new image, the daemon replaces the list with the plugins of that image. Thus up cannot set the plugins in the same run that sets a new image: 1. The first up sets the pending image and does not set the plugins. compose status reports plugins pending: applied after the agent adopts image NAME:TAG; run up again, and counts it as drift. 2. The agent adopts the image at the start of its next iteration. Until the next up, the agent runs with the plugins of the image. 3. The next up sets the plugins of the file. Then status reports no drift. After a re-provision of a stopped agent, up always sets the plugins of the file, because compose cannot predict the list after it. A rebuild of the image in up with a new digest also replaces the list when the agent adopts the image. status then reports plugin drift, and the next up sets the list again. For a schema-v1 image, the daemon adds the core plugins to the list. To make up idempotent (a second run changes nothing), list the complete result, core plugins included. Otherwise every up writes the list again. Agent secrets Agent secrets follow the rules of queue secrets. The file holds only the name of the variable. compose reads the value from its own environment when it writes the secret, and an empty variable counts as not set. The value never appears in the output of up, up --dry-run or status, in an error, or in the archive of compose pack. | Variable | Secret on the agent | status | up | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Set | Yes | secret GH TOKEN ok (value not compared) | Writes the value again and reports ok. | | Set | No | secret GH TOKEN MISSING | Writes the value and reports changed. | | Not set | Yes | secret GH TOKEN ok (DEV GH TOKEN not set, kept) | Keeps the secret. | | Not set | No | secret GH TOKEN MISSING (DEV GH TOKEN not set) | Fails the agent. The error names the variable and the tariboy secret set command. | up --dry-run prints secret GH TOKEN=from DEV GH TOKEN for a write and does not list a rewrite. up never removes a secret. status and up --dry-run list a secret of the agent that the file does not declare as agent dev secret OLD not declared. Group settings A group has two fields. The groups phase applies them: | Field | Rules | Call | | --- | --- | --- | | lead | Must be a member of the group in the file. A group without lead keeps its lead. | PATCH /api/groups/{name}/lead, after the members are assigned | | budget | limit usd, period, mode. | POST /api/budgets | The members of a group are the agents whose group names it. Agent settings outside compose These agent commands have no compose field: | Command | Reason | | --- | --- | | context set, script and its schedules, the iterations, agent mail clear, agent file | They hold the working state of the agent, not its configuration. | | agent start, stop, restart, kill, rm, reprovision, exec, send-keys, iteration extend-timeout, agent image cancel, group rename, group member rm | They are actions, not settings. Compose verbs cover the lifecycle actions. | | retention set default, daemon agent-shell-script set | They are daemon settings, not agent settings. | | agent budget set (the calendar budget with hour, day, week and month limits) | budget already limits the spend of the agent. A second budget mechanism in the file would give two sources for one purpose. | | agent shell-script set | The shell script is a Bash file in the directory of the agent, which is code, not a parameter. | | secret rm, env keys that the file omits with env mode: merge | up never removes them. Use env mode: replace for env. | | agent messages instant-senders --reset | The file cannot express "not set". Run the command. | Task queues and pools Compose can declare task queues with every setting of a queue: | Field | Meaning | | --- | --- | | name | The queue name. Required. | | description | The queue description. | | owners | The agents that own the queue. The daemon does not check that they exist, so an owner can be outside the file. | | responsible agent | The agent responsible for the queue. It must be declared in agents. | | pools | The agent pools of the queue. Each agent must be declared in agents. | | workflow | The workflow image the queue follows. See Queue workflows. | | triggers | Letters that create tasks: pattern is a sender such as plugin:telegram or plugin: , correlation key is optional, and action is create task, the default. | | env | Plain variables for workflow scripts, for example CUSTOMER AGENT POOL and AUTO MERGE. | | secrets | Secrets for workflow scripts. from env names the variable of the compose process that holds the value. | An env or secret key holds letters, digits and underscores, does not start with a digit, and does not start with TARIBOY . A key is either env or a secret, not both. CUSTOMER AGENT POOL is always env. compose validate checks these key rules, that each secret has a valid from env, and that each trigger has a valid pattern and action and is declared once. It does not check that the from env variable is set, because a file is checked without its secrets. compose up applies a queue in two phases: 1. The queues phase runs before the agents. It creates the queue with its name, description and owners, or changes the fields that differ in one update. Then it sets the env keys, except CUSTOMER AGENT POOL, and the secrets. 2. The queue bindings phase runs after the agents and groups. It binds the pools. Then it sets CUSTOMER AGENT POOL, because the daemon accepts it on a bound queue only when the pool exists. Then it sets the responsible agent, binds the workflow and creates the triggers. The workflow binding comes after the env and the secrets, so a secret that the workflow requires (requires secrets) exists before the bind. The triggers come after the binding, so a task from a new letter follows the workflow. Secrets The file never holds a secret value. compose reads the value of secrets.KEY.from env from its own environment when it applies the secret, and an empty variable counts as not set. The value never appears in the output of up, up --dry-run or status, or in an error. The daemon never returns a secret value, so compose cannot compare it: | Variable | Secret on the queue | status | up | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Set | Yes | secret GH TOKEN ok (value not compared) | Writes the value again and reports ok. | | Set | No | secret GH TOKEN MISSING | Writes the value and reports changed. | | Not set | Yes | secret GH TOKEN ok (DEV GH TOKEN not set, kept) | Keeps the secret. | | Not set | No, but the daemon environment holds the key | secret GH TOKEN ok (daemon environment) | Does nothing. | | Not set | No | secret GH TOKEN MISSING (DEV GH TOKEN not set) | Fails the queue. The error names the variable and the ttasks queue secret set command. | Because up writes each set secret again, a second up reports ok and a new value of the variable reaches the daemon on the next up. Each write adds a secret set event to the queue history. up --dry-run does not list such a rewrite. When a secret fails, up skips the workflow binding and the triggers of that queue. The other queues and the agents still apply. What up does not change up never removes a pool, an env key, a secret or a trigger that the file does not declare. compose status and up --dry-run list them as not declared (see Removing an entity from the file). An empty description, owners or responsible agent in the file keeps the value of the daemon. To clear one, use ttasks queue update. The API cannot change a trigger. If you change a trigger in the file, up creates a new trigger, and the old trigger stays and shows as not declared. To remove it, use ttasks queue trigger delete. If a key is in env in the file but is a secret on the queue, up makes it env, as the daemon does for ttasks queue env set. Queue settings outside compose These queue operations of ttasks queue have no compose field: | Operation | Reason | | --- | --- | | pool delete, env rm, secret rm, trigger delete, workflow clear | up never removes anything. Use ttasks queue to remove. | | Turn a trigger on or off (enabled) | The API cannot change this flag. A trigger is always on. | | source ls, source log | These read state and set nothing. The workflow image declares its sources. | | revision | The daemon uses it to refuse concurrent writes. compose reads the current revision itself. | Pools and parsing The file is parsed strictly: a misspelled or unknown field fails instead of being ignored. Queue prefixes and pool names use URL-safe ASCII identifiers (A-Z, a-z, digits, ., , and -; the first character must be alphanumeric). A pool is an explicit list of compose agents, normalized by agent name, and independent of groups: putting an agent in a group does not put it in a pool, and a pool does not alter group membership. An agent no longer takes a subscribe: key: the mailbox replaced channel subscriptions, so the key fails as an unknown field. Remove it from older files; group mail and task notifications need no declaration. In version 1, the top-level workflows: map belonged to the removed task workflow engine. A non-empty value is rejected with an error that names the key and tells you to declare version: 2. In version 2, workflows declares workflow sources; see The compose file. compose up uses the Native Tasks API of the daemon. A second compose up on a converged file changes nothing. compose status changes nothing and reports drift of each queue field, pool, env key, secret, trigger and workflow, next to agent, group and budget drift. It prints env keys, never env values. Existing compose files without task queues keep their previous behavior. Queue workflows A queue may name the workflow image it follows: workflow takes one of four forms: | Value | compose up | | --- | --- | | NAME | Binds the already built NAME:latest. The queue follows latest. | | NAME:TAG | Binds the already built NAME:TAG. The queue follows the tag. | | STORE/NAME | Builds the workflow source NAME from the registered Store STORE, then binds the digest that build produced. The binding is pinned. | | STORE/NAME:TAG | Builds STORE/NAME, then binds NAME:TAG. The queue follows the tag. | A tag of . or .. is a validation error. In version 2, NAME is the key of a workflows entry. up builds the entry in the workflows phase and binds the queue after that build. A failed build or a version conflict skips the binding, and the queue keeps its workflow: | Value | compose up in version 2 | | --- | --- | | NAME | Binds the entry's tag (latest by default). The queue follows the tag. | | NAME:TAG | Binds NAME:TAG. The queue follows the tag. | | STORE/NAME | Binds the digest of the entry's build. The binding is pinned. STORE must be the store of the entry. | | STORE/NAME:TAG | Binds NAME:TAG. The queue follows the tag. | The paragraphs below describe the version 1 forms. Each Store workflow is built once per run in the workflows phase, before any queue is bound, and a bind runs after the queue's pools exist, since a bind needs the pools the workflow names. A queue already bound to the resolved digest and tag is left alone. A queue that follows a tag moves to each new build of that tag; see Binding a queue. A form without a Store prefix fails when the image is not built. Rebinding a queue to a newer version leaves its existing tasks on the version they pinned. Compose never clears a binding: removing workflow from the file leaves the queue bound; unbind with ttasks queue workflow clear. Declare the secrets that the workflow requires in secrets with from env (see Secrets). When the workflow lists requires secrets that the queue does not have, the bind fails with workflow secret missing, and the error names the secrets and the command to set one: compose status never builds. A STORE/NAME workflow is compared with the workflow version of its Store source, as the daemon reads it from the Store, and reported as (Store source); when the Store or the source cannot be read, and for every other form, status resolves the declared workflow through NAME:TAG, latest when no tag is given. It reports a queue whose binding is missing, differs, or names an image that is not built yet. A bound queue whose file declares no workflow is listed as not declared. When the daemon fails to return a queue's binding, that queue shows workflow UNKNOWN (<error code ) and status goes on with the next one. See Task workflows.
description: Bring up a whole set of Stores, workflows, images, task queues, agents, and groups declaratively from a Tariboycompose.yaml.
title: The compose workflow

content: This page gives one entry for each special case of tariboy compose. Each entry gives the case, the decision, what you see, and the section of Compose with the details. scripts/compose-e2e.sh runs most of these cases on an isolated daemon (see Development). A failure in the middle of up | | | | --- | --- | | Case | An action of up fails, for example a build, a create or a secret. | | Decision | up does not stop and does not undo. It skips each action that depends on the failed action, in every later phase. Independent actions still run. | | What you see | One line for each resource: ok, changed, failed with the first error, or skipped. up exits non-zero and prints compose up: N resource(s) failed. The daemon is partly converged. Correct the cause and run up again. | | Details | When an action fails | An error while up reads the live state or plans stops up before any change. A Store that is not available | | | | --- | --- | | Case | The daemon cannot reach a Store: no network, a wrong URL, a ref that does not exist, a path that does not exist, or another source under the same name. | | Decision | The Store fails. Each workflow and image from it is skipped, and so are the agents on those images and the queue bindings of those workflows. Entries from paths and from other Stores still apply. up never changes the source of a registered Store. | | What you see | failed store:NAME and skipped lines for its dependents. up exits non-zero. After you correct the Store, the next up applies the skipped resources. | | Details | A Store that is not available, Stores | A version conflict | | | | --- | --- | | Case | The version of a workflow or image entry differs from the version that its source gives. | | Decision | The entry fails before the build, and its tag stays on the build it had. If the source changes during the build, the entry fails after the build.
