content: This path is for the 0.111.0 alpha on an Apple Silicon Mac. Allow ten minutes after the DMG is available. Before you begin - macOS 12 or newer on Apple Silicon; - a verified Tariboy 0.111.0 aarch64.dmg; - for remote use, an SSH config alias resolving to Linux x86 64/aarch64 or Apple Silicon macOS; - a writable /.local, flock, and python3 on that remote host; - at least one supported harness installed where the agent will run. 1. Install Verify the release checksum: Open the DMG and drag Tariboy.app to Applications. The alpha is ad-hoc signed. If Gatekeeper says the developer cannot be verified, close that dialog, Control-click the exact /Applications/Tariboy.app, choose Open , and confirm once. If that action is unavailable on the installed macOS version, open System Settings → Privacy & Security , find the blocked Tariboy notice, choose Open Anyway , and confirm the exact named app. This temporary alpha exception applies only to /Applications/Tariboy.app. Never disable Gatekeeper globally and never run spctl --master-disable. Desktop opens the workspace directly. Daemon startup and saved-host reconnect continue in the background, with their state visible in the workspace. On the first start, the home screen shows Getting ready . The daemon connects the Tariboy catalog, builds the starter image basic, and looks for the coding tools installed on the host. Each row turns green by itself. If a row fails, it says why in one sentence, with Details and Retry . A missing coding tool is shown in that list with its install hint, not as an error banner. To take the tour of the interface, or to read the changelog, open the ? (Help) menu in the titlebar. The tour does not start by itself. After the first agent exists, the home screen shows what needs you, the agents that run now, today's numbers, and your recent agents. The sidebar has six items: Home , Agents (your agents, opened in place), Tasks , Inbox , Library (images, workflows, and sources), and Settings . The numbers next to Tasks and Inbox count what waits for you. The search field in the titlebar finds agents and tasks; press ⌘K or Ctrl+K to use it. The line at the foot of the sidebar shows your hosts and opens Settings → Hosts , where you add a host. This alpha includes WebView developer tools in release builds. Open them with Option-Command-I on macOS or choose Inspect Element from the WebView context menu. To expose the bundled local commands on your shell PATH, choose Install/Update CLI from the Tariboy menu-bar item. It updates six Tariboy command links under /.local/bin and restarts the local daemon. The bundle has five real payload files; ttasks is the alias for tariboy-tasks. Running agent shims continue; their harnesses retry through the brief proxy outage. When upgrading a running daemon older than 0.10.1, Desktop first verifies that it is idle and refuses to change links or restart it while work is active. Finish or stop that legacy work and choose Install/Update CLI again. Future updates use the persisted handoff state and do not require an idle daemon. 2. Add a host Open Settings → Hosts → Add SSH host . Enter a label and an existing SSH config alias such as build-box. Tariboy runs system ssh, so ProxyJump, ssh-agent, known hosts, and interactive authentication work as they do in a terminal. Run preflight. Review the detected platform, architecture, disk, flock, python3, tmux, and harnesses. Choose Install when the host reports Linux x86 64/aarch64 or macOS arm64 and the required install prerequisites are green. Provisioning ends by opening a loopback-forwarding tunnel and checking daemon health. For local-only use, keep the default Local host and continue. Later, Edit host → Update Tariboy performs upload, activation, daemon restart, and reconnect as one operation. The update click is the restart confirmation. Running agents on daemon 0.10.1 or newer survive through shim handoff; legacy daemons fail closed when active work cannot be preserved. 3. Create or select an image For the first agent you do not have to do anything here: the daemon builds basic by itself. To use another image, open Library → Images : - use basic:latest: at its first start the daemon registers https://github.com/alekzonder/tariboy-store.git as the Store tariboy and builds tariboy/basic in the background. The build is in Settings → Maintenance . If you removed the Store, click Add tariboy Store in Library → Sources , then click Build on the basic row of its card (or run tariboy store add tariboy https://github.com/alekzonder/tariboy-store.git and tariboy image build tariboy/basic); or - choose an existing built image and click Run agent . Images that no agent uses yet are under Show unused ; or - choose Add image → Build from directory , enter the path to an original directory containing Tariboyfile.yaml, set a required name such as reviewer, validate the exact plugin/prompt template, and build reviewer:latest. An image is a reusable template. It is not an agent and does not start work. 4. Create an agent On a host with no agent, the home screen has the card Run your first agent . Later, use New agent in the sidebar; it opens the same form. 1. In Folder , type the path of your repository, for example /code/my-app. If the folder does not exist, click Create it . 2. Keep Image basic and the selected Coding tool . The form selects a coding tool that it found on the host. 3. Keep the suggested Name , for example my-app-basic, or type another. 4. Click Start agent . The agent opens on its Terminal tab. The line above the terminal says what happens while the coding tool starts, and the reason with Retry if it did not start. Every other setting has a default and is under Advanced . Model and effort are shown as one line under the coding tool; click change to edit them. They suggest values in two groups: From harness lists what the harness CLI on the selected host reports, and Saved lists values entered earlier for that harness. They are runtime settings, not schema-v2 image content. A successful create remembers the model and effort locally for that harness. An agent has one on/off switch. Start agent , or Start in the agent header later, turns on the whole agent: Terminal and timer/message-triggered iterations. Advanced → Create without starting creates it stopped. Advanced → Headless (no terminal) creates an agent without Terminal. For the first walkthrough, keep the terminal and use a non-bare image. From the CLI, tariboy agent run IMAGE:TAG creates an interactive agent too; pass --interactive=false for a headless one. A --cwd that does not exist is rejected; add --create-cwd to make the directory first. tariboy agent cwd NAME PATH --create does the same for an existing agent. 5. Use Terminal Open the agent's Terminal tab. This is a real terminal to the selected harness. Use it to work with the agent by hand. For work that the agent must do on its own, give it a task in Work ; the agent runs it while it is on. Startup can take a few seconds while the shim socket appears; Terminal retries during that bounded window. Leaving the tab does not hide or stop the session, and returning attaches a new terminal client to the same tmux session. The line above the terminal always says what the screen shows: - Starting Claude Code in /code/my-app… while the coding tool starts. - Working on DEV-1 — this is its live screen. while a run works on a task. - Idle. The screen appears when a run starts. when the agent waits for work. What you type here is not recorded in a task. - Off. with a Start button when the agent is off. - Claude Code did not start: and the reason, with Retry and Open settings . - No interactive terminal. Enable it in Settings → Autopilot. for an agent without a terminal. The toolbar under the terminal has Send files , Compose , Scrollback , Keys , and ? (help). Click Keys to show the Esc , Enter , Ctrl-C , ↑ , and ↓ keys. To try an ordinary terminal with no image instructions, create a separate agent from bare:latest. Bare requires Interactive and runs no autonomous iterations. 6. Let Autopilot run 1. Open the agent's Settings tab. 2. Under Autopilot , select Also every and enter the interval in minutes. 3. Set Stop a run after to a soft timeout in minutes. 4. Under Spending limit , set daily and monthly limits in USD. 5. Click Save changes at the top. To run only for tasks or messages, select Only when given tasks or messages . A separate schedule can still start runs. Open Advanced → Schedule and timeouts to edit that schedule, the hard timeout in seconds, and timeout and error policies. While the agent is started, a letter stays open in its inbox and nudges the loop. To give the agent work, open Work . Type a title in the Give \ a task… field and press Enter. If the agent is off, the button reads Start & give and also starts the agent. Details sets the queue, the priority, and a description. The task shows under In progress , Queued , or Done . When the agent asks you something or waits for your decision, a card shows under Needs you . Answer there, or choose an outcome, without opening the task. 7. Inspect and stop safely The agent header says in one sentence what the agent does or waits for. Its primary button follows that state: Answer , Give task , Start , or Restart . Answer opens the first Needs you card in Work , and Give task puts the cursor in the task field. Open Activity to see the tasks done, runs, and cost of the period, with Today as the default. Under More , the Runs log shows the trigger, outcome, and audit of each run; Usage and Status history are there too. Then: - use Stop in the agent header to turn the agent off and prevent new runs; - use ⋯ → Force-stop current run to stop only the current work, after you confirm; - use ⋯ → Run once… to start one run now while the agent is on. Quitting Tariboy leaves daemons and remote data running. Removing a host stops its local tunnel and removes local metadata, but does not delete the remote installation or agent data. Next Read Images, Remote hosts, Autopilot, and Security and controls.
description: Install Tariboy, connect a host, build an image, and run one agent interactively and on Autopilot.
title: Ten-minute quickstart

content: tariboy command reference tariboy has four command surfaces: 1. Operator commands — tariboy <group <command (sa below is a convenience alias you define yourself, e.g. alias sa=tariboy; the build ships no such symlink), run by a human or CI against the daemon. Global flags: --json, --help, --help-json, --version. --json counts as the global flag wherever a flag may appear, but not as the value of another flag. The list below is generated from the binary's registry (tariboy --help-json). 2. Agent capability scripts — the applicable packaged skill's scripts/ .sh launcher, run inside an agent over $TARIBOY TOOLS SOCKET. 3. Native Tasks — tariboy-tasks, installed as ttasks, runs shared task verbs for an operator or an identity-bound agent. ttasks --version reports its build and ttasks --json … requests JSON output. tariboy tasks … runs the same client, always in operator mode; the table below does not list it. 4. Mail — tariboy-mail, installed as tmail, reads, sends and answers letters for an identity-bound agent or an operator. tariboy mail … runs the same client, always in operator mode. 5. Scripts — tariboy-scripts, installed as tscripts, runs and inspects the durable scripts of an identity-bound agent. It has no operator mode. The skill launcher scripts/scripts.sh stays a thin launcher, exec tscripts "$@", like tasks.sh and mail.sh. automatic refresh and build policy | | tariboy store list | List registered Stores | | tariboy store ref NAME REF | Check a Git Store out at a branch, tag or commit | | tariboy store refresh NAME | Refresh a Store | | tariboy store remove NAME | Remove a Store registration | | tariboy store show NAME | Show a Store and its images | | tariboy team compose NAME | Render a group as tariboy-compose.yaml | | tariboy team import archive apply ID | Build images and create a staged portable team | | tariboy team import archive plan ID | Validate and plan a staged portable team import | | tariboy team import archive status ID | Inspect portable team import progress | | tariboy team import yaml YAML | Preview pasted tariboy-compose.yaml | | tariboy transcript NAME ID | Show the AI proxy transcript for an iteration (parsed; ?raw=1 for bytes) | | tariboy update | Install a published release over this installer-managed installation | | tariboy usage | Aggregate AI usage and cost from ai requests | | tariboy user-prompt get NAME | Read the agent's standing user-prompt | | tariboy user-prompt set NAME TEXT | Set the agent's standing user-prompt | | tariboy version | Print the Tariboy version | | tariboy workflow build | Start a background build of a workflow image from a Workflowfile.yaml | | tariboy workflow inspect NAME | Show a workflow image manifest | | tariboy workflow ls | List built workflow images | | tariboy workflow rm NAME TAG | Remove a workflow image tag, and its content when no tag remains | | tariboy workflow validate | Validate a workflow source directory without building it | | tariboy workflow version get | Print workflow version from a local Workflowfile.yaml | | tariboy workflow version update PART | Bump workflow version in a local Workflowfile.yaml | A test keeps this table equal to tariboy --help-json. Each row shows the command's required positional arguments; tariboy COMMAND --help lists its flags. After adding, removing or renaming a command, regenerate the table: Host-local commands Some of the commands above run in the CLI process instead of calling the daemon API. They act on the host the CLI runs on and work while the daemon is down: - tariboy daemon start|stop|restart|status|logs control and inspect the local daemon process. daemon status prints running (pid N, version V) and exits 0, or prints stopped and exits 1; with --json it prints the daemon's full status, or {"running":false}. The API still serves GET /api/daemon/status. daemon logs [-f] [--tail N] prints the last N lines (default 200) of /.tariboyd/tariboyd.log. - tariboy update [VERSION|latest] [--force] [--cleanup [--keep N]] installs a published release over this installer-managed installation, restarts a running daemon, and with --cleanup deletes all but the newest N releases (default 5). - tariboy compose VERB reads a compose file and drives the daemon API. Without -f FILE, it reads Tariboycompose.yaml, else tariboy-compose.yaml, from the current directory; if both files exist, it stops with an error. compose up starts the daemon first unless --no-start or TARIBOY NO AUTOSTART is set, and applies the file phase by phase. compose up --dry-run prints that plan from reads only: it does not start the daemon, build or change anything. compose status and compose up --dry-run also list the agents, groups and task queues tied to the file that it does not declare. If the file has a tariboy version range, a verb that calls the daemon stops before any change when the daemon version is outside the range. tariboy compose validate [-f FILE] [--daemon] checks the file and changes nothing; only --daemon makes it read the daemon version. tariboy compose pack -o FILE writes the file and its images and workflow images to one compose archive. tariboy compose unpack FILE checks the whole archive, then imports and applies it without network access or a build. tariboy compose validate --archive FILE checks an archive offline. pack and unpack need a running daemon. compose archive and compose import are deprecated aliases of pack and unpack. See Compose. The compose flags may also come before the verb, as in tariboy compose -f FILE up. tariboy update updates only an installer-managed linux-x86 64 or linux-aarch64 installation and is described in Remote hosts. Removing an agent tariboy agent rm NAME has three modes. A running agent needs --force. | Mode | Command | The daemon deletes | The daemon keeps | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | remove | agent rm NAME | the agent row, secrets, budgets, schedules, scripts and their runs, the script result outbox, the retention policy, the letters in the inbox, image/, bin/, workdir/ | iterations with their tags, ai requests, iterations/, CONTEXT.md, audit.jsonl, assessments, the letters that the agent sent | | keep | agent rm NAME --keep | image/, bin/, workdir/ | the stopped agent row (enabled=false) and all other data | | purge | agent rm NAME --purge | all rows of the agent and the agent directory | assessments, the letters that the agent sent | The answer gives the mode in mode and lists what the mode deleted and kept in deleted and kept. A partly deleted table, such as mail, is in both lists with its part. purged is true only in mode purge. --keep and --purge together fail with bad args, and the agent does not change. After mode remove, agent inspect NAME answers not found, and agent ps does not show the agent. image rm can then delete the image of the agent if no other agent uses it. tariboy iteration ls NAME and GET /api/assessments?agent=NAME&history=true still return the kept history. If the agent is in a task queue agent pool, modes remove and purge fail before the daemon stops the agent. The error names each queue and pool. An agent that you create later under the same name gets the kept history: CONTEXT.md, audit.jsonl, and the iterations. For a clean start, run tariboy agent rm NAME --purge first. --purge also works when only the kept history of a removed agent is left. If nothing of the agent is left, it answers not found. An older daemon left a removed agent as a stopped row. Run tariboy agent rm NAME again to delete that row. tariboy compose down uses mode keep, and compose down --volumes uses mode purge. After mode keep, agent ps shows the stopped agent with image removed: true, and compose up re-provisions only such an agent. A daemon older than mode keep ignores keep and keeps the row as before. An older compose client sends no keep. Then a new daemon deletes the agent in mode remove, and the next compose up creates the agent again with its kept history. Secrets, budgets and schedules that you set outside the compose file are then lost. Update the CLI and the daemon together. Iteration tags Tags annotate an iteration without changing it: one agent marks the iterations of another agent it has already handled. An iteration can carry several tags. A tag is at most 64 characters and contains no comma, whitespace, or control character. The three mutations take a batch of iteration ids and a batch of tags, and apply in one transaction — the whole batch succeeds or nothing is written. An id that belongs to another agent fails the batch with not found. tariboy iteration ls searches by tag and by iteration start date. --tag takes a comma-separated list and matches an iteration carrying any of them. Both date bounds are inclusive and accept RFC3339 or a bare YYYY-MM-DD day: iteration ls rows and iteration inspect both report a sorted tags list. Metrics tariboy metrics reports task metrics that the daemon computes from tasks, workflow visits, AI requests, iterations and assessments. Metrics defines each value, its unit and its source. - tariboy metrics task KEY prints the metrics of one task. KEY is the current key or an old key of the task. - tariboy metrics server prints the report of a period: the total and one row for each agent, image version and workflow version. metrics server takes these flags: | Flag | Value | | --- | --- | | --since, -s | RFC 3339 time, inclusive. The default is 30 days before --until. | | --until, -u | RFC 3339 time, exclusive. The default is the time of the request. | | --agent, -a | Only the iterations and tasks of this agent | | --image, -i | NAME or NAME:VERSION. Only the iterations and tasks on this image. | | --workflow, -w | NAME or NAME:VERSION. Only the iterations and tasks under this workflow. none selects work without a workflow. | Both commands print tables, with times in hours and minutes. The global --json flag prints the API response, with times in seconds and costs in US dollars. Agent capability scripts Run inside an agent; the socket comes from $TARIBOY TOOLS SOCKET. | Tool | Purpose | | --- | --- | | scripts/whoami.sh | Print agent, cwd and current iteration | | scripts/status.sh | Print the agent status | | scripts/loop.sh done | Signal this iteration is finished (i-am-done) | | scripts/context.sh get | Print the durable working memory (CONTEXT.md) | | scripts/context.sh set <text | Overwrite the durable working memory | | scripts/schedule.sh add --kind cron\|oneshot --spec S [--message JSON] | Schedule a future letter; without a recipient it writes to you | | scripts/schedule.sh ls | List your schedules | | scripts/schedule.sh cancel ID | Cancel a schedule | | tscripts ls | List your scripts | | tscripts run NAME [--description TEXT] -- COMMAND | Queue exactly one local run | | tscripts schedule NAME --every SECONDS -- COMMAND | Run now and repeat after each completion; a run that exits 111 (TARIBOY QUIET EXIT) stays quiet | | tscripts runs SCRIPT ID / logs RUN ID | Inspect run history and bounded logs | | tscripts rerun SCRIPT ID | Run a completed one-shot or idle recurring definition immediately | | tscripts cancel SCRIPT OR RUN ID / rm SCRIPT ID | Cancel work or remove inactive history | | scripts/image creator.sh build --name NAME [--tag TAG] --path DIR | Build a schema-v2 image from a daemon-readable source directory (image-creator only); relative paths start at the managed workdir | Mail (tmail …) tariboy-mail is the real executable and tmail its managed alias. A non-empty TARIBOY TOOLS SOCKET selects agent mode: the sender is the calling agent and every read is scoped to its mailbox. Without the variable, the client uses the host Unix daemon socket and acts as the customer unless --as names another principal. tariboy mail … is the same client, always in operator mode. See the Mail reference for flags, routes and debugging. | Command | Purpose | | --- | --- | | tmail inbox [--all] [--limit N] [--before TIME] | List open letters, oldest first; --all lists every letter, newest first | | tmail sent / tmail archive | List the letters you sent / your closed and dead letters | | tmail show ID | Show one letter and its reply | | tmail send --to P[,P] --subject S --text T [--kind K] [--deadline D] [--notice] [--data JSON] | Send a letter; a request unless --notice | | tmail reply ID TEXT [--ask] | Answer a letter, which closes it | | tmail requeue ID | Return a dead letter to the inbox | | tmail close ID [--note T] | Archive without a reply (operator only) | | tmail read ID... | Mark letters read; a read notice to an agent closes (operator only) | | tmail unread | Count open letters by sender and kind (operator only) | | tmail clear --as agent:NAME [--yes] | Delete an agent's open letters (operator only) | Native Tasks (ttasks …) tariboy-tasks is the real executable and ttasks its managed alias. A non-empty TARIBOY TOOLS SOCKET selects agent mode; it uses only that socket and fails closed if it cannot connect. Without the variable, the client uses the host Unix daemon socket as the customer actor. The bare tasks command is only the optional capability-controlled legacy agent shim. tariboy tasks … is the same client with the same commands, flags, output, and exit codes. It always runs in operator mode on the daemon socket (--socket or the default path) and ignores TARIBOY TOOLS SOCKET, so an agent that runs it sees every task and acts as the customer. Its help names tariboy tasks; tariboy tasks --help-json prints the ttasks tree. These shared verbs are available in both modes; in agent mode every mutation derives identity from the socket. | Command | Purpose | | --- | --- | | ttasks list [--status S] [--text T] [--sort ORDER] [--limit N] [--after KEY] | List and search visible tasks; Native Tasks lists every filter | | ttasks mine | Alias of ttasks list | | ttasks ready [--queue Q] [--claim] | List ready work; --claim requires agent mode | | ttasks show KEY | Show task detail, comments, waits, and relations | | ttasks create --queue Q --title T [--assignee A] | Create a queue-root task | | ttasks create --parent KEY --title T | Create a child inheriting queue/context | | ttasks update KEY [--title T] [--description D] [--status S] | Update fields with optimistic revision | | ttasks assign KEY ASSIGNEE | Hand work to an agent name | | ttasks comment KEY [TEXT \| --body TEXT \| --file PATH] (stdin when absent; up to 64 KiB) | Add a task comment | | ttasks ask KEY agent:name\|user:login [TEXT \| --file PATH] (stdin when absent; up to 64 KiB) | Mention a principal and record an open answer wait | | ttasks move KEY [--parent KEY] [--before KEY] [--to-root] | Reparent/reorder in the same queue | | ttasks block KEY --by BLOCKER | Add a directed, cycle-checked blocking relation | | ttasks relate KEY OTHER | Add a symmetric related link | | ttasks done KEY [--complete-anyway] | Complete, optionally overriding active descendants | These verbs drive a task that follows a queue's workflow image. Agent mode sends advance, request get, artifact set, artifact ls, artifact show, workflow get, workflow runs, and workflow run log over the identity-bound socket; operator mode calls the REST routes as the customer. | Command | Modes | REST route | | --- | --- | --- | | ttasks advance KEY --outcome NAME [--from STATUS] [--message TEXT] [--no-wait] (--from refuses with status changed when the task has moved on; waits for the transition's checks, polling GET /api/tasks/{key}/workflow/requests/{id}, unless --no-wait) | agent, operator | POST /api/tasks/{key}/advance | | ttasks artifacts set KEY NAME [VALUE \| --file PATH] (stdin when absent; stored as given, up to 64 KiB) | agent, operator | PUT /api/tasks/{key}/artifacts/{name} | | ttasks artifacts ls KEY | agent, operator | GET /api/tasks/{key}/artifacts | | ttasks artifacts show KEY NAME | agent, operator | GET /api/tasks/{key}/artifacts/{name} | | ttasks workflow get KEY | agent, operator | GET /api/tasks/{key}/workflow | | ttasks workflow runs KEY (newest first) | agent, operator | GET /api/tasks/{key}/workflow/runs | | ttasks workflow log KEY RUN [--max-bytes N] (last 64 KiB by default, at most 1 MiB; queue secrets redacted; customer and the task's holders only) | agent, operator | GET /api/tasks/{key}/workflow/runs/{id}/log | | ttasks workflow move KEY --to STATUS [--reason TEXT] | operator only | POST /api/tasks/{key}/workflow/move | | ttasks workflow upgrade KEY [--reason TEXT] (pins the task to the queue's current workflow version and restarts it at that version's initial status; artifacts and holders stay; errors workflow current, workflow unbound, workflow closed, workflow pool empty, workflow secret missing, forbidden) | operator only | POST /api/tasks/{key}/workflow/upgrade | | ttasks workflow resume KEY --decision continue\|release (resolves the pause of a task the daemon paused: continue keeps the holder and zeroes the counters; release takes a pool task from its holder and dispatches it to another member, or leaves it open and unassigned; errors invalid decision, workflow not paused, forbidden) | operator only | POST /api/tasks/{key}/workflow/resume | | ttasks workflow watch KEY (starts the watch script of a script status now instead of at its next scheduled time and returns the pending run; errors workflow no watch, script running, workflow closed, workflow paused, forbidden) | operator only | POST /api/tasks/{key}/workflow/watch | | ttasks cancel KEY | operator only | POST /api/tasks/{key}/cancel | | ttasks requeue KEY --queue QUEUE [--revision N] (creates a new task in QUEUE and cancels this one; errors task closed, same queue, queue not found, requeue has children) | operator only | POST /api/tasks/{key}/requeue | | ttasks queue workflow set QUEUE REF [--revision N] | operator only | PUT /api/task-queues/{queue}/workflow | | ttasks queue workflow get QUEUE | operator only | GET /api/task-queues/{queue}/workflow | | ttasks queue workflow clear QUEUE --revision N | operator only | DELETE /api/task-queues/{queue}/workflow | | ttasks queue secret set QUEUE KEY [--value V] (stdin when absent, one trailing newline stripped; up to 64 KiB) | operator only | PUT /api/task-queues/{queue}/secrets/{key} | | ttasks queue secret ls QUEUE (keys only, never values) | operator only | GET /api/task-queues/{queue}/secrets | | ttasks queue secret rm QUEUE KEY | operator only | DELETE /api/task-queues/{queue}/secrets/{key} | | ttasks queue env set QUEUE KEY [VALUE \| --value V] (stdin when absent; the value is not secret) | operator only | PUT /api/task-queues/{queue}/env/{key} | | ttasks queue env ls QUEUE (keys and values) | operator only | GET /api/task-queues/{queue}/env | | ttasks queue env rm QUEUE KEY | operator only | DELETE /api/task-queues/{queue}/env/{key} | | ttasks queue source ls QUEUE | operator only | GET /api/task-queues/{queue}/sources | | ttasks queue source log QUEUE RUN [--max-bytes N] (redacted tail, 64 KiB by default) | operator only | GET /api/task-queues/{queue}/source-runs/{id}/log | On a workflow task ttasks done, ttasks update --status, and ttasks ready --claim are refused with workflow managed; the error lists the status's outcomes and the ttasks advance form to use, with --from set to the current status. For an outcome that declares checks, ttasks advance exits 0 when the transition applied and 1 when a check rejected it, a check failed, the request was cancelled, or the wait ran out; the output names the next command. ttasks show prints status (the workflow status), category, and waiting on. See Task workflows for the scripts behind checks and watch statuses. The following administration roots are operator-only and are documented by ttasks --help-json: queue (including pools and triggers; see Task workflows), events, principals, and activity (GET /api/task-activity: the work on tasks in a --since/--until window, optionally for one --agent). They are unavailable to agent mode. Resource identifiers are positional (or named flags), for example: Use each administration command's --help for its required fields.
description: The full command reference — operator commands and agent capability scripts.
title: Command reference

content: Mail Every message in Tariboy is a letter from one principal to another. This page is the reference for working with mail: the tmail client, its operator form tariboy mail, the HTTP routes, the prompt block an agent sees, the agent settings, and debugging. The mailbox architecture page explains the model: principals, requests and notices, closing rules, dead letters, the wake path and the producers. Mental model - A letter has a sender, a recipient, a subject, a body, a kind (default message) and a JSON data object. A send to several recipients writes one letter per recipient. - A letter is a request , which its recipient answers with a reply, or a notice , which closes when an agent has read it or when the customer archives it. A reply is a notice unless --ask makes it a request. - Inbox is the open letters addressed to you, Sent the letters you sent, Archive the closed letters addressed to you, including dead ones. - An open letter in an agent's inbox wakes the agent's loop and is rendered into its prompt until it closes. A letter rendered five times without closing is dead-lettered. tmail and tariboy mail tariboy-mail, installed with the managed link tmail, is one client with two modes: - Agent mode. When TARIBOY TOOLS SOCKET is set, every command is POST /tools/mail/<command on the agent's identity-bound socket. The daemon fixes the sender to the calling agent and scopes every read to that agent's mailbox. Agent provisioning puts tmail on the agent's PATH. - Operator mode. Without that socket, tmail calls the operator routes on the host daemon socket. tariboy mail … runs the same client and is always in operator mode, also inside an agent. Operator mode acts as the customer, user:<customer login , unless --as <principal names another principal. tmail --help and tmail <command --help print local help and never run a command; tmail --help-json prints the whole command tree. --json prints results as JSON, --version prints the client build. Pass long or multi-line text with --text -, which reads standard input. | Command | What it does | Agent mode | | --- | --- | --- | | tmail inbox [--all] [--limit N] [--before CURSOR] | Open letters, oldest first; --all lists every letter to you, newest first | yes | | tmail sent [--limit N] [--before CURSOR] | Letters you sent, newest first, with their state | yes | | tmail archive [--limit N] [--before CURSOR] | Closed letters, newest first; dead ones tagged dead:REASON | yes | | tmail show ID | One letter and the reply that closed it, if any | yes | | tmail send --to P[,P] --subject S --text T [--kind K] [--deadline D] [--notice] [--data JSON] [--instant] | Send a letter; a request unless --notice. --instant sends an instant letter | yes | | tmail reply ID TEXT [--ask] [--instant] | Reply to a letter addressed to you, which closes it | yes | | tmail instant [--format FORMAT] | For a harness hook: print the instant letters that wait for the running iteration | agent only; prints nothing in operator mode | | tmail requeue ID | Put one of your dead letters back in the inbox | yes | | tmail close ID [--note TEXT] | Archive a letter without a reply | operator only | | tmail read ID... | Mark letters read; a read notice to an agent closes | operator only | | tmail unread | Count open and unread letters, and open letters by sender and kind | operator only | | tmail clear --as agent:NAME [--yes] | Delete every open letter of an agent; asks for confirmation unless --yes | operator only | Every operator command takes --as. In agent mode --as and the operator-only commands are refused: an agent always acts as itself and answers its letters instead of archiving them. - --to takes a comma list of agent:<name , user:<login , plugin:<name , system:<component , queue:<prefix and group:<name . A group expands to every member except the sender. - --deadline is a Go duration such as 5m or an RFC 3339 time. When an agent's request is still open at that time, the agent receives a deadline notice from system:schedule with data.request id. A reply or an archive cancels it. A deadline on a request from any other principal is stored and listed but sends no notice. - reply also takes the text as --text; a TEXT of - reads standard input. With tariboy mail reply ID TEXT --as agent:NAME an operator replies on an agent's behalf; the reply carries data.on behalf = "operator". - sent, archive and inbox --all print a last next: line with the command for the next page when a page is full. The open inbox does not page: raise --limit instead. Examples: Routes Operator routes are registry commands on the daemon socket and the loopback listener; the OpenAPI snapshot describes their arguments and results. as defaults to the customer. | Route | Purpose | | --- | --- | | GET /api/mail?box=inbox\|sent\|archive&as=&limit=&before= | One mailbox view; a full page returns next before, an opaque cursor to pass back as before. The inbox pages oldest first, the other boxes newest first, and letters sharing one created at are never skipped | | GET /api/mail/{id}?as= | One letter and its reply | | POST /api/mail | Send: to, subject, text, kind, data, deadline, notice, instant, as | | POST /api/mail/{id}/reply | Reply: text, ask, instant, as | | POST /api/mail/{id}/close | Archive without a reply: note, as | | POST /api/mail/read | Mark read: ids, as | | POST /api/mail/{id}/requeue | Requeue a dead letter: as | | GET /api/mail/unread?as= | Open and unread counts, open letters by sender and kind | | POST /api/agents/{name}/mail/clear | Delete an agent's open letters | | POST /api/agents/{name}/messages/instant-senders | Read or set mail instant senders: senders, reset | | GET /api/mail/ws | Live hints, one frame {id, from, to, kind, ts} per written letter and per change of instant state | Agent routes: POST /tools/mail/<action with a JSON body, where the action is inbox (all), sent, archive, show (id), send (to, subject, text, kind, data, deadline, notice, instant), reply (id, text, ask, instant), requeue (id) or instant (no body; see the hook command). The mail capability gates them. An image declares it as plugin mail with the packaged skill mail; an image built before the mailbox declares messages with its messages skill, which the image contract accepts as an alias. Plugin routes: a plugin sends with POST /api/plugin/mail (to, subject, text, kind, data, notice, instant, idempotency key), authenticated by its plugin token, and receives the letters addressed to it at its own POST /deliver. See Plugins. Every route returns letters in one JSON shape: The prompt block The platform-owned # Task Processing Order block has a ## Messages section. When the agent has open letters, it lists them oldest first, up to messages batch, requests first and notices after them: A letter shows deadline: and data: lines only when they are set. A task.question letter carries one more line, answer: ttasks comment <task-key "<answer ". The subject of a task letter has the task key and title, for example Question on DEV-1: Ship the release. The body of a task.question or task.answered letter has the full text of the comment after its first line. With no open letters the section reads No incoming messages for this iteration. Requests the agent sent with a deadline and no answer follow under ### Awaiting replies, one line each with the id, the recipient, the age and the deadline. The image placeholders messages and awaiting-replies keep their names and map to the mail capability. The standing instruction is platform text, so an agent whose image still ships the old messages skill is told tmail reply. Instant letters An instant letter goes into the recipient's running iteration at the next end of a tool call. A tool call is one action of the harness, such as a shell command or a file edit. An ordinary letter waits for the next iteration. Send one with --instant on tmail send, tmail reply, tariboy mail send or tariboy mail reply, or with instant: true on the send and reply routes. If the agent has no running iteration, the letter wakes it like any other letter. Who may send an instant letter The daemon checks the flag in Send and in Reply, before it writes the letter: 1. A system: sender, a plugin other than plugin:telegram, and every other principal get instant not allowed (HTTP 403). 2. After group expansion, each recipient must be agent: . Another recipient gives instant recipient (HTTP 400). 3. The customer, user:<customer login , and plugin:telegram may always send. The Desktop operator sends as the customer. 4. An agent may send only when each recipient agent allows it. The recipient setting mail instant senders is a list of agent:<name principals. When the list is set, only the agents in it may send, and an empty list refuses every agent. When the list is not set, only the lead of the recipient's group may send, and never to itself. Set the list with tariboy agent messages instant-senders NAME --sender agent:LEAD, repeat --sender for more agents, and pass --sender '' for an empty list. --reset returns the setting to not set. Without flags the command prints the list. agent run takes the same list as mail instant senders. The agent view returns it, or null when it is not set. Delivery state Each letter has four fields for instant delivery. instant is the flag. instant state is empty on a letter without the flag. instant iteration and instant at are the iteration and the time of the delivery or of the prompt render. | instant state | Set when | | --- | --- | | waiting | The letter arrives while the iteration of the agent runs. It waits for a tool call | | queued | The letter arrives while no iteration runs, and the agent starts iterations on its own. The next iteration reads it | | stopped | The letter arrives while the agent cannot start an iteration on its own: it is stopped, halted by on error or on timeout, or on the bare image | | delivered | A hook gave the letter to the running iteration | | read | The letter was rendered into the prompt of an iteration before a hook gave it | | not delivered | The letter became dead before a hook gave it or a prompt rendered it | Each change of state sends a hint on /api/mail/ws. A requeued instant letter starts again with waiting, queued or stopped. The hook command tmail instant [--format FORMAT] is for a harness hook that runs after each tool call. Run it in agent mode: 1. The daemon sets TARIBOY INSTANT MAIL FLAG in the environment of each iteration. Its value is <base-dir /agents/<name /iterations/<iteration /instant-mail. 2. When an instant letter arrives in the waiting state, the daemon creates that empty file with mode 0600. 3. Without the file, tmail instant stops at once and does not call the daemon. 4. With the file, it calls POST /tools/mail/instant and waits at most 1.5 seconds. The daemon removes the file. Then, in one transaction, it marks each open instant letter in waiting, queued or stopped as delivered, adds one to its attempts, and records the audit event mail instant shown. A letter whose sixth attempt this would be becomes dead with reason attempts. 5. It prints the letters in the format that --format names: | --format | Output | | --- | --- | | text (default) | The block below | | json | {"ids":[...],"text":"..."} | | claude-post-tool-use | {"hookSpecificOutput":{"hookEventName":"PostToolUse","additionalContext":TEXT}} | | claude-post-tool-use-failure | The same, with "hookEventName":"PostToolUseFailure" | | claude-stop | {"decision":"block","reason":TEXT} | | codex-post-tool-use | The same as claude-post-tool-use | | codex-stop | The same as claude-stop | | opencode-tool-after | A blank line, then TEXT, for the OpenCode plugin to add to the tool result | TEXT is the block below. tmail builds the JSON itself, so a hook needs no jq, python or node. If the iteration already called loop.sh done, the daemon takes no letter and keeps the flag file. A Stop hook therefore never continues a finished iteration. The letter stays waiting, and the next prompt reads it. No letters, an error, the timeout and operator mode print nothing and exit 0. tmail instant writes nothing to standard error, because a hook can show that output to the model. A letter that a hook delivered stays open in the inbox: - A notice closes with close note read when the iteration finishes done. After an error, a timeout or a kill it stays open and the next prompt shows it. - A request stays open until tmail reply. The next prompt shows it again, with one more attempt. A hook never gets a letter that the prompt of the iteration already rendered, and it never gets the same letter twice. The release is frozen. Do not push. The body is in a code fence that is longer than every run of backticks in it. A body longer than 8,000 Unicode code points is cut to its first 8,000 and ends with the line (cut; full text: tmail show ). The text goes to the model only as the output of the hook, in the next request of the harness. The AI proxy does not change requests. Harness support | Harness | Interactive | Batch | | --- | --- | --- | | claude | hook | hook | | codex | hook | hook | | opencode | plugin, after a successful tool call | plugin, after a successful tool call | A turn that ends without a tool call does not get the letter in opencode. The letter stays waiting, and the next prompt reads it. For claude, the daemon writes a plugin with three hooks into /agents/ /harness-hooks/claude/. It passes the plugin with one more --plugin-dir flag, after the plugin of the image skills. The interactive mode and the batch mode get the same flag. | Claude Code event | Command | | --- | --- | | PostToolUse, every tool | tmail instant --format claude-post-tool-use | | PostToolUseFailure, every tool | tmail instant --format claude-post-tool-use-failure | | Stop | tmail instant --format claude-stop | The PostToolUse hooks add the letters to the context of the model after the tool call. The Stop hook stops the end of the turn, and the model continues with the letters. Each hook calls the absolute path of tmail that the daemon finds on the PATH of the iteration, and has a timeout of 5 seconds. The agent shell prologue therefore cannot change which tmail runs. For codex, the daemon writes no file. It adds the two hooks to the codex command as -c configuration overrides, which codex reads as one more configuration layer. CODEX HOME, HOME and XDG CONFIG HOME do not change, and no file goes into /.codex or the working directory. The interactive mode and the batch mode (codex exec) get the same arguments: | Codex event | Command | | --- | --- | | PostToolUse, every tool | tmail instant --format codex-post-tool-use | | Stop | tmail instant --format codex-stop | Codex runs PostToolUse also after a failed tool call. It has no separate failure event. Codex runs only trusted hooks, and it keeps the trust in the config.toml of the user. --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust lets the hooks run without that trust, for this run only. The flag also runs every other enabled hook without review: the hooks in /.codex/config.toml and the hooks of a trusted repository. Codex shows a warning about the flag in the codex exec event stream and on the TUI screen. The warning does not stop the iteration. The Codex approval mode section gives the security effect. The daemon connects the hooks only when all of these are true: - The harness is claude, version 2.1.227 or newer, or codex, version 0.141.0 or newer. The daemon runs claude --version or codex --version before each iteration. A version that the daemon cannot read counts as too old. - For codex, the daemon codex approval mode is yolo. In approve-for-me, the trust bypass would let an unreviewed hook run outside the sandbox. - The image is not bare, and the agent has the mail capability (or its old name messages). - tmail is on the PATH of the iteration. If a condition is false, or the daemon cannot write the plugin, the iteration starts without the hooks. Except for a missing capability or another harness, the daemon log has a warning. An instant letter then stays waiting or queued, the next iteration reads it, and its state becomes read. The same is true for a harness without hooks. For opencode, the daemon writes the plugin file /agents/ /harness-hooks/opencode/tariboy-instant-mail.js. It adds the file:// URL of that file to the plugin key of the configuration overlay in OPENCODE CONFIG CONTENT. It adds the key after its checks of the proxy routing, so these checks still refuse every other plugin. The daemon writes nothing into the working directory, into /.config/opencode or into the directory of the image skills, and it does not change HOME or XDG CONFIG HOME. The batch mode and the interactive mode run the same opencode run command with the same overlay. The plugin has one hook, tool.execute.after. After each successful tool call, it does these steps: 1. If the file in TARIBOY INSTANT MAIL FLAG does not exist, it stops. It starts no process. 2. It runs the absolute path of tmail with instant --format opencode-tool-after. It uses Bun.spawn, the process API of the runtime inside opencode, so the agent needs no node, bun, jq or python. 3. If tmail exits 0 and prints text, the plugin adds the text to the end of the tool result. The model reads it in the next request. If tmail fails, runs longer than 5 seconds or prints only to standard error, the tool result does not change. The plugin writes nothing to standard error. opencode does not call the hook after a failed tool call, so the letter waits for the next successful call or for the next prompt. The daemon connects the opencode plugin when all of these are true: - The harness is opencode, version 1.19.5 or newer. The daemon runs opencode --version before each iteration. A version that the daemon cannot read counts as too old. - The image is not bare, and the agent has the mail capability (or its old name messages). The image skills are not necessary. - tmail is on the PATH of the iteration, after the agent shell scripts ran. With any plugin, opencode installs the npm package @opencode-ai/plugin into each of its configuration directories, also into /.config/opencode, and waits for the install before it starts. opencode does this itself, and it has no setting to turn the install off. If the package is already there, the start takes no extra time. The first start after a new opencode version installs the package of that version. With network access, this took 13 to 70 seconds on a test host. Without network access, the install fails after about 72 seconds, and opencode then starts with the plugin. Each later start waits again, until an install succeeds. No timer of the daemon stops an iteration in this time, unless the agent has a timeout shorter than the wait. The image skills bridge of the agent is one of these configuration directories. Tariboy keeps the bridge with the installed package, so the install does not repeat in each iteration. The limits that stay with a hook or a plugin: - A long tool call holds the letter until the call ends. Nothing stops model output that has no tool call. - A letter that arrives after loop.sh done, or after the iteration ends, waits for the next prompt. - A failure to create the flag file is logged. The next iteration reads the letter. - Codex does not document hooks in -c overrides or the trust bypass as a stable interface. If a newer codex changes them, the hooks do not run and the next iteration reads the letter. The version check finds only an older codex. Agent settings | Setting | Default | Effect | | --- | --- | --- | | messages batch | 10 | Most letters rendered into one prompt; a value of 0 or less falls back to 10 | | messages max queue | 100 for new agents | Most open letters in the agent's inbox; a letter beyond it is stored dead with reason queue limit | | mail instant senders | not set | The agents that may send this agent an instant letter. Not set: the lead of its group. An empty list: no agent | | enabled | — | Set by agent start, cleared by agent stop. A stopped agent keeps its letters open and does not run for them. A stop-policy halt has the same effect until the next start | | interval s | — | Timer interval. A letter wakes a started agent without a positive interval | | group | — | Membership that group: expands over | Set the two mail fields with tariboy agent messages batch NAME VALUE and tariboy agent messages max-queue NAME VALUE, in the Desktop agent configuration, or with the compose messages block. Existing values and values copied by Clone are not rewritten when a default changes. Agent status reports the open inbox count as messages pending and messages queue full when it is at the cap. Schedules and scripts A schedule sends a letter from system:schedule each time it fires. It stores agent, kind (oneshot or cron), spec, its recipient, a message template, next fire at and enabled. The agent route POST /tools/schedule/add takes to, a principal; without it the schedule writes to the owning agent. The template may set subject, text, kind (default schedule.fire), data and notice; a schedule letter is a request unless notice is set. An older skill that still sends channel is mapped: chat:service: and agent: :inbox become agent: , and any other channel the owning agent. Scripts run only local commands. A non-quiet run sends a script.result request from system:scripts to the owning agent. Its data holds the script and run ids, name, mode, status, optional exit code and the absolute log path; the log starts with the resolved working directory, and the combined output stays in that file. Sending the result also stops a recurring definition, so one failing command cannot flood the inbox; tscripts rerun scr-... resumes it once the agent has handled the letter. A quiet run, one that exits 111, sends nothing and keeps the schedule running. Errors | Code | When | | --- | --- | | unknown recipient | A recipient is not an existing agent, the customer, an enabled plugin that declares mail.receive, a system: principal, an existing queue or an existing group | | unknown sender | --as names a principal that cannot send | | empty group | The group has no member other than the sender | | forbidden | Reply, close, read or requeue by a principal that is not the recipient; show by one that is neither sender nor recipient | | answer on task | A reply to a task.question; the message names the ttasks comment command | | queue limit | A requeue while the agent's inbox is at its cap (HTTP 409); close letters first | | inbox full | POST /api/plugin/mail to an agent whose inbox is at its cap; the letter is stored dead | | instant not allowed | An instant letter from a sender that may not set the flag (HTTP 403). The message is instant delivery is not allowed from this sender | | instant recipient | An instant letter to a recipient that is not an agent, also after group expansion (HTTP 400) | | bad mail instant senders | A value of mail instant senders is not an existing agent: | | not found | No letter has that id | | invalid argument | A missing recipient, a reply without text, a bad deadline, a requeue of a letter that is not dead | Debugging an agent through its mail An agent's mail is its message history. Read it as the agent with --as: - A letter was sent, the agent does not act on it. - Check the agent is started; a stopped agent keeps its letters open. - Check the letter is in its inbox, not in its archive as dead. Requeue a dead letter with tariboy mail requeue ID --as agent:NAME. - Check messages queue full in agent status. At the cap new letters are stored dead with queue limit; plugins receive 409 inbox full. - A letter appears in every prompt. It is a request nobody answered, or a notice rendered into iterations that failed. The agent closes a request with tmail reply; an operator can reply on its behalf or archive it with tariboy mail close ID --as agent:NAME. After five renders it is dead-lettered with reason attempts. - A task.question letter does not close. It closes only when the question is answered on its task or a workflow outcome resolves it; tmail reply refuses it with answer on task. - A send fails with unknown recipient. Check the principal prefix and name; a channel name such as agent:worker:inbox is not a principal. - An old image fails with unknown route. Its scripts/messages.sh calls routes the mailbox removed. The prompt still names tmail reply; rebuild the image with the mail skill. - A plugin does not receive replies. Read tariboy mail inbox --as plugin:NAME: open letters there are waiting for a successful /deliver, and dead ones in its archive failed five times. - An agent's inbox must be emptied. tariboy mail clear --as agent:NAME deletes its open letters after a confirmation prompt (--yes skips it); tariboy agent mail clear NAME` does the same without a prompt. Closed and dead letters stay.
description: The tmail and tariboy mail commands, the mail routes, the prompt block, the agent settings, and how to debug an agent through its inbox, sent and archive.
title: Mail reference

content: Tariboy manages a remote daemon through the SSH configuration already used by the operator. The desktop does not implement a second SSH stack. Compatibility | Component | Alpha support | | --- | --- | | Desktop | macOS 12+, Apple Silicon | | Automatic remote install | Linux x86 64 and aarch64, macOS arm64 (Apple Silicon) | | SSH | system ssh | | Server download | outbound HTTPS from the host to github.com and its release file domain | | Remote install root | /.local/lib/tariboy | | Remote CLI links | /.local/bin | | Daemon HTTP | remote loopback only | | Tunnel | local loopback forwarding over SSH | | Android app | signed arm64 APK in each release; forwarded loopback port or HTTPS server, no SSH hosts | Automatic installation requires a writable /.local, python3, curl or wget, tar, and sha256sum or shasum. Linux hosts also need flock. Preflight names each missing program, and Desktop does not start the install. The desktop app package carries only the binaries of its own platform, which run the local daemon. It carries no server builds. The server downloads its build from the GitHub release of the Desktop version. Desktop selects the archive from the uname -s and uname -m of the host: | Host | Archive | | --- | --- | | Linux x86 64 | tariboy <version linux-x86 64.tar.gz | | Linux aarch64 or arm64 | tariboy <version linux-aarch64.tar.gz | | macOS (Darwin) arm64 | tariboy <version darwin-arm64.tar.gz | Install and update read the platform and architecture again in preflight every time. Desktop reports any other combination as unsupported, and nothing changes on the host. Examples are 32-bit armv7l and an Intel Mac (Darwin/x86 64, also a shell that runs under Rosetta). macOS ships neither flock nor sha256sum, so on a Mac the installer takes its lock through python3 and verifies checksums with shasum -a 256. On macOS, /usr/bin/python3 works only once the Command Line Tools are installed (xcode-select --install). Homebrew installs tmux and harnesses under /opt/homebrew/bin; that directory must be on the login shell's PATH or the daemon reports them as missing tools. A daemon started over SSH does not start again after the Mac reboots; connect from Desktop to start it. The Python runtime executes the standard-library agent tool scripts. Preflight also reports tmux, git, npx, Claude, Codex, OpenCode, and the Cursor CLI (its agent executable) so you can see which workflows are available; a missing harness is listed as an optional tool and does not block installation. At least one chosen harness must be installed on the remote host. Account PATH and harness launch A Desktop-managed local daemon is started inside the account's login shell, so it inherits the whole environment a new terminal gets — PATH and every other variable your shell startup files export. Desktop reads the login shell from the operating-system account record, so this works even when Finder supplied no useful SHELL. A daemon launched through SSH or an ordinary terminal already inherits that environment from its launcher. When no usable account shell exists, the daemon is started directly with a bootstrap PATH: whatever the launcher had, plus /.local/bin and the standard system and package-manager locations. Such a daemon then resolves the account PATH itself, once, from a bounded interactive-login-shell probe. If that probe fails the daemon stays available with the inherited PATH and logs one stable warning naming only the class of failure — never the path or shell startup output. Before each iteration, Tariboy checks the selected harness executable using the final agent environment. For non-bare images it resolves python3 from the same environment and passes that absolute interpreter to skill launchers. An agent's explicit PATH overrides the daemon baseline and therefore must retain both prerequisites; non-bare images then prepend their agent bin directory, while bare images do not. After resolving PATH, the daemon appends /.local/bin when it is missing, so agents find the managed tariboy and ttasks links. Daemon host tools Every GET /api/daemon/status checks the daemon PATH, the one iterations start from, for the commands the daemon and its agents need: | Tool | Needed for | Install | | --- | --- | --- | | tmux | agent terminal sessions | system package manager | | bash | running iterations | system package manager | | python3 | agent tool scripts | system package manager | | git | adding and refreshing Stores | system package manager | | npx | building images that carry skills-lock.json | Node.js (npm ships npx) | | tariboy, ttasks, tmail, tscripts | Tariboy commands inside agents | Tariboy CLI links in /.local/bin | | claude, codex, opencode or agent | at least one agent harness | the harness vendor's installer | The response carries state (ready or error), missing tools (name, purpose and install hint for each missing tool) and message, for example missing required tools: tmux, npx; install them on the daemon host. The check only looks for an executable on PATH; it does not install anything, because install commands differ between systems. The error state blocks nothing: the API, tunnel and running agents keep working, and the state returns to ready on the next status read after you install the tool, without a daemon restart. Desktop shows a connected SSH host whose daemon reports missing tools as error with the message, and the local daemon banner names the missing tools in the desktop app and in a browser. A host's state is read when its tunnel connects, so reconnect it after installing the tools. Add a host 1. Confirm the alias works in Terminal: ssh build-box. 2. Add the same alias under Settings → Hosts . 3. Choose one of the two setup modes: - Install Tariboy (default) runs preflight, has the host download and install the matching release, starts the daemon, and connects the tunnel. - Connect to existing Tariboy saves the host and connects without uploading, installing, activating, starting, or restarting anything. Both modes use system OpenSSH and its existing host-key, ssh-agent, ProxyJump, and authentication rules. Connect to existing Tariboy creates an independent dynamic local forward from 127.0.0.1 to the remote daemon at 127.0.0.1:9990, then checks daemon health through that tunnel. A successful probe marks the host Ready, and the ordinary saved-host reconnect restores the tunnel after Desktop restarts. If no daemon answers at the remote loopback port, Desktop keeps the saved host and does not install or start anything automatically. The dialog offers to retry the connection or run Install Tariboy explicitly. A daemon version different from Desktop is allowed to connect; the existing Update indicator reports the mismatch without triggering an update. System OpenSSH honors /.ssh/config, ProxyJump, ssh-agent, hardware-backed keys, known hosts, and organization authentication. Tariboy never adds StrictHostKeyChecking=no, copies private keys, or stores prompt replies. Install and update behavior Update Tariboy on a Linux host whose CLI supports tariboy update --cleanup runs on the server: Desktop runs tariboy update <Desktop version --cleanup on the server over SSH. The server downloads and verifies that release from GitHub, installs it with the same fixed installer, restarts the daemon, and deletes old releases, keeping the five newest and the active one. Desktop then checks the reported version, as below. When the command fails after the managed links already moved to the new release, Desktop reactivates and restarts the previous release; a failure before the switch leaves the host unchanged. The first install, every macOS host, and a host whose CLI predates --cleanup use the Desktop installer path below. After one such update, the next update of a Linux host runs on the server. Desktop uploads no binaries. Over SSH, it runs two fixed scripts that are built into Desktop: 1. remote-download.sh downloads SHA256SUMS and the archive for the host from <base URL /download/v<Desktop version / with curl, or with wget when curl is missing. It makes sure that the archive checksum matches the line in SHA256SUMS. It accepts only plain file names at the archive root. Then it unpacks the archive into a staging directory. 2. remote-install.sh installs the staged release. The base URL is https://github.com/alekzonder/tariboy/releases. If TARIBOY UPDATE BASE URL is set in the environment of the desktop app, it replaces the base URL, for example for a mirror. tariboy update reads the same variable. The base URL must start with https://, and it can contain only letters, digits, and . :/-. The server needs outbound HTTPS to GitHub, and the Desktop version must be a published release with a server archive. A build of an unpublished version, for example a local development build, gets a 404 response. Set TARIBOY UPDATE BASE URL to a mirror that has the archives of that version. The download has a budget of ten minutes. If the download or the checksum fails, the step Download release fails with the URL in the message. Desktop removes the staging directory, and the active release on the host does not change. Desktop does not fall back to an upload. The archive holds the seven binaries, a version marker, checksums, and a copy of the installer. Desktop does not run that copy. It runs its own built-in remote-install.sh, which: - validates checksums; - serializes installs with flock, or with a python3 file lock where flock is absent (macOS); - publishes a versioned release directory; - atomically switches managed CLI symlinks; - verifies the daemon reports the requested version; - rolls back the previous release on activation failure. Reactivating a release that predates tariboy-tasks removes both newer Tasks links transactionally. Selecting the newer release again restores them; every selected release must contain its required payloads before links switch. An update refuses to replace unrelated regular files in /.local/bin. Choosing Update Tariboy authorizes the version switch and daemon restart; connect, download, activation, restart, and reconnect remain one operation with one operation ID. Daemon 0.10.1 and newer preserves running shims across that restart, so active agents do not require a second confirmation. A legacy daemon older than 0.10.1 instead fails closed before activation when active work exists or cannot be checked. Update a host from its own shell A Linux host can also fetch and install a release itself, without the desktop app: latest resolves the newest published GitHub release; an explicit version installs exactly that release. The command downloads the archive for its own architecture, tariboy <version linux-x86 64.tar.gz or tariboy <version linux-aarch64.tar.gz, and the release SHA256SUMS, verifies the archive checksum before unpacking, stages it under /.local/lib/tariboy/.stage-<token , and then runs the same fixed installer the desktop app runs — so checksum validation, flock serialization, atomic symlink switching, and rollback are identical. A running daemon is restarted onto the new release and must report the installed version; a stopped daemon is left stopped. The command updates only an installer-managed linux-x86 64 or linux-aarch64 installation, where /.local/bin/tariboy is a symlink into /.local/lib/tariboy/<version /. It refuses anything else — a hand-placed binary or a macOS installation belonging to the app bundle — and changes nothing. A Desktop-managed macOS server is updated with the Desktop update button instead. --force reinstalls a version that is already active. TARIBOY UPDATE BASE URL overrides the GitHub releases root for a mirror. --cleanup deletes older releases from /.local/lib/tariboy after the update succeeds, or right away when the version is already installed. It keeps the newest five releases by version number, or --keep N, and always the active release among them. It removes only release directories whose VERSION file matches their name, leaves staging directories and other files alone, and holds the installer lock while it works. A failed daemon restart skips the cleanup so the previous release stays available for rollback, and a cleanup error is only a warning: the update itself has already succeeded. Releases published before this archive existed cannot be fetched this way: move to the first release that carries it through the desktop app once, then tariboy update works from there. The host dialog presents provisioning and updates as one vertical sequence: 1. Connect to host. 2. Check server. 3. Download release, or Get release for an update. The server downloads the release in both cases. 4. Install release. 5. Start or restart Tariboy. 6. Connect or reconnect to Tariboy. Only one step is current, and a failure remains attached to the step that failed even when rollback successfully reconnects the previous daemon. Process stdout and stderr are diagnostic streams; stderr by itself does not mean that the command failed. The main flow shows only the actionable result. Checksums, raw JSON, and command output are available under the closed Technical details disclosure and cannot expand the dialog horizontally. The dialog offers one primary action for its current state: add, save and reconnect, update, or retry. If update reports that a path such as /.local/bin/tariboyd is an existing non-symlink, move that file out of the way yourself and retry. Desktop does not delete or overwrite it automatically. Host and agent lists show their compact Update action only when tunnel health has reported a non-empty remote daemon version that differs from the current Desktop bundle version. Matching or unknown versions do not show the indicator. The manual Edit host → Update Tariboy action remains available when an operator deliberately wants to reinstall the current release. Inside an SSH agent workspace, Open in VS Code opens the displayed effective working directory through VS Code Remote SSH using the same saved SSH config alias in a new editor window. Local agents open as ordinary local folders in a new editor window. HTTPS hosts do not show the action because they have no SSH identity. Missing harnesses, tmux, git and npx are reported separately as agent workflow prerequisites. They do not make an otherwise successful Tariboy update appear failed. Platform, architecture, writable install root, python3, and, on Linux, flock remain installation requirements. Connection lifecycle The remote daemon binds 127.0.0.1. The desktop starts an SSH local-forwarding tunnel, probes health through it, retries bounded transient failures, and treats authentication or host-key mismatch as terminal until the operator acts. Quitting the app stops local tunnels but leaves remote daemons running. The next launch reconnects saved hosts. Removing and uninstalling Removing a host from Settings stops its tunnel and deletes local host metadata and any Keychain token. It intentionally does not stop the remote daemon or delete remote data. To uninstall remotely after confirming no work is active: Deleting /.tariboy removes remote agents, images, audit, and database state. Back it up first and perform that separate destructive step only when data removal is intended. Android app The Android APK runs the same UI without a local daemon, SSH hosts, tunnels, or host provisioning. Each release attaches Tariboy X.Y.Z android-arm64.apk; the release notes give its signing certificate fingerprint (see Android release APK). It connects to two kinds of servers: - A forwarded loopback port. You forward a daemon's listener to the phone yourself, for example ssh -L 9990:127.0.0.1:9990 host in Termux or adb reverse tcp:9990 tcp:9990 from a computer. Then Add host with base URL http://127.0.0.1:9990 and an empty token. Forward a token listener instead if you prefer, and enter its token. - An HTTPS server with a bearer token, as in the browser. Plain http:// is accepted only for 127.0.0.1, localhost, or [::1] with a port; Android blocks cleartext to every other host. The app does not start or restart the forward: while it is down the server shows as unreachable. A forward can accept a connection and never answer, for example when the SSH session behind it lost the server. The app stops each read after 30 seconds and keeps the last data on screen. When you come back to the app, for example after you restart the forward in Termux, it opens its live connections again and rereads the screen. You do not have to restart the app. If the forward comes back while the app stays open, reads recover in 30 seconds, but live task updates can wait until you leave the app and come back. The daemon must be this release or newer, because only it allows the Android app's origin http://tauri.localhost on its loopback listener. An older daemon answers, but the WebView blocks its responses; forward its token listener instead. Any app on the phone can reach a forwarded tokenless port while the forward is up. A token lives in WebView session storage and must be entered again after Android stops the app; the server list is kept. Web links open in the phone's default browser, never inside the app: links in chat messages and task descriptions on a tap, and http:// or https:// text in the Terminal tab on a tap (there is no Command key). Other link schemes open nothing. If no browser can open the address, nothing opens and the app shows no message. On a phone or a tablet narrower than 768 CSS pixels the sidebar is a drawer: the menu button at the left of the titlebar opens it, and picking an item, an agent, a host or a team closes it. See Web UI.
description: Connect, provision, update, and remove Linux and macOS hosts through system OpenSSH.
title: Remote hosts

content: The alpha is designed for named internal partners and trusted hosts. It has no built-in product analytics. OTLP export is disabled by default and activates only when an operator explicitly sets OTEL EXPORTER OTLP ENDPOINT or the persisted otlp endpoint daemon setting. Network boundaries - Local and remote daemon HTTP listeners bind loopback. - Remote access uses an SSH local-forwarding tunnel. - System OpenSSH owns host-key verification, agent use, ProxyJump, and 2FA. - Tariboy never disables strict host-key checking. - Non-loopback daemon TCP requires a bearer token file. - The tokenless loopback web listener echoes CORS only for loopback http origins, the macOS app origin tauri://localhost, and the Android app origin http://tauri.localhost, each matched exactly. Browsers resolve .localhost to loopback, so the Android origin is that app's WebView or a loopback port-80 page, which http://localhost already covered. The Host check is unchanged. - Every daemon HTTP server (the unix socket, daemon TCP, the loopback web listener, the agent tools socket, and the AI proxy) closes a connection whose request headers take more than 10 seconds, closes idle keep-alive connections after 120 seconds, and refuses headers larger than 64 KiB. The servers set no read or write timeout for the whole request, because SSE, websockets, terminals and model responses stay open for a long time. - A command request body is limited to 1 MiB and a larger body gets HTTP 413 too large. A route raises its own limit only where it needs to: file uploads, queue secrets (512 KiB), and the two text-file editors (the agent file editor and image source files), whose limit fits their largest file after JSON escaping. The agent tools API limits every body to 1 MiB. - The operator API and the agent tools API map a domain error to an HTTP status and code in one place, so both give the same answer. For example, an unknown script is 404 not found and an active script is 409 script active on both. Any other error is HTTP 500 internal with the fixed text "internal error, see daemon log", and its detail goes only to the daemon log. A body that is not valid JSON gets 400 bad json with a fixed text, not the text of the JSON decoder. - Every websocket route (Tasks, message and agent-state hints, and the agent terminal) checks the browser Origin when the request has no bearer token: only the web listener's allowed origins above may open it, and any other origin gets HTTP 403 forbidden origin. A request with a valid bearer token may come from any origin, because a federated /terminals page on one daemon opens sockets on another. A terminal websocket accepts frames of at most 8 MiB (one paste); a larger frame closes the socket with "message too big". - The Android app permits cleartext only to 127.0.0.1, localhost, and ::1 through its network security config, and its WebView has no Tauri IPC permissions. It keeps server tokens in WebView session storage, not a keystore. - The Android app's native navigation guard decides every top-level WebView navigation. Only the app's fixed origin tauri.localhost (and, in a debug build, its configured dev server) loads inside the WebView. The page that is shown now never widens that. Any other http or https address is cancelled and given to the system browser through the opener plugin in a background task. The navigation callback returns without waiting for the browser. If opening fails, navigation stays cancelled and the current page stays in place. Every other scheme (javascript:, file:, intent:, and the rest) is cancelled and opens nothing. The guard never logs the address or raw opener error, because either can carry a token. An opener failure logs only the fixed message could not open a web link in the browser. Credentials SSH private keys remain with OpenSSH and are never copied. Interactive prompt replies live in memory only and are redacted from events. Manual HTTPS host tokens live in macOS Keychain under service app.tariboy.desktop.host, keyed by host ID. Host registry JSON contains no tokens. The AI proxy gives scoped short-lived tokens to harnesses/plugins and scrubs upstream provider keys from plugin environments. Audit transcripts contain model traffic and are sensitive operator data even though support bundles exclude them. Active iteration tokens and the stable loopback proxy address are carried across a daemon restart in /.tariboy/aiproxy-handoff.json. The base directory is owner-only and the handoff file plus atomic temporary files use mode 0600. Tokens are never logged, audited, stored in SQLite, or included in support bundles. Startup prunes leases that no longer map to a running iteration; adoption revokes the remaining lease when its shim finishes. OpenCode leases also carry the prepared provider addresses. Routes cannot be chosen from request-supplied URLs, and cross-origin upstream redirects remain blocked. OpenCode retains its own API-key environment and authentication files; the proxy forwards those credentials to the bound provider without persisting them in the lease. OAuth and external OpenCode plugins are unsupported because their transport hooks can bypass the configured SDK address, so preparation rejects them. The check has no exception: it refuses a plugin from the user configuration, the project, OPENCODE CONFIG DIR and the original OPENCODE CONFIG CONTENT. Tariboy adds its own instant mail plugin to the overlay only after the check passed. The plugin file is in the agent directory, <base-dir /agents/<name /harness-hooks/opencode/, with mode 0700 on the directory. The plugin only adds tmail instant output to tool results, and model requests still go to the proxy addresses of the overlay. Tariboy writes nothing into /.config/opencode and does not change HOME or XDG CONFIG HOME. opencode itself installs the npm package @opencode-ai/plugin into its configuration directories when a plugin is loaded, also into /.config/opencode and the image skills bridge. The integrity check of an OpenCode skills bridge skips only these install entries at the bridge root: node modules/, package.json, package-lock.json, bun.lock and .gitignore. Without this exception, each install made the bridge invalid, and the next iteration rebuilt it and waited for the install again. The check still covers the modes and contents of the skills, the generated files and each other entry. Bridges of other harnesses have no exception. The complete temporary OPENCODE CONFIG CONTENT value is masked in launch logs and audit, and probe output is never included in failures. The handoff file remains owner-only and excluded from diagnostics. This routing controls ordinary harness requests, not arbitrary network commands an agent can execute.
