The compact panel above it owns the current decision and pause controls. The workflow assigns pool work, so Save never changes the assignee. In an open, unpaused pool status the Assignee field is a list of the members of that status's pool: choosing one runs workflow reassign at once (see Changing the holder), and a refusal shows its message under the field. In any other status the assignee is read-only text. The sheet has no Move to another server… , because the daemon refuses to export a workflow task. Its actions menu offers Move to queue… instead (see Tasks). The panel follows the task's events as well as its revision: a rejected request, a script run, or another event refetches the view while the sheet is open, and an older response never replaces a newer one. The workflow view retains these controls and details: - Problem. Appears when something needs a person and the task is not paused, with a title, the script's own message as text, how close the task is to a pause (2 of 5 rejections, from the visit counters and the status limits), and a line that says what to do. The first that applies is shown: a failed request of the current visit (a check could not run: the run's log opens by itself, and Retry sends POST /api/tasks/{key}/workflow/requests/{id}/retry and follows the new request like an outcome button, unless the task is paused); a rejected request of the current visit (the advice names the agent in a pool status and the artifact or a return to the agent in a customer status; the run's Log is on demand); a failed watch in a script status, with its log open; a pool status with no agent free; and, quietly, a holder that ended iterations without a transition request. A request from an earlier visit, a closed task, and a pending request show nothing here. - Workflow. The statuses of the pinned image in manifest order: the current one marked, the visited ones ticked, and a return count on a status the task came back to from a later one. A status opens to show its owner, its instruction file, its watch script with the image's description, schedule, and timeout, each way out with the artifacts it requires and its checks (script, description, run as, and timeout), and the effective limits. The row wraps on a narrow screen. - Header. name@version, step k of n, the status, the owner, and the holder, with the labeled actions Run watch now , Return to agent… , Upgrade to NAME@VERSION… , Move to status… , and Cancel task ; see below. - Outcomes. The workflow details show each declared outcome, its target, required artifacts, and checks. Each check keeps its description, resolved run as, and timeout. The compact decision panel owns customer outcome buttons and the Outcome message. Pool and script outcomes remain available for reference, because the agent or watch script decides. - Artifacts. Decision materials list the artifacts required by transitions into and out of the current status, with their transition names. The lower workflow details retain all declared artifacts. Each artifact shows its description and current value as Markdown, with a Markdown / Text switch. Long values collapse to six lines or 600 characters and expand in place. Edit and History remain available, and History loads earlier values on demand. A declared artifact with no value shows Set. Editing is disabled once the task is closed. - Runs. The latest 20 script runs with kind, script, state, verdict, exit code, and times. The verdict carries the tone: a failure or rejection is red, a pass or outcome green, a quiet run dim. A Log toggle loads the log on demand and says when it is truncated; while a run is pending or running, an open log has Refresh . Who may read a log is described in Runs and logs; a refusal is shown in place of the log. - Visits. Every stay in a status, with who entered it, when it was left and by which outcome, and the message. A visit made under an earlier workflow version carries that version, as @VERSION. - Return to agent. Sends the task back to a pool status with an optional message the agent reads in its Goal as the transition message. The targets are the pool statuses a declared outcome of the current status leads to, the pool statuses the task visited before, newest first, and, for a paused pool status, the status itself as a restart; the most recently visited one is chosen first. In a customer status a declared outcome is sent as an advance with the message; everywhere else, and for a paused task, the operator's move is sent with the message as its reason, after a confirmation that says so. The action is hidden on a closed task and on an unpaused pool status an agent already holds. - Run watch now. Starts the watch script of the current status at once, without a confirmation; see Watch scripts. The action is shown only on an open, unpaused task in a script status that has a watch. It is disabled while a script run of the task is pending or running. After the request the panel reloads, and the new run shows under Runs . A refusal shows the daemon's message under the header. - Move and cancel. Move to status… offers every declared status but the current one, terminal statuses grouped last, and takes an optional reason; a move to a terminal status closes the task. Cancel task is hidden once the task is closed. Both ask for confirmation, because they skip outcomes, checks, and required artifacts and stop the current scripts. The header actions are shown only to a principal that may edit the task. - Upgrade. Upgrade to NAME@VERSION… is shown on an open task whose queue is bound to another version than the task's. It takes an optional reason and asks for confirmation, then restarts the task at the first status of that version; see Upgrading a task to the queue version. A refusal shows the daemon's message in the form. The step marks, the return counts, and the targets of Return to agent… read only the visits of the task's current version. Messages and logs are text; Desktop never interprets them as Markdown or HTML. Artifact values render as Markdown without raw HTML, or as text when switched. After an action in the sheet the task list reloads as well, so its row agrees with the sheet. Queue settings Manage queues… opens a large dialog; on a phone it fills the screen. The left side lists the queues. Each row shows the queue prefix and name, the bound workflow as name@version (or flexible ), and a red dot when a pool that the bound workflow uses has no agents. New queue opens the create form on the right. Choose a queue to open it on the right, in tabs. On a phone the list and the queue take turns, and Back to queues returns to the list. Closing the dialog drops every unsaved edit. - General. The queue name, description, owner agents, and responsible agent, saved with Save and the queue revision. - Workflow. The bound image's name, version, and the first 12 characters of its digest, or No workflow . The name links to the image's page in Workflow images , by its version tag when one names the bound content and by digest otherwise. A binding made by a tag ends with follows and the tag, for example follows latest: new tasks get the version that tag names. Choose an image as name:tag and press Bind . Choose name:latest to follow each new build; Clear asks for confirmation and unbinds. A binding changed elsewhere (revision conflict) is reloaded with a notice so you can retry. Below the binding, Statuses lists every status of the bound image in manifest order: its owner and its outcomes as outcome → status. A pool owner shows its number of agents; a pool without agents is red. Click a pool to open the Pools tab. When you choose an image in the select, the list shows that image's statuses before you bind it, so you can see which pools it needs. A bind refused with workflow pool empty or workflow secret missing lists the names with Open Pools or Open Environment ; a pool leaves the list once it has agents. - Pools. One row per pool: first the pools the bound workflow uses, also before they exist, and the pools a refused bind named, then the queue's other pools. A row shows the statuses that use the pool and its agents. Remove an agent with its × , type a name (the server's agents are suggested) and press Add , then Save . Save sends the complete list with the pool revision. Add pool adds a row for a pool by name. A pool changed elsewhere is reloaded with a notice; any other refusal, for example emptying a pool the workflow uses, shows on the row and keeps your edit. - Environment. Two blocks. Env lists the plain env vars with their values and update time, a form to Set one, and Remove with confirmation. Secrets lists the secret keys with their update time, a form to Set one, and Remove with confirmation. A secret value is write-only: it is cleared from the form when sent and is never read back or shown. Setting a key that the other block holds asks first, then moves the key. A bind refused with workflow secret missing lists the missing names in the Secrets block until either block sets them. Each secret the bound image requires that the global env holds shows as NAME present in global env, with overridden by the queue secret when the queue sets it too. For a bound queue, the key field of each block suggests the names the Workflowfile declares: env keys for Env and requires secrets for Secrets . Below the form, Declared in Workflowfile: shows one button for each such name that has no value in either block. Click it to fill the key, then type the value. Hover over an Env name to see its default. - Sources. Only for a bound queue: the sources of the workflow and their runs; see Sources. What Desktop does not do - There is no filter by workflow status. The Active, Closed, and All segment uses the daemon's categories. - It does not edit a workflow. The statuses in queue settings are read from the image; change the Workflowfile.yaml` and build a new image instead. - It does not delete a pool. Save with no agents empties it, and the daemon refuses that while the bound workflow uses the pool.
description: Bind a workflow image to a queue so its tasks move through statuses with one owner each, gated by check scripts and driven by watch scripts; queue secrets, run modes, commands, routes, and troubleshooting.
title: Task workflows

content: Native Tasks are Tariboy's central work domain. They live in the existing host-local tariboyd.db. Every daemon starts with a default TASK queue named Tasks, with no owners and no responsible agent. At each start tariboyd creates it when it is absent and records a task.queue created event by system:tariboyd; an existing TASK queue, whether created by hand or by compose, is left unchanged. A queue with no workflow holds flexible tasks, the model described below. A queue can instead be bound to a workflow image: a task created there pins that version and follows its statuses, each owned by an agent pool, the customer, or a script. See Task workflows. Every task has a category field, which is one of the five statuses below and equals status for a flexible task. Work model Every task belongs to a queue and receives an immutable queue key such as TEST-fkt3: the queue prefix, a dash, and four random characters drawn from 23456789abcdefghjkmnpqrstuvwxyz — the digits and lowercase letters that cannot be confused for one another when a key is read aloud or copied by hand. The key is random rather than a per-queue counter so that two daemons never mint the same key, which is what lets a task keep its key when it moves to another server. Keys are matched case-insensitively, so test-FKT3 finds the same task. Daemons upgraded from a numeric key such as TEST-12 rewrite every task to a random key on first start and keep the old key as a permanent alias, so a key already written into an agent context, a branch name, a pull request title or a comment keeps resolving to its task. A task records its author, customer, assignee, optional group, status, priority, pull request URL, block reason, parent, ordered siblings, comments, dependencies, and principals whose answers are still required. A pull request is an optional normalized absolute http or https URL without embedded credentials; an empty value clears it. Priority is one of P0 Critical, P1 High, P2 Normal (the default), or P3 Low. Root and nested sibling sets sort by priority, then manual position, then task key. Parent/child depth is unlimited. Assigning or authoring an ancestor exposes its descendant subtree in the same queue to that agent; otherwise an agent sees only nested tasks it authored, tasks assigned to it, and tasks visible through its current group. Authoring alone does not expose a root task: see Filing a task into a queue below. Ancestors needed to render an allowed descendant are returned as read-only context. Group membership is resolved when access is checked, not copied into the task. A queue boundary stops both rules. Write access does not pass from a parent to a child in another queue, and the read-only ancestor chain stops at a parent in another queue. See Subtasks in another queue. An agent explicitly mentioned in an open answer request receives response-only access: it can read the task and add the answering comment, but cannot edit, complete, move, or change relations unless another ACL rule also grants write access. blocks is directional and cycle-checked; related is symmetric. A task is ready when it is open, unassigned, has no manual block, and has no active incoming blocker. Completing a parent with active descendants returns a conflict unless the caller explicitly chooses complete anyway . This check counts every descendant, also one the caller cannot see. Reading one task also returns descendants and active descendants for the part of its subtree that the reader can see, so a tree that keeps growing instead of closing is visible without walking it. The same read (tasks.get, also ttasks show --json) also returns the direct family of the task. The visibility rule of tasks.list decides what the reader sees: | Field | Content | | --- | --- | | parent | key, title, queue, and access of the parent. The field is absent for a root task and for a parent that the reader cannot see. | | children | The direct children that the reader can see, from every queue and every category, closed ones included. Each item has the fields of a tasks.list row. The order is the tree order: priority, position, key. | | hidden children | The number of direct children that the reader cannot see. The response gives no key, title, or queue for them. | Flexible tasks use open, in progress, wait customer, done, or cancelled status. When the assigned agent asks the task customer a question, the same comment transaction moves a non-terminal task to wait customer. The last customer answer returns it to in progress, unless an operator made an intervening status change. A customer comment that mentions the assigned agent (@agent:NAME) also returns a wait customer task to in progress once no question to the customer stays open. Questions for another principal do not change status. A task that follows a workflow reports the workflow status (plan, review, ...) as status and one of those five values as category, which the daemon derives from the status owner; waiting on says whether a wait customer task waits on the customer, on a script, or on a pause. A pause is a task the daemon stopped because it stalled (too many idle iterations, rejected requests, or script failures, or a holder that cannot work): it keeps its status and assignee, shows for the customer as a task in wait customer with an open wait and a comment that names the reason and the three commands to decide, and resumes only with ttasks workflow resume KEY --decision continue|release or ends with ttasks cancel; a plain reply does not resume it. See Pauses. The daemon assigns the task, so ttasks done, ttasks update --status, ttasks assign, and ttasks ready --claim are refused with workflow managed. The agent or customer that owns the status leaves it with ttasks advance; a transition that declares checks applies only after the workflow's check scripts pass, and a status owned by a script is left when its watch script reports an outcome. Status filters, blocking relations, and the active-descendants check use the category for every task. See Task workflows. Filing a task into a queue Any agent identity may create a root task in any existing queue. Creating one never grants queue ownership or triager status, and the queue's own tasks stay hidden. What the agent gets back depends on whether it runs that queue — that is, whether it is the queue's responsible agent or one of its owners: - Runs the queue. Ordinary create: the agent may set an assignee and a group, and keeps write access through queue ownership. - Does not run the queue. A create without an assignee is filed : the created task is unassigned and ungrouped, and its author has no access to it afterwards. The create response carries filed: true and no access, and ttasks create prints that the task is recorded but no longer visible, so the agent does not read the following not found as a failure and file it twice. An explicit assignee, including the creating agent, instead owns that task and its descendants without gaining access to the rest of the queue. A group remains forbidden and is rejected with report cannot assign. Filing is how an agent hands over work it should not schedule for itself — a defect it noticed outside its current assignment. Triage stays with the queue's responsible agent, who receives a task.triage notification; when the queue has none, that notification goes to the customer instead. To let a specific agent triage a queue, the customer adds it to the queue's owners. The same rule applies to a child that an agent creates in a queue it does not run (ttasks create --parent KEY --queue OTHER). A filed child differs in one point: its author keeps read-only (context) access to it, and the create response carries filed: true and access: "context". The author cannot change, claim, comment on, or complete that child. ttasks move KEY --to-root detaches a task from its parent, which is the inverse operation: the task becomes a root, and the mover loses access to it unless it is the assignee or runs the queue. A move without --parent, --before, or --to-root is refused rather than treated as a detach. Subtasks in another queue A task can have a child in another queue. The child keeps its own queue, key, workflow, and status. Only its parent link crosses the queue boundary. Create a child in another queue with --parent and --queue: The creator must have write access to the parent. In the child's queue, the ordinary rules of that queue apply: - If the creator runs the queue, the create is ordinary. --assignee and --group are allowed. - If the creator does not run the queue, a create without --assignee is filed (see Filing a task into a queue ). A create with --assignee gives that agent the task and its same-queue descendants. --group is refused with report cannot assign. - If the queue has a workflow, the child enters the workflow's initial status, and an explicit --assignee is refused with workflow managed. The child takes the parent's customer. It does not take the parent's group, because a group gives write access without the tree. Without --queue, or with the parent's queue, a child takes the parent's queue and group as before. Access stops at the queue boundary: | Who | Access to the child in another queue | Access to the parent | | --- | --- | --- | | An agent that writes the parent, by queue, assignment, or group | None | Unchanged | | The child's assignee, or an agent that runs the child's queue | Write, and write on its same-queue descendants | None | | The child's author, with no other rule | Read-only (context) | Unchanged | | The customer | Write | Write | A workflow task keeps its workflow rules: the status holder, the customer pool, and workflow managed. A visible child shows its parent key even when the reader cannot see the parent. ttasks list --subtree KEY returns only the descendants that the reader can see, each with its queue and status. Move an existing task under a parent in another queue with --parent: A move changes only the parent. The task keeps its queue, key, workflow, and status. To change the queue of a task, use ttasks requeue, which creates a new task (see Moving a task to another queue). These rules apply to the move: - The mover must have write access to the task and to the new parent. - The task and the new parent must have the same customer. Otherwise the move is refused with scope change. A group mismatch is refused only when the new parent is in the same queue. - The same-queue descendants of the task move with it. Its children in other queues stay under it. - Order is kept per queue under a parent. --before KEY must name a task of the moved task's queue with the same priority. A task of another queue is refused with invalid before. Without --parent, the task moves under the parent of the --before task, even when that parent is in another queue. - --to-root on a task whose parent is in another queue also needs write access to that parent. Otherwise the owner of the child could take ordered work out of a tree that it does not run. For a parent in the same queue, write access to the task is enough. Events for the child, such as task.created and task.moved, are recorded on the child. Only a reader that can see the child receives them. The owner of the parent who cannot see the child gets no event and no notification about it. A hidden active child still blocks the completion of its parent with active descendants. The error gives only the count. The customer sees the keys. The export for Moving a task to another server refuses a tree with a task in another queue with cross queue subtree. Move or detach those tasks first. Questions and notifications Comments recognize typed principals only: Each mention creates or refreshes a durable waiting for row on the task. The mentioned principal's next comment resolves only its own open wait. This makes “where is my answer required?” directly filterable for both agents and the customer. The customer can also close a question without an answer, for example a question an agent asked after the task was done. POST /api/tasks/{key}/waits/dismiss (tasks.waits.dismiss) works for a task in any status. Only the customer can call it; another caller gets forbidden (HTTP 403). In one transaction it: - closes each open wait on the customer, with no resolving comment; - closes the matching task.question letters with close note = task-wait-dismissed; - moves a flexible task from wait customer to in progress when no question to the customer stays open, as an answer does. A workflow task gets the state an answer gives it. A done or cancelled task keeps its status; - records a task.waits dismissed event and sends each asker a task.answered letter that says no answer is needed. The workflow's own wait on the customer stays open: an outcome or workflow resume resolves it. Questions to agents stay open too. With no open question to the customer, the call changes nothing and returns an empty resolved waits. A mentioned name starts and ends with a letter or a digit. A dot, or - inside the name is part of the name. Punctuation after the name is not part of it, so @agent:worker. and (@agent:worker) both mention agent:worker, and @agent:a.b mentions agent:a.b. A mention opens a wait only on a principal that exists. An agent principal exists when the daemon has an agent with that name. A user principal exists when its login is the customer login. A comment that mentions a missing principal is saved as plain text: it opens no wait, the mentions of its task.comment added event do not list that principal, and the task status does not change. ttasks ask on a missing principal fails with principal not found (HTTP 400) and saves no comment. A question to a principal opens one wait on it, also when the question text mentions that principal again. An older daemon also opened waits on principals that do not exist, for example agent:tariboy-pm. with the closing dot of a sentence. No answer can resolve such a wait. When tariboyd starts, it closes each open wait on a principal that does not exist or that has a name a mention cannot match. It also closes the open question letters of that wait. The daemon log gets one Info record for each closed wait, with the task key, the wait ID, the principal and the reason (principal not found or invalid principal name). One more record gives the number of closed waits. Waits on the customer and on existing agents stay open, and the task status does not change. If the customer login is empty, all waits on user: principals stay open. An enabled agent normally follows one sticky assigned task as its Goal. It releases that selection when the task is done, cancelled, loses assignment or visibility, remains in wait customer beyond the agent's configured grace period, or eligible assigned work has a strictly higher priority. A task's pull request URL does not affect Goal selection or release. The goal is daemon-owned and read-only to the agent; see Agents and the iteration loop. Assignment, question, answer, and queue-triage events enter a transactional outbox and are sent as letters from the principal that caused them: the asker, the assigner, or system:workflow. An agent notification goes to agent:<name ; a customer notification goes to user:<login , the configured customer login. The kinds are task.assigned, task.question, task.answered and task.triage, and data carries task key, queue and notification id. A notification therefore wakes an enabled agent like any other letter; a disabled agent keeps it open in its inbox. A task.question letter is a request that is answered on the task, never by mail: tmail reply refuses it with answer on task and names the ttasks comment command. When the wait resolves, the tasks service closes the matching question letters with close note = task-comment:<id , for an agent recipient and the customer alike; a workflow outcome that resolves the customer's wait closes them with task-outcome:<status . The other three kinds are notices; the agent's Goal letter drives the work. Desktop Tasks in the sidebar opens /tasks, the tasks of one host. With two or more hosts in the workspace, a host selector at the start of the toolbar picks the host, and the URL carries it as ?host=<id . The number next to Tasks counts the tasks that need you on every host of the workspace: a workflow task that waits for you past its first status, or a paused workflow task. The layout is Tree-first: - one toolbar row that does not wrap: search, the Active/Done/All segment, a Filters menu with Queue (with its Manage queues… dialog), Assignee ( Anyone , My tasks , or one agent), Waiting for me , and Columns , then refresh and New task . The Filters button shows how many filters are on; - full width: dense expandable tree ordered by priority at every depth, with inline task/child creation and same-queue drag reparenting; manual before/after drag order is limited to the task's current priority bucket. In-progress tasks show an explicit In progress label, while open and done tasks retain their existing row presentation. A small red indicator marks each task with an unread task.question letter in the customer's mailbox; opening that task marks those letters read and clears the indicator. A question letter stays open until it is answered on the task. tariboy mail inbox lists the customer's open letters, the questions among them. A task in a queue bound to a workflow shows its workflow status, for example Approval , instead of one of the five fixed labels; a long status ID is clipped and its full text is the tooltip. The colour of the label follows the task's category (open, in progress, wait customer, done, cancelled), not the status ID, so a closed workflow task reads as closed whatever its last status was. Beside the label an open task shows its step as 3/6, its position among the workflow's statuses (hidden on a phone), then a small customer or script marker that says who the task waits on. A problem mark takes the marker's place when something needs a person: red when a check could not run or the status's watch script failed, accent-coloured when a check rejected the request; its tooltip carries the script's words and the count behind it (see Attention summary). A red paused marker outranks both when the daemon paused the task (its tooltip gives the reason). Active, Closed, and All use the category too. There is no filter by workflow status. Flexible tasks keep the labels described above. A subtask in another queue stands under its parent in the tree, as a subtask of the same queue does: - If its parent is in the tree and in another queue, the Key cell shows a queue marker (a layers icon) between the chevron and the key. Its tooltip and accessible name give the queue, the queue name, the workflow, and the parent queue, for example Queue TARIDESIGN · Design · workflow design-flow (parent queue TARI). A queue without a workflow reads flexible tasks. A root task and a subtask in its parent's queue have no marker. - Each row shows the status by the model of its own task. A workflow subtask under a flexible parent shows its workflow status, step, and markers. A flexible subtask under a workflow parent shows a flexible label. - A subtask in another queue cannot move among its siblings with the mouse. It cannot go inside a row of another queue either. A drop on the tree root detaches it from its parent and keeps its queue. A refused drop shows Tasks can only move inside their queue and outside their own subtree. - The + button of a row makes the new subtask in the queue of that row. The form shows Queue: {PREFIX} in place of the queue select. The Desktop does not make a subtask in another queue. The Queue filter keeps each task of the chosen queue with its whole subtree from every queue. A subtask in the chosen queue under an ancestor in that queue stays in the subtree and does not repeat as a root. Rows of other queues in the subtree are not dimmed. A task of the chosen queue whose parent is in another queue becomes a root. After its title it shows in {KEY}, a link that opens the parent in the sheet. On a phone the link is only an icon with a 24×24 px target. If the parent is not in the loaded list, the link is text with the tooltip You cannot open this task. The parent queue then comes from the parent key, up to its last -. The queue counts in the menu do not change with the filter: each task counts only in its own queue. Clicking a task opens a right-side sheet over the tree. The sticky header shows the key, one title, status, and assignee. The pencil edits the title in that same place. Save task appears only while task fields have unsaved changes. For a workflow task, a compact decision panel sits directly below the header in the same sticky block. It shows the current stage, owner, wait reason, and available outcomes, including the initial customer action that starts work. The block has a height limit and scrolls on a short screen. Decision materials appear below the sticky block, before the description and comments. View plan and the named material links open and focus their artifacts there. An Outcome message belongs to the chosen outcome. To answer a question or add a comment, use the comment form. Completed tasks offer no transitions, and flexible tasks have no workflow decision panel. The header of a subtask shows Subtask of {KEY} {title} above the title, on one line. The line is a button that opens the parent in the same sheet. If the parent is in another queue, a queue marker with the text Parent queue {PREFIX} · {name} stands before the key. If the reader cannot see the parent, the line is Subtask of {KEY} as text, with the tooltip You cannot open this task. A Subtasks section follows the description and comes before the comments. Its heading gives the number of visible direct subtasks, for example Subtasks 3. Each row shows a queue marker for a subtask in another queue, the key, the title, the status as the tree shows it, and the assignee without agent:. The rows come from the children field in tree order. Closed subtasks stay in the list in every Active, Done, or All view. A row opens its subtask in the same sheet. On a phone a row has two lines: the marker, key, and status, then the title. The assignee is hidden there. If the reader cannot see some subtasks, a line under the list says 1 more subtask is hidden from you. or {N} more subtasks are hidden from you. The section is hidden for a task without subtasks. Two placeholder rows show while a list loads. If a later read of the task fails, the section shows Could not load subtasks. and Retry in place of the list. Realtime task events refresh the section with the rest of the sheet. Opening the parent or a subtask from the sheet asks for confirmation first when the sheet holds unsaved drafts, as closing does. After the move, the key of the opened task takes the focus. If that task is hidden or no longer exists, the sheet says You cannot open {KEY}. It is hidden from you or no longer exists. A task sheet opened from an agent, usage, or a letter moves the same way. A collapsed Details section holds the author, customer, queue, group, blocked state, parent, flexible status, priority, assignee, pull request URL, block reason, and dependencies. The parent is a button that opens it, or text when the reader cannot see the parent. History is collapsed by default. The flexible status wait customer reads Waiting for you. The flexible assignee list contains Unassigned, me, and each agent. You cannot type a principal. In the comment form, Ask an agent mentions an agent, and Reply Ok to the question posts Ok. When a question to you is open, the "Waiting for an answer" banner at the top of the sheet has Dismiss question , in every status, also for a done or cancelled task. The Needs you card has the same button. The sheet starts at half the viewport width. Drag its left separator or use its keyboard controls to resize it. The chosen width survives reloads. Back, Close, Escape, or a backdrop click returns to the still-mounted tree with its expansion and scroll position preserved. Unsaved task, comment, relation, or outcome-message drafts require confirmation before the sheet discards them. A pending decision prevents closure until it finishes. A workflow task has no flexible status select, Done action, or Move to another server action. Its lower Workflow disclosure holds the status graph, artifacts, runs, logs, visits, and operator actions. Existing confirmations still protect actions that override the workflow or cancel the task. In an open, unpaused pool status, the Assignee control can reassign the holder to a member of that pool. See Desktop in the workflow guide. Queue bindings, pools, environment variables, and secrets remain in the Manage queues dialog. Descriptions and comments render as Markdown. Their visual editor supports headings, bold, italic, strikethrough, links, lists, checklists, code, and tables. Switch to Source Markdown to edit the source directly; content the visual editor cannot represent stays in source mode so unsupported syntax is preserved. Both modes save the same Markdown strings used by the API and ttasks. Send files beside Description and Comment uploads selected files to the task's server and appends their absolute paths to that editor's current draft. It works without an assigned agent. Uploading does not save the task or send the comment; use Save task or Send comment . If a later file fails, paths for files already uploaded are kept in the draft. Files are stored on disk under $TARIBOY BASE DIR/files (normally /.tariboy/files), with a unique directory per upload so matching names never overwrite earlier files. Each file is limited to 1 GiB. Files remain after a draft is discarded or a task is closed; remove unneeded files manually on the server when their paths are no longer needed. Desktop streams each selected file directly rather than creating a base64/JSON copy in memory. The Desktop establishes a silent baseline when it first observes a host, and again when an unavailable host recovers. Existing unread questions appear as dots without replaying stale native notifications. A question first observed later in the current Desktop session can send one native notification; repeated realtime hints and identical HTTP snapshots do not send it again. Notification permission denial or an unavailable native service does not remove the in-app dots. Opening a native question notification marks that exact question letter as read and selects its task on its original server. The Desktop route is exactly /tasks?host=<hostId &task=<key (for example, /tasks?host=local&task=ASK-1); in the packaged single-page application it appears after the URL hash as #/tasks?host=local&task=ASK-1. An older /servers/<hostId /tasks?task=<key link opens the same page. Routing keeps the notification's explicit host identity and never substitutes the local daemon for a missing remote host. The task still opens if the read request is interrupted, so the customer can answer it and mark the letter read later. HTTP remains usable if realtime is disconnected. GET /api/tasks/ws?after=N replays visible durable event hints after N, then streams new hints. The client reconnects with its last accepted sequence and performs a full refetch when the server requests a reset. Revision conflicts (409) also refetch the authoritative tree/detail before another edit. The Tasks toolbar starts in Active view. Its GET /api/tasks request sends status view=active, and the daemon applies that predicate to the task's category before it builds the response. A flexible task's category equals its status; a workflow task's category is the one its workflow status maps to. Active returns the categories open, in progress, and wait customer; Closed (status view=closed) returns the finished categories, done and cancelled; and All (status view=all) returns every category. An omitted status view is Active when no explicit status filter is present; an explicit status without a view keeps its legacy authoritative semantics. When both are supplied, their predicates intersect. Other task filters and access rules are applied alongside the selected view, so excluded rows are never shipped to the client. An invalid view is rejected with 400 invalid status view. Filtering by category may exclude an otherwise visible parent while retaining an eligible child. In that response the child keeps its parent key, but the client renders it as a root-level filtered orphan; the excluded parent is never included merely to reconstruct the tree. Switching views always refetches the authoritative selected view, and realtime refreshes retain that selection. The agent's Work tab The Work tab of an agent shows the tasks assigned to that agent. It does not use the Tasks tree. At the top, a field reads "Give \ a task…". Type a title and press Enter to create a P2 task. Details reveals the queue, the priority, and the description. The queue is the last one you used for this agent, else TASK. In a flexible queue the task is assigned to the agent. In a queue bound to a workflow the task has no assignee: the composer says that the workflow dispatches it to a pool member, and after the create it shows a link to the task. When the agent is off, the button reads Start & give : it creates the task, then starts the agent. If the start fails, the task stays. When the agent's Goal setting is off, the composer says that the agent does not pick up tasks and links to Settings. Below the composer, the tab has these sections: - Needs you : each card has a key and title button that opens the task sheet on the agent's host. Opening it sends no answer. The card's answer fields, outcomes, and links work independently. Closing the sheet restores focus to the button and retains the card's draft. Home and Inbox keep their expandable Needs you cards. - In progress : the other active tasks. - Queued : open tasks, and workflow tasks in their first status. Such a workflow task has one button per outcome of that status, so you can start it from the row. - Done · last 7 days : closed tasks, with a search box for the key and the title. Show all shows every closed task. A row shows the key, the title, the status in words (for example Not started or Waiting for you ), the age, and the cost when it is known. Click a row to open the task sheet. The agent header's Answer button opens the tab at the first task's card, and Give task focuses the composer. Task budget A task budget is a USD limit on the AI spending of a task and all of its subtasks. The field budget usd holds it. The value 0 means no limit, and every task starts with 0. Only the customer sets the limit, with ttasks update KEY --budget-usd 5, with tariboy tasks update, or in the Budget, USD field of the task panel. An agent that sends --budget-usd gets forbidden. An agent sees the limit in ttasks show. The panel shows under the field what the task and its subtasks spent, from GET /api/tasks/{key}/budget. The spending of a task is the sum of cost usd of every AI request whose task id is the key of the task or of one of its subtasks. Old keys from task key aliases count too. The limit has no time window. Before the AI proxy sends a request upstream, it checks the task of the request and each of its parents. If the subtree of one of them spent its limit or more, the proxy answers 429 with budget exceeded: task KEY and records the request as budget block. Then the daemon reacts on the task of the request: | Task | Reaction | How the customer lifts it | | --- | --- | --- | | A workflow task | The task pauses with the reason budget exhausted. The pause question names the task with the limit, the spending and the limit. | Raise the limit or set 0, then resume with ttasks workflow resume KEY --decision continue or release. While the limit is still spent, the resume fails with budget exhausted. | | A flexible task | The task gets the block reason budget exhausted: task KEY spent $X of $Y, and a comment by system:budget mentions the customer. A blocked task is not a Goal, so the agent takes other work. | Raise the limit above the spending or set 0. The daemon then lifts, in the same write, each block in the subtree that names this task. A block with other text stays. The customer can also clear a block with ttasks update KEY --manual-block-reason "". An agent cannot clear a budget block. | A task that is already paused, blocked or closed does not change. A parent with a limit is not blocked itself: each task of the subtree is paused or blocked at its own first refusal. Limits of a task budget: - Requests that already started can go over the limit, because the proxy knows the cost only after the answer. Several agents in one subtree can go over it at the same time. - Requests without a price, such as Cursor requests, cost 0 and are not limited. - A request of an iteration without a Goal has no task id and does not count. - If the database read of the check fails, the proxy lets the request through and logs the error. - A move to another queue creates a new task without the limit. A move to another server does not carry the limit. Moving a task to another queue A task key names its queue, so a task that belongs in another queue of the same host is moved as a new task. In the task panel, the header actions menu opens Move to queue… for any open task, workflow or not. The dialog lists the other queues of this host and says what happens; for a workflow task it says that the current workflow stops. After the move the Tasks workspace opens the new task. The same move is ttasks requeue KEY --queue QUEUE for the operator; agents cannot move tasks between queues. The daemon does the whole move in one transaction: it creates the new task in the target queue with the same title, description, priority, pull request, group, and comments, and cancels the old task. If the old task followed a workflow, its scripts stop and its questions close, as with ttasks cancel. If the target queue has a workflow, the new task enters it like any new task there; if not, the new task is a flexible open task. The two tasks are related and each has a comment that names the other. A task with open subtasks is refused (requeue has children); move or close the subtasks first. See Operator move, retry, and cancel for the details. Moving a task to another server Each host keeps its own tasks, so work that belongs with another host is moved rather than copied by hand. In the task panel, the header actions menu opens Move to another server , which lists the other hosts registered in the desktop app. The desktop app is the only component authenticated against both daemons, so it drives the move: it exports the task tree from this daemon, imports it into the chosen one, then comments on the task here and sets it to cancelled. Nothing is deleted — the original task, its history and its events stay on the source host — so a failure part-way leaves the task readable on both sides. What moves: the task, its whole descendant subtree, their comments with the original authors and times, and the relations whose two ends are both inside that subtree. What does not move: the event log, notifications, reminders, relations pointing outside the subtree. This daemon refuses the export when the subtree has a task in another queue (cross queue subtree) or a task that follows a workflow (workflow managed). The target daemon refuses the import, changing nothing, when: - it has no queue with the same prefix (queue not found); - a task or a retired key alias already uses one of the keys (task key taken). The two endpoints behind the menu are GET /api/tasks/{key}/export and POST /api/tasks/import. Both are customer-authenticated; agents do not transfer tasks. Agent capability Tasks are native daemon functionality, but prompt and command exposure is optional per image: tariboy-tasks is installed globally as ttasks; it uses identity-bound agent mode only when TARIBOY TOOLS SOCKET is non-empty and otherwise uses the host Unix daemon socket as the customer actor. Agent mode fails closed rather than falling back to operator access. tariboy tasks … runs the same client and always uses operator mode, also when an agent runs it, so it sees every task. When enabled, the tasks capability also provisions the bare legacy tasks shim. Schema-v2 images must still package the Tasks image skill; capability selection never packages instructions automatically. See the Tasks built-in reference for the complete boundary. Every agent mutation is identity-bound by its per-agent socket. Body fields cannot forge the author, customer, or acting principal. Command help ttasks and tariboy-tasks provide the same local help. Run either without arguments or with --help / -h for the command list and mode descriptions. Every command and nested group accepts those help flags; a bare group lists its subcommands. Command help explains its purpose, syntax, arguments, flags, required fields, and examples: Help never executes the command, resolves a daemon socket, or requires a running daemon. It lists both modes and labels operator-only administration and agent-only operations; showing help does not grant execution access. Root --help-json returns the complete command tree with descriptions and examples. Shared commands retain their flags name array and add flag help descriptions, usage, arguments, help, and examples. --json controls command results; use --help-json for machine-readable documentation. Write task descriptions and comments as valid Markdown: use real newlines, blank lines before lists, closed code fences, and no raw HTML. Typed mentions and explicit ttasks ask retain their existing answer-tracking behavior. ttasks create --queue works in any existing queue. In a queue the agent does not run, omitting --assignee files an unassigned task the agent can no longer see; passing --assignee creates work owned by that agent without exposing the rest of the queue. --group remains forbidden there. See Filing a task into a queue . Listing and searching tasks ttasks list lists the tasks the caller can see: in agent mode the agent's visible tasks, in operator mode every host task. ttasks mine is an alias with the same flags and output. Search is list --text, which matches the key, title, and description without regard to case. Filters combine with AND, and a comma-separated value matches any of its items: | Flag | Selects | | --- | --- | | --status S | The status show prints: the workflow status of a workflow task, the stored status of a flexible task. A category value also finds workflow tasks in that category. | | --category C | Only the category: open, in progress, wait customer, done, cancelled | | --priority P | P0 to P3 | | --queue, --assignee, --group | The queue prefix, the assigned agent, the task group | | --author, --customer | A principal, user:login or agent:name; a bare name means agent:name | | --parent KEY, --subtree KEY | Direct children, or every descendant, of KEY; not both | | --waiting-for P | Tasks with an open question to P; me is the current agent | | --blocked true or false | Blocked or unblocked tasks | | --view V | active (the default without --status), closed (done and cancelled), or all | --sort is tree (the queue tree order, the default), updated or created (newest first), or priority (P0 first, then newest). A page holds --limit tasks, 50 by default and 500 at most. The output is a table of key, priority, status, assignee, update time, and title. A B before the key marks a blocked task, and a workflow task shows its category in brackets. When more tasks remain, a last line next: prints the command for the next page: the same filters with --after KEY. --json prints the page as tasks, next cursor, and sequence. Every filter applies inside the caller's visibility. A --parent or --subtree key the caller cannot see gives an empty list, the same as a key that does not exist, and a subtree never shows a descendant the caller cannot see. On a task in a queue bound to a workflow, use the workflow commands instead of done, update --status, and ready --claim: advance waits for the transition's checks and prints rejected: with the script's message or failed: with the run log to read. workflow move, workflow upgrade, cancel, queue workflow, and queue secret are operator-only. See Task workflows for the full flow. Create, comment, and relation actions accept stable idempotency keys internally so transport retries return the original result without duplicating a task, comment, wait, relation, event, or notification. Relation changes also use the same optimistic task revision guard as field and tree mutations. They require write access to both endpoint tasks, hide relations whose other endpoint is not visible, and emit realtime history events for both endpoints.
description: Queue-owned, infinitely nested work shared by customers and agents, with comments, dependencies, answer tracking, and realtime Desktop updates.
title: Native Tasks

content: A workflow image is a versioned, immutable artifact built from a source directory that holds a Workflowfile.yaml, status instructions, and scripts. The manifest declares a status graph: who owns each status, which outcomes lead to which next status, and which artifacts and checks a transition needs. A queue binds a workflow image, and its tasks then follow the image's statuses; see Task workflows for binding, the runtime, and the script protocol. Everything in the manifest drives queue tasks. owner, transitions, requires, and artifacts shape the status graph; the daemon runs checks when a holder requests a transition and runs each watch while a task is in its script status; requires secrets names queue secrets that must be set before the image can be bound and that the scripts receive; env sets non-secret variables for every script; limits set when the daemon pauses a stalled task (see Limits). Source layout A Store holds workflow sources next to image sources. Any source directory works with --path. The whole directory is the image: every regular file in it is stored, not only the files the manifest names. A .git directory is skipped. A file named manifest.json at the source root is rejected because that name is reserved for the stored manifest. Workflowfile.yaml The loader is strict: an unknown field is an error, and a second YAML document is an error. Thus a daemon that is older than a field rejects a Workflowfile.yaml that uses it. For example, daemon v0.106.0 rejects sticky holder; see Dispatch. Root fields | Field | Required | Meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | schema version | yes | 1. | | name | yes | Workflow name; matches ^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9. -]{0,63}$. | | workflow version | yes | SemVer 2.0.0 without a v prefix. | | initial status | yes | ID of a non-terminal status. | | statuses | yes | The status graph; at least one status. | | artifacts | no | Declared artifact names with descriptions. | | requires secrets | no | Names of secrets the scripts need; each matches ^[A-Za-z ][A-Za-z0-9 ] $, must not start with TARIBOY , and is listed once. | | env | no | Non-secret environment defaults for scripts. A name matches ^[A-Za-z ][A-Za-z0-9 ] $ and must not start with TARIBOY . | | limits | no | Workflow-wide defaults; see Limits. | | watch spacing | no | Least time between the starts of two watch runs of this workflow, from 1s to 10m; default 5s. See Watch scripts. | | sticky holder | no | true gives a task that comes back to a pool status to the previous holder of that pool, however busy that agent is. Default false: the previous holder gets the task first only when it is free. A pool status can override it. See Dispatch. | | sources | no | Queue-level scripts that create tasks; see Sources. | Status IDs, outcome names (on), artifact names, and pool names match ^[a-z][a-z0-9 -]{0,63}$. Status fields | Field | Applies to | Meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | id | all | Unique status ID. | | owner | non-terminal | {pool: NAME}, customer, or script. | | instructions | pool, customer | Source-relative Markdown file shown to the owner. Not allowed on a script status. | | watch | script | script, every, timeout, and description of the watch script. | | transitions | non-terminal | List of on, to, and, for pool statuses, requires and checks. | | limits | non-terminal | Per-status overrides of the workflow limits. | | sticky holder | pool | true or false. Replaces the root sticky holder for this status. Without it, the status uses the root value. | | terminal | terminal | true. A terminal status has no owner, transitions, watch, instructions, or limits. | | cancelled | terminal | true when the result counts as cancelled rather than done. Allowed only on a terminal status. | A watch has a required script, a required every duration of at least 1s, an optional positive timeout (default 60s, maximum 30m), and an optional description. The daemon runs it once when a task enters the status, then every after each run finishes. A check has a required script, an optional run as (queue, the default, or agent), an optional timeout (default 60s, maximum 30m), and an optional description. The checks of a transition run in declared order when the holder requests it. A description is one line of plain text of at most 200 characters that says what the script verifies or waits for. Desktop shows it next to the script's name, and the agent's Goal block names each check with it, so write it for the reader who sees the script fail: "The pull request exists and is open", not "runs pr-open.py". How scripts are run, their exit codes, result file, environment, and run modes are described under Script protocol. Sources A source is a script the daemon runs on a schedule for every queue bound to the workflow, outside any task. Each item it reports with a key the source has not reported before becomes a task in the queue, in initial status; the task then moves through the statuses like any other. A reviewer that waits for pull requests, an alert, an issue, or an email are examples. | Field | Required | Meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | name | yes | Matches ^[a-z][a-z0-9 -]{0,63}$; unique among the sources. It keys the items already seen, so keep it across versions. | | script | yes | Source-relative executable; follows the path rule. | | every | yes | Duration of at least 10s between the end of one run and the start of the next. | | timeout | no | Positive duration, default 60s, maximum 30m. | | description | no | One line of plain text, at most 200 characters, shown next to the source in Desktop and by queue source ls. | The result file, the environment, and the commands that show a source's runs are described under Sources. Paths A path in instructions, watch.script, checks[].script, or sources[].script: - starts with ./, is not absolute, contains no backslash or NUL byte, and stays inside the source directory; - is not inside the top-level .git directory, which a build does not store; - names a regular file; a symlink anywhere on the path is rejected; - for a script, has an executable bit. Limits | Limit | Default | Value | | --- | --- | --- | | idle iterations | 3 | Positive integer. | | rejected requests | 5 | Positive integer. | | script failures | 3 | Positive integer. | | unavailable grace | 5m | Non-negative duration such as 5m; 0 is allowed. | A status limits block overrides the workflow-wide block, which overrides the defaults. The daemon counts idle iterations, rejected requests, and script failures per visit of a status and pauses the task when a limit is reached; see Limits and Pauses. Validation validate and build report every independent error as an object with a stable code, a path that uses YAML field names and indexes (for example statuses[2].transitions[0].to), and a message. Errors are ordered by path, then code. | Code | Reported when | | --- | --- | | schema version unsupported | schema version is not 1. | | name invalid | name does not match the workflow name rule. | | version invalid | workflow version is missing or not SemVer 2.0.0 without a v. | | secret name invalid | A requires secrets name is malformed, starts with TARIBOY , or is repeated. | | env name invalid | An env name is malformed or starts with TARIBOY . | | limit invalid | A count limit is zero or negative. | | duration invalid | unavailable grace, watch.timeout, a check timeout, or a source timeout is not a valid duration of the required sign, watch.every is not a duration of at least 1s, or a source every is not a duration of at least 10s. | | artifact name invalid | An artifact name does not match the identifier rule. | | artifact duplicate | An artifact is declared twice. | | artifact unknown | A requires entry names an undeclared artifact. | | status missing | There are no statuses. | | status id invalid | A status ID does not match the identifier rule. | | status duplicate | A status ID is used twice. | | initial status unknown | initial status names no status. | | initial status terminal | initial status is a terminal status. | | status unreachable | No path from initial status reaches the status. | | terminal unreachable | No terminal status is reachable. | | terminal has work | A terminal status has an owner, transitions, watch, instructions, or limits. | | cancelled not terminal | cancelled is set on a non-terminal status. | | owner missing | A non-terminal status has no owner. | | owner invalid | A pool owner's name does not match the identifier rule. | | watch missing | A script status has no watch. | | watch not allowed | A status that is not script has a watch. | | instructions not allowed | A script status has instructions. | | sticky holder not pool | A customer, script, or terminal status sets sticky holder, also to false. | | transitions missing | A non-terminal status has no transition. | | outcome invalid | An outcome name does not match the identifier rule. | | outcome duplicate | An outcome is used twice in one status. | | transition target unknown | A to names no status. | | requires not allowed | requires appears on a transition out of a customer or script status. | | checks not allowed | checks appear on a transition out of a customer or script status. | | run as invalid | A check's run as is neither queue nor agent. | | timeout too long | A check timeout, watch.timeout, or source timeout exceeds 30m. | | description invalid | A check, watch, or source description exceeds 200 characters or is not one line of plain text. | | source name invalid | A source name does not match the identifier rule. | | source duplicate | A source name is used twice. | | path invalid | A path breaks the path rule. | | file missing | A named file does not exist or cannot be read. | | file not regular | A named path, or a component of it, is a symlink or not a regular file. | | script not executable | A named script has no executable bit. | | source invalid | The source directory itself is refused: a symlink or special file anywhere in it, a root manifest.json, or a file, file-count, or total-size limit exceeded. Checked only once the manifest has no error. validate reports it with path source; build refuses with workflow invalid and the same message. | validate runs the same checks as build, so a source validate accepts is one build accepts, apart from a version already published with other content. tariboy workflow validate prints the whole result and exits 1 when the source is invalid, so a script can gate on it. A manifest that cannot be read or decoded (including an unknown field) is reported as workflow invalid without a per-field list. Build, storage, and versions tariboy workflow build validates the source and publishes it. The built artifact is stored once, addressed by a SHA-256 digest over one line per stored file, sorted by path: <path \0<executable 0|1 \0<SHA-256 of the content \n. Workflowfile.yaml is one of those files, so the definition is covered through its exact bytes, and the digest of an unchanged source does not change between releases. Timestamps, ownership, and other permission bits do not change the digest. A build publishes two tags that point at the digest: the workflow version and latest. The stored tree is owner-only and read-only: directories are 0500, regular files 0400, and executable files 0500. manifest.json holds the schema version, name, version, digest, build time, the definition as parsed, the path, SHA-256, executable flag, and size of every file, and the role from ROLE.md when the source has one. A source may hold at most 256 files, at most 4 MiB per file, and at most 32 MiB in total. Symlinks and special files anywhere in the source are rejected. A published workflow version is immutable. Rebuilding the same version with identical content is a no-op and reports created: false. Rebuilding it with different content fails with workflow version published. This is stricter than agent images, where a rebuild moves the ref, because a workflow must stay reproducible. To change a workflow, bump the version with tariboy workflow version update and build again; latest then moves to the new digest. Removing the version tag does not free the version. While any tag, such as latest, still names content of that version, a build of the same version with different content fails with workflow version published. A version may be reused only after its content is gone: every tag that named it is removed, which deletes the content and its database row. The manifest of every published digest is also recorded in the task workflow images table of the daemon's SQLite database. Removing the last tag of a digest deletes its row in a transaction that commits only after the content is deleted. At startup the daemon inserts any missing row for stored content and deletes any row whose content is gone, unless a queue binds or a task pins its digest, so a crash between a disk write and its row heals. See State model. Describe the role with ROLE.md ROLE.md is an optional Markdown file that describes what the workflow is for. Put it next to Workflowfile.yaml. The build copies its text into the manifest field role. Tariboy does not put this text into the Goal block, the status instructions, or any agent prompt. The text is metadata for people and for the UI. Write ROLE.md in English. Say only what the role is and why the workflow exists. Do not describe the process, skills, commands, or rules. The daemon does not check the language or the content of the text. The build applies these rules: | Case | Result | | --- | --- | | No ROLE.md | The manifest has no role field. | | Only white space | The same as no file. | | Not valid UTF-8 | The build fails with workflow invalid and the text ROLE.md is not valid UTF-8. | | Up to 500 characters | role.text is the full file. | | More than 500 characters | The build fails with workflow invalid. The error gives the file size in characters and the limit of 500. | A character is one Unicode code point, so 500 Cyrillic letters are in the limit. ROLE.md is one of the stored files, so it is part of the digest like any other file. The role field does not change the digest rule. tariboy workflow inspect and GET /api/workflow-images/{name}/{tag} show the field: A workflow image built before this feature has no role field. If you build the same content again, the build adds role to the stored manifest and to its database row. The digest and the build time do not change. An import of a workflow archive reads role from the ROLE.md in the archive and applies the same rules, so a file of more than 500 characters fails the import. Commands The daemon commands act on the selected daemon. STORE/NAME selects a workflow source in a registered Store; --path selects a Workflowfile.yaml or its directory. A manifest file under any other name is refused. The two are mutually exclusive. | Command | HTTP route | Result | | --- | --- | --- | | workflow validate | POST /api/workflow-images/validate | valid, name, version, pools, files, and errors (empty when valid). Validation errors are returned in the result, not as an HTTP failure; the CLI prints them and exits 1. | | workflow build | POST /api/workflow-images/build | {operation}: the started build operation. The build result (name, version, digest, tags, and created) is operation.workflow result once the build succeeds; with wait: true the request answers with the finished operation. The CLI prints the operation log to stderr until the build ends, then the result; --detach prints only the operation id. See Build as an operation. | | workflow ls | GET /api/workflow-images | workflows (one row per tag with name, tag, version, digest, built at) and count. | | workflow inspect NAME [TAG] | GET /api/workflow-images/{name}/{tag} | The stored manifest. TAG is a tag or a full digest and defaults to latest. | | workflow rm NAME TAG | DELETE /api/workflow-images/{name}/{tag} | name, tag, removed, and content removed. Removing the last tag that names a digest also deletes its content and database row. | | (Desktop) | GET /api/workflow-images/{name}/{tag}/export | A portable archive of the image; see Copying to another server. | | (Desktop) | POST /api/workflow-image-imports | Imports such an archive; the same result as workflow build. | Removing the last tag that names a digest is refused with workflow in use (HTTP 409) while a queue is bound to that digest or any task, open or closed, is pinned to it; the error says which holds it and how many. Removing one of several tags is not guarded, because the content stays and tasks keep running from it. Unbind the queue (ttasks queue workflow clear) and finish or cancel its tasks first. A closed task keeps reading its workflow and artifacts through the image, so the image stays until nightly task retention removes the closed task trees that pin it. workflow version get and workflow version update read and rewrite the local workflow version, default to the current directory, and need no daemon. update increments the SemVer component, resets the lower ones, removes any suffix, and preserves the rest of the file. Errors: | Code | Meaning | | --- | --- | | workflow invalid | The manifest failed validation or could not be parsed, or the source breaks a source limit. Validation failures carry the error list in error.details.errors. | | workflow version published | The workflow version is already published with different content. | | workflow in use | workflow rm would delete a digest that a queue binds or any task, open or closed, pins. | | not found | No workflow image has that name and tag or digest. | | bad source | Both a Store selector and --path were given. | | missing path | Neither a Store selector nor --path was given. | | bad archive | An import is not a readable workflow-image portable archive. | | archive too large | An import has no Content-Length or is larger than 64 MiB. | | workflow digest mismatch | An imported archive does not hold the content its digest names. | Copying to another server An image moves between daemons as content, not as tags. GET /api/workflow-images/{name}/{tag}/export takes a tag or a full digest and returns tariboy-workflow-image.tar.gz: a portable archive of kind workflow-image holding every stored file (not manifest.json), with the name, version, digest, and the paths of the executable files in its metadata, because the archive format does not keep permission bits. POST /api/workflow-image-imports takes that archive as the request body, with a Content-Length of at most 64 MiB. The daemon stages it under <base-dir /workflow-image-imports/, which the archive limits and path checks of the portable format guard, restores the executable bits, and publishes it like workflow build: the same validation, the version tag and latest point at it, and latest moves if it named other content. Before anything is written it computes the digest of the staged files and refuses the import with workflow digest mismatch when it differs from the one the archive names. The staged copy is always removed. The result is the workflow build result; an archive whose digest the daemon already holds reports created: false. A version already published there with other content is refused with workflow version published. built at on the receiving daemon is the import time, and queue bindings do not move. Desktop Open Library → Workflows (/library/workflows). With two or more hosts, the Library header has a host selector. Every request goes to the selected host. The old /servers/:hostId/workflows/… URLs redirect to the same page. - The list has one row per workflow name, with the version of its first tag (latest first, then the other tags newest version first) and Bound to : the queues bound to any digest of that name. A queue whose binding cannot be read adds unknown, with the queue named on hover; the rest of the page still works. The name opens the page of that first tag. - Add workflow opens Build from directory in a dialog. It takes a Workflowfile.yaml, or the directory holding it, on that server. Validate shows the name, version, pools, and files, or every validation error as code · path: message. Build reports built NAME:VERSION, or NAME:VERSION already built when nothing changed, and lists the errors of a refused build; a version already published with other content suggests bumping it. - Upload to servers , on the tag page and on each row of its Versions , copies that tag to other ready servers through the export and import routes: the archive is downloaded once and imported on each selected server in turn. Each server reports Completed , Already present , or Failed with the daemon's message, and a failure does not stop the others. Cancelling skips the servers not yet started. - A tag's page (/library/workflows/:name/:tag, where the tag may also be a full digest) shows the status graph as a table (owner, instruction path, outcomes with their required artifacts and checks with run as and timeout, watch), the effective limits of the workflow and of each non-terminal status with where each value comes from, the declared artifacts, required secrets, env, and the stored files. Instruction files are shown by path only. Remove tag asks for confirmation; a workflow in use refusal is shown in place with the bound queues. A page opened by digest has no Remove tag . Below, Versions lists every tag of the name with its version, build time, and bound queues, and marks the tag on screen. Building from a Store selector stays in the CLI and Compose. Official workflow images A Store holds workflow sources at workflows/<name / beside its images/. The official Store provides two: - development: the pull request flow with the statuses plan, approval, implement, review (watched by a script), complete, and done. It requires the GH TOKEN queue secret and a pool named developers. - research: one pool status, research, for a pool named researchers; the agent stores a report artifact and the task is done. The graphs are in Task workflows. To use development on a queue DEV: The secret is read from standard input so it never shows in the process list. The bind is refused with workflow pool empty or workflow secret missing until the pool and the secret exist. For research, build tariboy/research, create a researchers pool, and bind research:0.1.0; it needs no secret and runs on any image that enables the tasks plugin, such as tariboy/basic. The queue secret and the agents' tokens are independent. The queue secret GH TOKEN is what the workflow's scripts (pr-monitor.py, pr-open.py) read. It needs read access to pull requests, issues, checks, and commit statuses of the repository. Each agent of the developers pool needs its own GH TOKEN agent secret as well: the skill's ensure and preflight commands run in the agent's environment and use the agent's token, which also creates the pull request. Only github.com is supported. Every agent of the developers pool must: - run the image tariboy/tariboy-developer; - have its own GH TOKEN agent secret, as above; - have git push credentials for the repository; - have the repository checkout as its working directory; - have the loop and the Goal block enabled, because the Goal block carries the status instructions. Using an image A published image is bound to a queue with ttasks queue workflow set, or from Compose with task queues.<PREFIX .workflow; tasks created in that queue pin the version and follow its statuses. A queue bound by NAME or NAME:latest follows latest: after a new build, new tasks pin the new version, while existing tasks keep theirs. See Task workflows for binding, queue secrets, the Desktop panel, dispatch, artifacts, outcomes, scripts, and the operator commands, and Compose for the Compose form.
description: Build, validate, store, and inspect versioned, immutable workflow images from a Workflowfile.yaml source directory.
title: Workflow images
